issues.title: How Ten National Book Award Finalists Tackle Writer’s Block
issues.summary: This first appeared in Lit Hub’s Craft of Writing newsletter—sign up here. Some of this year’s National Book Award finalists and winners share their best advice for dealing with writer’s block, from writing by hand to reading widely. * Edwidge Danticat, author
issues.author: Literary Hub
issues.content_html:
This first appeared in Lit Hub’s Craft of Writing newsletter—sign up here.

Some of this year’s National Book Award finalists and winners share their best advice for dealing with writer’s block, from writing by hand to reading widely.

*

Edwidge Danticat, author of Dèy

I’ve never really had writer’s block, mostly because I refuse to acknowledge it. If something I’m writing and want to write isn’t coming, I simply tell myself it’s not ready yet, and I try to trust that it will arrive in its own time. During these times, I’ll read a lot or I’ll draft shorter pieces to keep my creative juices flowing. Middles are often where I get most stuck, after the excitement of a beginning fades, so I muddle through, writing very imperfect sentences and paragraphs until I find my way forward. I also try to use my down time from writing to reconnect with life beyond the page. Living more fully can sometimes bring the words back.

Morgan Thomas, author of Mad Eden

Writer’s block takes different forms for me, and so responding requires discernment. Generally, if I’m not eager to write there’s a good reason. It signals that I need to tend other parts of my life — explore new books or music, spend time with my family, spend time with trees, go for a walk, rest. I try to listen. But I’ve also found that I’m always reluctant to work on stories or novels when they are about 75% done. The early glamour has worn away, but I’m not yet near enough to sense the ending’s presence. I’ve learned that I have to push through here, continuing in spite of my reluctance.

Sara Nović, author of Mother Tongue

I go back to writing by hand. Usually my writer’s block manifests by me sitting at my laptop, deleting and rewriting the same sentence over and over again — which can have its merits — but if I need to generate new words, I go back to the notebook. Nothing to tweak on a blank page, so you just have to write something new. If there’s a clunky word choice or phrase I know I already hate, I just circle it as a reminder to fix it later, and I keep moving.

​Fady Joudah, author of Exhibit G: Poems, Essays, and Photographs of Gaza

I do not tackle writer’s block because I do not name it that or do not feel I have it. When I am not writing or not progressing with writing, I tend to accept it as a form of meditation, self-examination, or respite that almost always rewards me in the end. I trust that mode of silence. Much of our cultural language is based on negative emotions. Why block? Take survivor’s guilt, for example. I think it is survivor’s love. Not everything has to be a pathology that serves a market reflex.

Intan Paramaditha, author of Night of a Thousand Hells

I read. Good books spark ideas. Less good books remind me of the road I do not wish to take.

Elana K. Arnold, author of Holloway

I’ve learned that the cure for writer’s block is always this: Do more research. “Research” is an elastic word; it can mean that when I’m writing a book set in an asylum in 1946 France, I learn more about that asylum, that year, that country… but it can also mean that I spend some time thinking about how interesting it is that “asylum” has two meanings, and looking up the definitions in various dictionaries, and then reading other words that appear on those same pages, and wondering about them, and maybe re-naming one of the minor characters a derivative of one of those adjacent words… and actually, that gives me an idea for something that can happen with that minor character! Maybe she won’t be so minor after all… and I’m rushing back to my manuscript, ready to write. Research cures writer’s block because it allows my brain to unclench, to loosen from the chokehold it’s taken on my work. As I wander, unclenching, through research, I always — one hundred percent of the time — find something that clicks and reinvigorates my writing. Is this because I’ve discovered some sort of magic trick? Magic, yes; trick, no. I think it’s magical that everything is connected, and that any route I take can lead me back to my own story.​

David Levithan and Gabriel Duckels, co-authors of The Fight of Our Lives: AIDS in America

DL: I always leave myself a runway for what I want to write next.

GD: Reading.

Brenda Hillman, author of Still House in the Desert: An eco-contemplation

​I’ve never defined writer’s block. There are slower periods and periods when I write less or with less intense commitment. I adore writing, re-writing, and re-visiting old failed drafts; “fail better,” as Beckett says. I like revisiting the bone pile, the compost pile, the pile of folders or lines in notebooks, and just making the process pleasurable… so, I don’t really experience “blocks,” if the term refers to not working on writing. I like to play when I’m not following the scent of the real poem; sometimes the unreal poem and the real poem become the same thing. If writer friends or my students are being too hard or judgy on themselves, on ourselves, I always say a version of the same thing I say to myself when I’m worried: lower your expectations but not your hopes and dreams. Sometimes just getting out of bed, washing your face and writing a line in your journal is a tall order for the day, so just lower your expectation until the next day of your writing life is manageable; if writing a whole line in your journal is too much, maybe go for just one word.

​Colin Asher, author of The Midnight Special: The Secret Prison History of American Music

Being a nonfiction writer helps. I always start by revisiting my source material. If I’m working with interview transcripts, news reports, or books, I re-read them. If I’m writing about a piece of music, I put it on repeat. Often, I’m able to fill in the gaps I had been stumbling over that way. Other times, the process will make me curious about some minor point, or character, that hadn’t interested me earlier and when I investigate them I uncover new facets of my story that suggest ways forward that wouldn’t have occurred to me otherwise.

When none of that works, I go running. I’ve written some of my best lines while on long runs. And if I’m still stuck, I walk along my bookshelves, grab books at random, and flip them open to random pages. Then I read a paragraph or two before repeating the process. There’s something about dropping into someone else’s work, and thinking, that allows me to see my own writing with fresh eyes and knocks me out of whatever rut I had been lodged in so I can move forward.

Keala Kendall, author of That Which Feeds Us: A Hawaiian Gothic

When I start a project, I write a mock query letter and a like list, a running inventory of elements that make me excited about the story. I refer back to these and use them as a guiding star while drafting (though the story can always change). Whenever I get stuck, I check my list to see what I can add to the scene to spark momentum. To give you an idea of how simple this can be, here are a few items from my list for That Which Feeds Us: hiding in tall grass fields, scuttling sounds at night, luxury turning into rot in real time, and the cost of coming home.

Valeria Luiselli, author of Beginning Middle End

I read.

issues.title: Why Fiction Loves Family Drama
issues.summary: There’s a house in my family—or, a house that used to be in my family. A beautiful, crumbly chateau in the south of France that my stepfather’s stepbrother had inherited from a wealthy godmother. The place was laden with debt,
issues.author: Chloë Ashby
issues.content_html:
There’s a house in my family—or, a house that used to be in my family. A beautiful, crumbly chateau in the south of France that my stepfather’s stepbrother had inherited from a wealthy godmother. The place was laden with debt, and expensive to run, so he had to sell it—but that’s not the point. The point is that our family, like lots of families, is complicated, with enough steps to make a ladder. Which is perhaps why I’m drawn to reading, and writing, about other complicated families in fiction—see, we’re not the only ones.

Lucky for me, stories about dysfunctional parents, children, partners, ex-partners (the list goes on) are in good supply and always have been. The Greeks were all over family drama: in Euripides’ Medea, a mother murders her children to punish her faithless husband; there’s a bucketload of domestic bloodshed in Aeschylus’s Oresteia. The Old Testament is plagued with marital woes and sibling rivalries.

If Jane Austen were here today, she might tell us that we’re drawn to families under pressure because there’s no such thing as a family that isn’t under pressure; she might even say that it’s “a truth universally acknowledged” (etc). Which, together with her writing, witty and slyly funny, is surely the secret to the enduring appeal of her classic novels. Two hundred years on, they remain a hit at the box office, with new adaptations for every generation.

In Sense and Sensibility, newly directed for the big screen by Georgia Oakley, the Dashwood sisters navigate love and loss in the face of financial ruin. Coming soon to Netflix, with a fresh script from novelist and Sunday Times columnist Dolly Alderton, Pride and Prejudice follows the Bennet sisters, who must marry well because they’re unable to inherit. So far, so old-school. But in the words of Naoise Dolan: “We would all like to be as scathing as Lizzy and to marry rich.” Where do we learn how to love and negotiate, compromise and persuade, if not from the family unit?

Joining the modern reboots of Austen is a starry revival of Jon Robin Baitz’s Tony-winning Other Desert Cities, currently showing at the Hudson Theater in New York. The play sees a daughter return to the family home in Palm Springs on Christmas Eve threatening to publish a tell-all memoir exposing an old trauma involving her brother. It’s funny and sad, a family reunion that’s as salty as it is satisfying. There’s nothing like time apart to fuel our capacity to love and wound our kin.

I didn’t set out to write a book about messy families, but I am aware that squeaky-clean ones rarely make for good (let alone convincing) reading material.

Family dramas needn’t be high drama. Just look at Tessa Hadley, who repeatedly burrows into the ordinary lives of families in her novels and short stories. Her recent foray into non-fiction, Alone with a Book: On Reading, Writing and Lookingtraces her development as both a reader and a writer, and explores the literary and artistic works that have kept her company along the way. There’s a brilliant essay on Elizabeth Jane Howard, best-known for the Cazalet Chronicles, a sprawling family saga packed with family get-togethers and holidays—Hadley describes them as “a true record of a real thing.” This fall, Louisa Young has picked up the thread where her aunt Elizabeth left off: The Golden Hours brings the story of the Cazalet family into the 1960s with a realistic dose of drama that’s the same, but different.

I didn’t set out to write a book about messy families, but I am aware that squeaky-clean ones rarely make for good (let alone convincing) reading material. And no wonder. What’s gripping about husbands and wives politely interacting or siblings resolving conflict without hurling abuse—or cups and saucers—across the kitchen table? Enough of the niceties! Give us tension, silence, long-suppressed secrets (simmering beneath the surface, of course)! Plus, Tolstoy was surely on to something when he wrote the famous opening line of Anna Karenina: “All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.” Infinite possibilities with every fracture, twist, and tangle!

My novel, Family Friends, is set in a house similar to the one I described at the outset of this essay. It tells the story of two long-term couples and their thwarted efforts to deflect and avoid heartbreak, and unfolds during two climactic weeks, and the long, winding decades that preceded them. It’s about marriage and parenthood, the way friends and lovers change (and don’t change) over time, and families muddling through. During the writing process I was thinking about people making mistakes, and the point at which doing a bad thing makes you a bad person. Plus, what happens next? Do you carry on, because family is family, or do you reassess and walk away?

The setting may have been inspired by the beautiful, crumbly chateau in the south of France that briefly belonged to my stepfather’s stepbrother, but the seed of the book was planted several years earlier. When I was a child, we used to go on holiday with my parents’ friends and their friends’ children—big group holidays that were chaotic and loud. The parents had grown up together, and in some cases shared tangled pasts; the assumption was that us kids would rub along. We were left to our own devices in the way that children often are on holiday and would inevitably end up hearing and seeing things we shouldn’t….

Just something to bear in mind when your own family reconvenes this holiday season.

______________________________

Family Friends by Chloë Ashby is available from Pegasus Books.

issues.title: The Fall of China’s Last Emperor
issues.summary: Spring 1923: The Imperial Garden, Forbidden City, Peking A Peking spring is always brief but can be glorious. Temperatures rise after a long, deep winter, the skies are blue and cloudless, the distinctive citrusy scent of magnolia perfumes the air
issues.author: Paul French
issues.content_html:
Spring 1923: The Imperial Garden, Forbidden City, Peking

A Peking spring is always brief but can be glorious. Temperatures rise after a long, deep winter, the skies are blue and cloudless, the distinctive citrusy scent of magnolia perfumes the air in the hutongs, or alleyways. Peking residents shrug off their padded greatcoats and feel the sun on their skin once again.

Dominating the heart of Peking is the Forbidden City, a walled citadel surrounded by a wide moat, home to China’s emperors since 1420. A complex of great halls, elaborate pavilions and formal gardens, at 178 acres the imperial palace is roughly twice the size of Vatican City. The northern portions, known as the Inner Court, were traditionally the preserve of the emperor and his immediate royal family, assorted concubines, dowagers, close relatives and clan members, as well as the most trusted servants and palace eunuchs. Within the Inner Court, the Imperial Garden (Yu Huayuan) lies in the shadow of the Palace of Earthly Tranquility (Kunning Gong), where traditionally the Qing dynasty held weddings and other imperial ceremonies. The gardens themselves are not overly extensive but are private; secluded pathways twist and turn alongside small streams traversed by miniature footbridges.

It was here, in the fine spring of 1923, that four very different but intimately connected individuals gathered for midday picnics. Of the four, two were Manchu royalty, the Emperor Puyi and his new Empress Wanrong, fated to be last in the line of the Manchu Qing dynasty. Accompanying them were Reginald Johnston, the young emperor’s tutor, and Isabel Ingram, the empress’s English teacher.

They were a seemingly unlikely group: a Manchu emperor who would never rule his kingdom, his arranged bride, a fifty-year-old Scottish colonial official and a young American woman, who was the daughter of pious Pennsylvania missionaries. Yet Johnston, a highly capable sinologist and a linguist with a deep appreciation of Chinese tradition, was a broad-minded and affable man who, thanks to Puyi’s regard, had risen to great importance within the imperial household. Ingram, from the start of her employment the previous year, had become a close friend of the empress. She was nearer to the royal couple in age and brought a refreshing vitality and modernity to the ritualistic and hidebound Forbidden City.

*

Puyi and Wanrong were, in 1923, cognizant of their position as the end of the Qing royal line. China had been a republic since 1912, just over a decade. Puyi had been anointed in December 1908 at barely two years of age and forced to abdicate at six when he was demoted to emperor in name only, confined within the high walls of the Forbidden City ever since. In 1922 the couple’s wedding was celebrated; it was to be the last burst of imperial pageantry Peking would ever see. Thousands lined the streets at dawn to see Wanrong enter the Forbidden City to become empress. They were both just sixteen.

That night, for the first time in over five hundred years through Ming to Qing to republic, the Forbidden City closed its gates without China having an emperor.

Puyi and Wanrong were forced to live a sequestered existence in the gilded cage of the so-called “Great Within” (Da Nei). Only the noises of the city breached its ramparts, but Puyi knew little of its tumultuous society, or his country’s cacophonous mix of fractious politics.

Since then the young couple had sought to build a life together, isolated but for the remnants of the imperial family—Puyi and Wanrong’s brothers, some aging dowagers who had been concubines of long-deceased emperors and Puyi’s own consort, Wenxiu. Serving them were their closest courtiers, a detachment of the palace guard, approximately a thousand palace eunuchs and the two royal tutors. It was a strange, cloistered life while outside China’s young republic sought to establish and consolidate itself against foreign interference and the internal chaos of warlordism.

*

That spring of 1923 the impromptu picnics in the Imperial Garden were a new pastime. Wanrong spent hours dressing Ingram in Manchu costume, styling her hair in the traditional liangbatou (a two-handed headdress), where two bunches of hair were arranged over a frame to create a wing-like structure. Puyi and Johnston would join them for tea and dim-sum, often both clad in classical scholar’s robes. They ordered in cream cakes from a German bakery in the nearby Legation Quarter of Peking, where the city’s foreign population clustered. When Peking’s notorious humidity kicked in they would sip barley water instead of tea. They posed for photographs, a hobby Johnston had introduced to Puyi and which became a shared passion among the four. They snapped each other constantly and took group photos too, often joined by consort Wenxiu. They appear at ease, comfortable, taking what pleasure they can despite their isolation and political impotence.

Johnston termed the years between 1919, when he started to tutor Puyi, and the emperor’s expulsion from the Forbidden City in 1924 “the twilight period.” He related his version of events at length in the oft-reprinted memoir Twilight in the Forbidden City (first published in 1934). Johnston was brought to life in a sympathetic portrayal by Peter O’Toole in Bernardo Bertolucci’s film The Last Emperor (1987), which placed him at the heart of the story of the young Puyi. However, in the light of his previously unpublished personal correspondence with Ingram, Johnston’s recounting of events in his book might be viewed as somewhat vainglorious. He presents himself as the only foreigner close to the emperor and empress, whereas this was clearly not the case. Reticent and rather pedantic in his memoir, Johnston is familiar, chatty and affectionate in his letters to Ingram, the pretty, vivacious and well-educated missionaries’ daughter, with whom he was clearly smitten.

As we shall see, their relationship was evidently far more important to him than its absence from Twilight in the Forbidden City might suggest. It becomes apparent that they met regularly outside the Forbidden City, either at Johnston’s Western Hills retreat just beyond the city walls, or for tiffin at the Grand Hôtel des Wagons-Lit in the Legation Quarter, where they would discuss the welfare of their charges, plan guest receptions and organize garden parties in an attempt to ease the claustrophobia of life in the Forbidden City.

*

Just two years after their wedding, Puyi, Wanrong and Wenxiu were expelled into a harsh world of feuding warlords and a weak Republican government, and into the arms of Japan, which was already actively planning to conquer and rule China. Their tutors were also cast out, their relationships with the royal couple severed overnight. Cut off from Johnston and Ingram, their only contacts with the world outside the Forbidden City, the naive and politically unsophisticated Puyi and Wanrong were destined for disaster.

Warlord fighting all around Peking escalated in the autumn and winter of 1924. There was a mass of competing factions and fragile alliances, a combustible coalition of warlords who had controlled Peking since 1912, initially held together and led by Yuan Shikai. One warlord had replaced the previous one as they plotted, deceived or assassinated one another. To cut a long and twisted tale of machinations and disloyalties short, the warlord Feng Yuxiang, known correctly as the “Betrayal General,” staged a coup and seized Peking in the midnight hours of October 23, 1924.

Feng immediately ousted the widely disliked President Cao Kun, known as the “Bribing President” (having basically bought the job though massive bribes), and placed him under house arrest. Cao Kun’s brother committed suicide at the news. Warlord soldiers blocked access into the Legation Quarter to prevent their enemies seeking sanctuary in the foreign embassies. They blockaded the main roads leading out of Peking in all directions and cut the telegraph cables to Tianjin, meaning that effectively all communications out of the city were dead. The Peking Leader described it as “unquestionably one of the most extraordinary coup d’états in Chinese history.” Johnston wrote that the Forbidden City was in “consternation.”

Foreigners and wealthy Chinese boarded up their homes, hired private guards and checked into the city’s foreign hotels—the Grand Hôtel de Pékin, the Grand Hôtel des Wagons-Lits, the Hôtel du Nord. Alternatively, they made for their weekend villas in the nearby Western Hills or at Paomachang just outside the city to wait out the chaotic interregnum, fully expecting a degree of bloodshed as there would inevitably be some revenge killings given all the betrayals and switching of sides among the warlords.

What Feng might do to Puyi, Wanrong and the Little Court was of paramount concern. Rumors swirled along the hutongs: Feng’s bloodthirsty troops would storm the Forbidden City and slaughter all inside; they would ransack the treasure cellars of the Great Within; they would do to the Aisin-Gioro clan what the Bolsheviks had done to the Romanovs. It wasn’t hard to be convinced by such rumors. Feng believed that the persistence of the monarchy in the Forbidden City was a block in the road to a full and proper Chinese Republic. He had good contacts with the new Soviet Union and the Bolsheviks. He had long opposed the Articles of Favorable Treatment and he had absolutely no time for monarchy in any form.

*

Puyi was immersed in the mourning ceremonies and funeral for Lady Tatara, the Dowager Imperial Noble Consort Duankang. Lady Tatara had famously criticized Puyi’s mother Youlan in 1921, prompting her suicide, yet the emperor was still expected to lead the elaborate and long-running grieving for her.

Johnston was summoned to the palace on November 2 for a conference with Puyi, Prince Chun, Zheng Xiaoxu and Wanrong’s father, Rongyuan. They were nervous that General Feng would decide to invade the Inner Court. Indeed his troops were already positioned on Coal Hill overlooking the Forbidden City. Johnston suggested evacuating the emperor and empress to safety in the Legation Quarter, but Zheng assured them all the gates of the citadel were closed and guarded by Feng’s troops on the outside facing the small band of Imperial Guards on the inside. Puyi handed Johnston a suitcase of ornate rings and jewelery—all Lady Tatara’s, he claimed. He told Johnston to deposit them at a bank as “they would all be stolen if left in her palace.”

Johnston returned to the Inner Court on November 3, noting “it presented a ghostly and forlorn appearance.” He found Puyi looking up towards Coal Hill at Feng’s troops through his telescope. “Many of the staff were in hiding or had disappeared. Others were engaged in carrying out the ceremonies connected with Tuan Kang’s [Duankang’s] funeral, and flitted about in the white garb of mourners.” He stayed overnight at the Lodge of the Cultivation of Nature and lunched the following day with the emperor. They then visited the empress in the Palace of Gathered Elegance. Johnston says they all, with Zheng Xiaoxu, discussed a plan to smuggle the emperor and empress wearing disguises out of the Forbidden City the following day.

As Johnston wrote: “The long twilight in the Forbidden City was deepening into darkness.”

But the plans came to nought. The following day, Wednesday, November 5, 1924, the telephone lines into the Forbidden City were cut. Feng’s troops surrounded the citadel, disarmed the Imperial Guards, marched into the Forbidden City’s Inner Court and occupied it. Johnston heard the news while having breakfast at Zhangwang Hutong. He immediately headed to the Forbidden City. At the gates he flashed his imperial pass but was prevented from entering by Feng’s soldiers.

*

Inside the Inner Court that morning the expulsion had been both swift and chaotic. They had all been expecting the axe to fall for so long that when it finally did Puyi and Wanrong seemed entirely stunned. Though servants had deserted, Imperial Household Department officials had not been showing up for work and troops had hauled cannon up onto Coal Hill facing down into the Inner Court, it was as if nobody thought it would ever actually happen. Puyi later admitted that he was scared and realized the situation was potentially mortally dangerous for the couple. When the troops arrived Puyi was chatting with Wanrong and peeling an apple for her in the Palace of Gathered Elegance. They were escorted out to the courtyard to await a decision on their fate—it was far from clear to them if they would survive the morning. Warlord troops took a photograph of Puyi’s hastily abandoned bedroom, the expulsion so swift “the imperial apartments were left in a state of disarray, with juvenile works of fiction, kung-fu novels and toys scattered around the formerly august dwellings.”

*

Forbidding him to contact Johnston, his father or Zheng Xiaoxu, General Feng’s officers dictated terms to Puyi: the final abolition of the title of emperor, a greatly reduced allowance of $500,000 a year, a factory to be established in Peking to employ any Manchu noblemen down on their luck, while Puyi’s person and private property were to be guaranteed by the Republic. The negotiation was effectively conducted at the barrel of a gun: Puyi had till midday to accept, or Feng threatened to fire the cannon on Coal Hill at the Forbidden City and destroy the palace. Puyi felt compelled to sign. The royal couple and Wenxiu were given three hours to leave the Forbidden City. They were not allowed to take more “than what a servant or two could carry.”

[Puyi] had hoped leaving would open a new world for him. It only passed him from one set of captors to another.

On hearing that Puyi had signed the revisions, effectively rendering the 1912 Articles of Favorable Treatment null and void, and that the royal couple had already left the Forbidden City, it is said that Prince Chun pulled off his hat with the peacock feather that distinguished his high rank, threw it on the floor and said, “It’s all over, it’s all over, I won’t need this again.”

Puyi left for his father’s house, the Northern Mansion. Feng’s troops provided five cars for the royal entourage. An officer in charge of the expulsion sat in the first, Puyi in the second, Wanrong and Wenxiu followed behind in the third, with two cars of armed guards making up the rear as they drove to the Beifu. As they prepared to leave the Forbidden City, General Feng’s commanding officer, Lu Zhonglin, shook hands with Puyi and asked him:

“Mr. Puyi, do you intend to be emperor in the future, or will you be an ordinary citizen?”

Puyi replied: “From today onwards I want to be an ordinary citizen.”

“Good,” Lu replied, “then we shall protect you.”

The procession left through the Gate of Divine Prowess into the Great Without.

*

Ingram later recalled that on the morning of November 5 her rickshaw had arrived as normal to take her for her daily lessons with the empress. But when she arrived at the Gate of Divine Prowess, she found the walls of the Forbidden City surrounded by grim-faced troops armed with bayonets pointing outwards. Concerned for Wanrong’s safety, she tried to face down the soldiers, demanding they stand aside and allow her in. She declared, “My business is with the Empress.” The soldiers laughed nervously, continued to point their bayonets in her direction and told her the empress was already gone from the Forbidden City. Their commander told her that Wanrong had departed “hatless, coatless and baggageless.” Ingram had no choice but to return home to Dengshikou and await news of Wanrong, Puyi and their fate. She later told the Philadelphia Record, “That day was the end of my beautiful China…”

Eventually, the historic day over, darkness fell on Peking. That night, for the first time in over five hundred years through Ming to Qing to republic, the Forbidden City closed its gates without China having an emperor.

*

Late that evening Johnston went to the Northern Mansion. He recalled in his memoirs that he found Puyi calm and resigned and Prince Chun typically floundering and chaotic. Johnston could think of little practical to do. He would not see Puyi again for over three weeks.

Then on November 29 Johnston arranged for Puyi to leave the Northern Mansion and travel the short distance to the Legation Quarter to seek sanctuary. Wanrong and Wenxiu remained behind; the plan was to smuggle them out to the Legation Quarter later once the emperor was secure.

Johnston sought sanctuary for Puyi, first with Willem Oudendijk at the Dutch Legation, but Oudendijk was not in residence and couldn’t be reached. Then at the darkly Gothic Japanese Legation on the eastern side of Canal Street, but Ambassador Kenkichi Yoshizawa was also out for the night and unavailable. Johnston rapidly crossed the road to the British Legation, the largest of all the foreign legations, with two over-sized stone lions at the gates. But it was a futile mission, and Johnston knew it. The ambassador, Sir Ronald Macleay, unequivocally told him that the legation did not accept political refugees. Johnston went back across the road to try the Japanese again, who historically had accepted Chinese political refugees and offered asylum (generally when it suited their political ends).

If there was a moment when Britain could have offered sanctuary to Puyi then that hope ended late that evening of November 29 with Macleay’s refusal to accept Puyi. A young man tutored by a Scotsman, who longed to be a student at Oxford, who adopted the name Henry after an English king and whose wife had taken the name Elizabeth after an English queen, was pushed back towards the Japanese—a fateful and tragic decision.

Ambassador Kenkichi Yoshizawa arrived back at the embassy. He accepted Puyi on November 30. The Last Emperor of China’s long years of exile began.

*

It was to be the end of an era for Reginald Johnston and Isabel Ingram too. Johnston, who shortly after the expulsion returned to his Colonial Service duties with the British government in China, was to keep in erratic touch with Puyi over the coming years. He visited him in his exile in the foreign concessions of Tianjin and Japanese-occupied Manchuria. They corresponded, though the letters are lost. Ingram was never to see the empress again.

Puyi had always maintained that he wanted to leave the Forbidden City, but the final expulsion was the beginning of the end for the royal couple. He had hoped leaving would open a new world for him. It only passed him from one set of captors to another.

Could a marriage that relied on joint support in internal exile, the curious persistence of the imperial household despite abdication and a decade of the Chinese Republic survive? The answer is it could not. It never stood a chance after the royal couple’s expulsion from the Forbidden City. From the day Puyi and then Wanrong left through the Meridian Gate for the final time, from the Great Within to the Great Without, they were both doomed.

___________________________

From The Last Emperor of China: Twilight of the Forbidden City by Paul French. Copyright © 2026 by the author and reprinted by permission of St. Martin’s Publishing Group.

issues.title: Everything You Need to Know About The Nightingale Adaptation
issues.summary: Now that we have a first look and a teaser trailer, here's everything you need to know about the adaptation of THE NIGHTINGALE.
issues.author: S. Zainab Williams
issues.content_html:
We have a teaser trailer and a first look at The Nightingale adaptation. Sony Pictures released the trailer and gave us a first look through Vanity Fair late last week. Information about this highly anticipated adaptation of Kristin Hannah’s bestseller has been trickling out.

Here’s what you need to know about the film, so far:

  • The film and the book focuses on women’s resistance and mobilization against the Nazis during WWII
  • Real-life sisters Dakota and Elle Fanning will play sisters on screen for the first time
  • The film is produced by Reese Witherspoon and her production company, Hello Sunshine, as well as the Fanning sisters’ production company, Lewellen Pictures
  • The book was a 2023 Reese’s Book Club selection
  • Reese’s Book Club and Lewellen Pictures shared a first look at the film tie-in cover
  • The film’s director, Michael Morris, recently worked on another adaptation: Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy, the fourth film in the series, based on Helen Fielding’s novel of the same name
  • March 19, 2027 marks the U.S. premiere
  • The teaser, just under three minutes, emphasizes the progression of the sisters from first-hand witnesses to the war to members of the resistance

On filming a scene together and playing sisters for the first time, Dakota Fanning told Vanity Fair,

We played together our entire lives and acted out scenarios, so it felt like clicking back into that. Like, ‘Oh, of course, this is what we do.’”

Hannah revealed to the publication that she’s unlikely to ever adapt one of her books for the screen.

“I would be afraid that my love for the story that I had written would in some way limit me from being able to see what the film really needed to be.”

You probably know someone who has read Hannah’s bestseller. That says it all about the popularity of her historical fiction set in Nazi-occupied France, and gives us big reason to believe the film will be an epic success.

issues.title: What to Watch This Weekend, YA Edition
issues.summary: In these Netflix adaptations you should watch this weekend , love gets messy and a sword-toting princess avenges her father.
issues.author: Community
issues.content_html:
Netflix has been having a time with adaptations lately. There are so many great ones that are either birthed from YA novels or that reimagine stories with younger protagonists.

The following YA adaptations are available on Netflix. In them, love gets messy, one bullied teen in Brazil gets a summer he’ll never forget, and a sword-toting princess avenges her father.

To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before: It feels like this adaptation of the 2014 bestselling release by Jenny Han came at a time when the Netflix adaptation game wasn’t as strong. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if the success of this movie encouraged more YA adaptations.

  • The 2018 release follows the book fairly closely, though there are also a few differences. High schooler Lara Jean’s world gets rocked when the love letters she wrote to her five crushes get mailed out to them.

Here the Whole Time: This Brazilian-set coming-of-age film was adapted from a 2017 YA novel of the same name in English, but originally titled Quinze Dias by Vitor Martins, translated by Larissa Helena.

  • Interestingly enough, the novel gets compared to To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before, except the main character is a fat gay teenager who finds out his crush is staying with him and his mother for 15 days one summer.

Scarlet: This fantastical anime adaptation of Shakespeare’s Hamlet looks gorgeous. It follows a teen princess on a quest to avenge her father.

issues.title: A Night at the 77th National Book Awards
issues.summary: The National Book Awards is arguably the year’s biggest night in books. It’s glam (Black-tie! Tuxedos! Champagne!), it’s fun (think cocktails on the dance floor next to literary all-stars), and, at its best, it’s political. It’s a moment for writers to take the stage and speak out against global injustice and the injustices we are […] The post A Night at the 77th National Book Awards appeared firs
issues.author: Katie Henken Robinson
issues.content_html:
The National Book Awards is arguably the year’s biggest night in books. It’s glam (Black-tie! Tuxedos! Champagne!), it’s fun (think cocktails on the dance floor next to literary all-stars), and, at its best, it’s political. It’s a moment for writers to take the stage and speak out against global injustice and the injustices we are facing from within our own industry. Last night’s ceremony was all of the above, and I got to experience it live, reporting the event with former Electric Lit intern Amulya Tadimety, who graciously helped me record the evening. (Shout out to Amulya, who even swapped phones with me so I could write down quotes while she took pictures using the higher-quality camera.)

This year featured a phenomenal set of finalists in all categories, many of whom Electric Lit is lucky to have featured in our digital pages. In Fiction, we featured an interview with Valeria Luiselli and a joint conversation with Morgan Thomas and Julián Delgado Lopera, the two trans novelists nominated for the award—an exciting and much-deserved first that I hope marks many more to come. In Nonfiction, we published interviews with Abdelrahman ElGendy, Sara Nović, and Camonghne Felix, as well as a reading list from Joseph Osmundson, who also helped us put together an article about Bret Stephens’ hideous New York Times hit piece about the diversity of the year’s longlist.

The event was hosted by Kyle MacLachlan, whose opening remarks set the tone for the night: at times, lighthearted, balanced with appropriate seriousness. He gave a much appreciated nod to library cards and referenced his love of Dune (MacLachlan’s appearance in the David Lynch adaptation was his break-out role). He also said he was confused about why the NBA wanted him to speak at their event, until he realized it wasn’t, well, that NBA, a joke sure to land with anyone who (like me) makes the annual mistake of googling “NBA finalists” when the shortlist drops.

MacLachlan also touched on a topic at the top of everyone’s mind, saying that while AI didn’t write his speech—that would be immoral—he was taking all the credit from the human who did, a more industry-accepted course of action. It was a lighthearted way to enter into the AI conversation, a hot topic, and for good reason. Many of the night’s speeches included rallying cries to reject the encroachment of AI on art, an admonishment implicitly directed at the publishing houses in the room (though perhaps meant less for the editors in attendance than for their boss’ boss’ boss). There were even references to outlets doing away with much-needed books coverage (from Kiran Desai, whose mother, Anita, once reviewed Salman Rushdie, the recipient of this year’s Medal for Distinguished Contribution to American Letters, in the now discontinued Washington Post books section). Interestingly, there was no mention of Catapult’s closure, however—a notable silence on a night full of adamant reminders about the importance of keeping literature alive.

Initially, I planned to introduce the winners and their statements one by one, but I would be remiss not to acknowledge up front that nonfiction winner Abdelrahman ElGendy was prevented from entering the country to attend the awards ceremony. His absence was acutely felt, an unignorable reminder of the violence of borders and the violence perpetuated by the current Administration. And, as if state-sanctioned harassment weren’t enough, ElGendy’s eligibility for the award was also questioned by The New York Times, before his win, and again afterward, despite the National Book Foundation issuing a statement affirming his eligibility.

ElGendy’s absence was also acknowledged by the first winners of the night, David Levithan and Gabriel Duckels, who won the category of Young People’s Literature for their book The Fight of Our Lives. Levithan opened his statement by saying, “We stand in solidarity with any author who is kept from being here tonight.”

Each of the night’s winners gave beautiful, moving speeches. Duckels and Levithan, whose book is a history of the AIDS crisis in America, also spoke about the censorship of queer stories. “The past, present, and future of HIV and AIDS cannot be erased,” said Duckels. Levithan gave a powerful statement on the ongoing erasure of trans and queer stories, saying, “Yes, there are people who want to erase our stories from the shelves, but know there are far, far, far more people who want our stories to be heard . . . We will not allow our youth, particularly our trans and nonbinary youth, to go unsupported. We will not let the noise of others drown out the music of who we are.”

Centroeuropa, a novel about a widower who uncovers the bodies of dead soldiers while digging up a field he intends to farm on, by Vicente Luis Mora, translated by Rahul Bery, won in Translated Literature. In his speech, Mora addressed the pain of ongoing war and his dream that one day countries standing for peace and protection for all people will be more than the stuff of fiction.

Bery cheekily addressed AI in his speech about the art of translation. Referencing an extremely specific element of Centroeuropa that he was tasked with recreating (the book doubles its page count for each chapter, down to the exact word), he said, “In a year where everyone’s talking about AI and its threat to all kinds of human creativity and endeavor, I like to think that, for now at least, this is something the computers couldn’t do.”

I was personally thrilled when Brenda Hillman, the poetry winner for Still House in the Desert, directly addressed the press in the room. “We’re grateful for you,” she said, looking at the press tables in the back where us journalists and magazine editors were gathered, “but you know, sometimes poetry gets kind of a short shrift . . . we ask the press to consider [that] best books include poetry too.” I felt immense pride sitting there, knowing that one day later, Electric Lit was publishing our annual list of our favorite poetry collections, a tradition I hope other outlets will adopt.

When ElGendy’s Huna won in nonfiction, the award was accepted on his behalf by his editor, Helen Thomaides. She read from a speech written by ElGendy himself, which began with a statement that if we were hearing his words, it meant that he’d achieved a lifelong dream, only to not be able to be in the room for the moment. It made his already towering absence even larger. Thomaides also gave her own speech, speaking of how ElGendy’s “commitment to speaking out against injustice put a target on his back,” and how, after having found refuge in America, he was once again forced to flee. “Now,” she said, “he’s not able to return even as a celebrated visitor.”

The final winner, Hannah Lillith Assadi, won in Fiction with Paradiso 17. Assadi shared that during the course of writing the book, she “experienced deep personal grief and unimaginable collective grief,” referencing cancer’s attack on her father, and the genocide waged against his people. She spoke of the pain woven with beauty in the novel, saying: “Perhaps this is the Palestinian story on this earth. So beautiful, so painful. And isn’t this story all of ours?” It was a fitting way to end the evening.

issues.title: A Call to Action from Electric Literature
issues.summary: Dear Reader, Last year, Electric Literature decided not to apply for funding from the National Endowment of the Arts. You might remember that our decision resulted from an Executive Order handed down by the Trump Administration and new compliance guidelines drafted by the NEA, both stipulating that applicants must not “promote gender ideology.” It was […] The post A Call to Action from Electric Li
issues.author: Denne Michele Norris
issues.content_html:
Dear Reader,

Last year, Electric Literature decided not to apply for funding from the National Endowment of the Arts. You might remember that our decision resulted from an Executive Order handed down by the Trump Administration and new compliance guidelines drafted by the NEA, both stipulating that applicants must not “promote gender ideology.” It was a blatant attack on trans people, period—and applying would have been a betrayal of the values held so closely by EL and its community. I was part of the decision to forgo funding, and while it was nerve-wracking to walk away from money we relied on, standing up for our beliefs was a no-brainer. We trusted that our community would have our back and fill the gap. And it did.

When I was preparing to take over as Executive Director and Publisher earlier this year, EL had the chance to speak publicly (in an amicus brief attached to a lawsuit targeting the NEA) about how the loss of NEA funding impacted our ability to practice free speech as an independent literary magazine. As I was interviewed by lawyers from the National Coalition Against Censorship, I took a moment to reflect on the prior year. I felt more sure of our decision than ever. Though our funding had been cut, though we had been forced to revise our financial strategy without notice, we stood with the communities whose rights, protection, and humanity we are forever committed to uplifting—trans people and the queer community, people of color, people with disability, immigrants, women. Rather than feeling fearful about what the future might hold, I only felt immense pride.

Over the course of this year, I’ve become acutely aware that independence is our greatest asset—which means community is our greatest resource. Because Electric Lit is completely independent, we retain the freedom to defy a government that sometimes wishes to silence us. That independence also means we rely on our people to keep us going. We need to raise $60,000 by the end of the year to ensure we remain a beacon for the writers and stories we most care about publishing.

Electric Lit is committed to safeguarding the freedom, dignity, and humanity inherent to creative expression, but we are only as powerful as the people standing with us. An anonymous donor has kicked off our campaign this year with a matching gift of $15,000. Helping us match that gift will get us halfway towards our goal. I believe in Electric Lit, but more than that, I believe in the people that power Electric Lit. Join us in this fight by making a gift today.

With warmth and gratitude,

Denne Michele Norris
Executive Director and Publisher

issues.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Poetry Collections of 2026
issues.summary: This year’s most interesting poetry collections keep circling one small word: we. In an era when we’re constantly sorted into us and them, these poets ask who does the sorting and what it costs. Is we a people, a piece of land, a family, a crowd, a database? And where does that leave the rest […] The post Electric Lit’s Top 10 Poetry Collections of 2026 appeared first on Electric Literature .
issues.author: Electric Literature
issues.content_html:
This year’s most interesting poetry collections keep circling one small word: we. In an era when we’re constantly sorted into us and them, these poets ask who does the sorting and what it costs. Is we a people, a piece of land, a family, a crowd, a database? And where does that leave the rest of us, trying to keep up?

Layli Long Soldier’s We (Wé) takes the question of we to its most elemental level. The Lakota word wé means blood, and Long Soldier uses it to explore family, nation, history, and language through poems, essays, and artwork. For Jake Skeets, we extends beyond people to the land and everything living on it. Horsesopens with 200 feral horses stuck in Arizona mud and unfurls into an elegy for a changing Navajo Nation. Fatimah Asghar’sDaughter of the Mountains asks what remains after exile, reckoning with estranged kin and the landscape of their ancestors in poems both funny and elegiac. In Assembled Audience, the ever-delightful Erika Meitner takes up the strange business of being together, on beaches and in airports, in mourning and in protest. William Lessard’s haunting /face turns patents for facial capture technology into unlikely poetry about what happens when a face becomes data. And Hieu Minh Nguyen’s Staying Still traces the distance between the people and places we long to belong to and the selves we’re trying to become.

So much about who counts as us is now decided by people and machines that don’t know us at all. Against all that flattening, these poems get stubbornly specific. Maybe we begins there, not in agreement or allegiance, but in the act of paying attention to what—and whom—we might otherwise overlook.
–Kelly Luce
Editor, The Commuter

Editor’s note: The following books were hand-selected by Electric Literature staff and interns, with the help of our community of contributors, readers, and friends of the organization. While books by current staff or board members are not eligible for consideration, we would like to informally recommend I Can Tell You the Version That Will Make You Take My Side by board member J Brooke, another collection we loved this year! The 10 titles below are presented alphabetically by title; they are not ranked.

/face by William Lessard

If there’s something slightly absurd about composing an ode to the misty beauty of landscape on a Macbook Pro while pausing intermittently to check Instagram, take a selfie, take a screenshot, /face pinpoints it. William Lessard’s poetry accomplishes the seemingly impossible feat of writing in the tradition of powerpoints, patent filings, and the whole chaos of social media-fueled data harvesting that defines so much of life in 2026. Lessard’s book is not so much filled with traditionally formed poems as with shocks to the idea of what constitutes poetry; with experiments in embracing the parts of modern life that seem unfit for art; and, in short, with an unashamed attempt at authenticity. Read Lessard’s meditations on /face in an EL interview . . . and read the book!
–Willem Marx, Associate Editor

America, A Love Storyby Camille T Dungy

In America, A Love Story, Camille T Dungy addresses the nation with the exasperated, clear-eyed intimacy of someone who knows its capacity to wound. Writing as a Black woman and mother, Dungy turns love into an interrogation, pushing away the easy comfort of a flag-waving tribute. Her poems move fluidly from strawberry fields tarped against frost to a father questioned on a roadside, from a grandmother’s willow switch to the sleepless, fragile early days of parenting. Love, through these poems, is an enduring tenderness for daughters, for soil and blooming lilacs, for the hard-won instinct to protect what is vulnerable. In Dungy’s hands, love is what keeps imagination alive when safety falters, an unflinching devotion that refuses to ignore danger while still demanding that America answer back.
–Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

Assembled Audience by Erika Meitner

In Assembled Audience, Erika Meitner looks straight at the conditions that make “staying present” feel like a moral demand: fracking, climate change, pandemic aftermath, gun violence, the erosion of reproductive rights. A peripatetic speaker moves from eschatology to a Hampton Inn, from Whitman-sized questions to Bud Light and dragonflies, making room for luck, wonder, and the strange comedy of being alive. Reading this collection, I was certainly reminded of the Whitmanesque impulse in “Song of Myself”—which is really the chorus of each other, the idea that to create and exist is to wonder, and that we celebrate our fractured world by relentlessly examining everything within it, finding interest even in the mundane. Meitner channels that expansive, defiant celebration into our own dizzying moment. In Meitner’s electric, unsentimental vision of all its gatherings, attention itself becomes a way of standing with others.
–Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

Daughters of the Mountainsby Fatimah Asghar

Unafraid of tackling the vastness of human experience from love to loss, Asghar asks how an exile can find their place in the world. What follows are meditative, at times humorous, and always introspective poems that embrace the complexities of lineage, environment, family, and nature in shaping and disrupting home and the self. If you’re a fan of poetry dealing with queerness, displacement, or searching for connection, there’s a lot to be said for Daughter of the Mountains.
–Rachel Maybee, Editorial Intern

Horsesby Jake Skeets

Beginning with the evocative image of 200 horses found dead in the mud of a former stock pond on Navajo land in Arizona, Navajo Nation Poet Laureate Jake Skeets faces down environmental apocalypse and dares to allow hope to blossom from grief. Queer, lyrical, and inextricable from Diné thought, Skeets’ poems span time and distance, blurring the artificial boundary set between people and place. This gorgeous, highly-anticipated second collection will leave readers marking Skeets as a poet to watch.
–Rachel Maybee, Editorial Intern

Maybe the Body by Asa Drake

In his introduction to EL’s interview with Asa Drake, Cameron Quan describes reading her gorgeous debut collection as not unlike “the experience of being cared for at a distance.” I, editor of that interview, rushed to read Drake’s book myself. Quan is right, a sense of care emanates from Drake’s words. Yet what continues to resonate now, as the year comes to a close and Drake’s book still lingers in my mind, is the way it demonstrates how to care. These poems tease out the crystalline threads that connect a self and a body, a body and a world, a place and a history, and in doing so, demonstrate a stunning capacity to observe. To observe this carefully is to care radically. Drake writes: “When I feed the animals / the rabbit stands up // so straight she falls over. / This is the part I want / you to know.” Maybe the Body is the kind of book that is both splash and ripple, sound and echo.
–Willem Marx, Associate Editor

Run It Back by Kortney Morrow

In Run it Back, Kortney Morrow’s debut poetry collection, nostalgia takes center stage. We float through a luminous remembrance of the early 2000s, a time when freedom felt inevitable and aspiration felt a mere breath away. Hope and heroics are the lifeblood of this collection, much like “the hero” (in this case, Lebron James) injects life into his community, uplifts the people, and they, in turn, become their own heroes. As a fellow Cleveland native, this collection was especially important to read; it is a tribute to the power of a place—and a people—that has long felt forgotten. Morrow reminds us, in this stunning and timely collection, that learning the past is the key to unlocking our future.
–Denne Michele Norris, Executive Director and Publisher

Staying Stillby Hieu Minh Nguyen

In Staying Still, Hieu Minh Nguyen treats remaining alive as an arduous, tender labor. Moving across packed dance floors, motel beds, and quiet doorways, these poems reckon with the isolation of queer boyhood, refugee inheritance, and the fraught bond between mother and son. There’s a gripping portrait of a boy secretly swaying in his mother’s floor-length dress before a mirror, discovering how beauty and shame can share the same hemline. Nguyen searches restlessly for an anchor, asking what it means to remain—in a body, a family, or a future—that has not always felt like home. Like the cover’s apartment windows glowing behind colored shades, these poems reveal how close we can be to one another while still remaining out of reach: turning small acts of attention (naming a landscape, sharing fruit, searching for the right color) into ways of keeping silence from taking over.
–Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

Tree of Knowledge by Victoria Chang

Victoria Chang’s latest collection is part art history course and part arboreal eulogy. Chang watches the eucalyptus across her street get cut down, then she continues to see cuts everywhere: in Picasso, in Joan Mitchell, in the Hilma af Klint paintings that give the book its title. At the center of the book is “Eureka,” a long poem about the California town that expelled its entire Chinese population in 1885. The color red runs through the poems, whether it’s paint, a body’s last few periods, and, in several poems, the actual ink itself.
–Kelly Luce, Editor, The Commuter

We (Wé)by Layli Long Soldier

In We (Wé), Layli Long Soldier takes we, meaning “first-person plural” in English, and wé, meaning “blood” in Lakota, and blends the two, looking closely at how language, as well as family, bear the communal meanings imparted by decades of shared experience. Likewise, Long Soldier blends artwork, essay, and poetry to emulate in-person spaces where knowledge is created and reinforced through mentorship and collaboration. History remains at the forefront of this unique, groundbreaking collection.
–Rachel Maybee, Editorial Intern

issues.author: Laura Wilson
issues.content_html:
The Taper Man by Nick Harkaway; Watch the Quiet Snow by Mick Herron; Revenge Plot by Stephanie Wrobel; The Voices of the Dead by Nicola Upson; The Bells of Fortune by Leonora Nattrass

The Taper Man by Nick Harkaway (Viking, £22)
The second George Smiley continuation novel from John le Carré’s son Nick Harkaway is set in 1965 and features early iterations of several characters who appear in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and Smiley’s People. The cold war is at its height, and British intelligence is keen to protect one of its most important sources, Red Army general Vladimir Vasilev. When a colleague is shot in Helsinki, Smiley discovers a connection to a group of Soviet agents who, through their links to a now defunct spying operation in the US, may jeopardise this key asset. Smiley travels to California to find the “Taper Man”, a sleeper agent whose job is to remain behind when the rest of the network is burned. Meanwhile, leftwing academic Roy Bland goes undercover in Moscow, but things do not go according to plan. Intricately plotted and densely written, The Taper Man takes time to get going, with a fair bit of cold war history and analysis to be digested, but it is a worthy and welcome addition to the le Carré canon.

Watch the Quiet Snow by Mick Herron (Baskerville, £22)
This beautifully presented collection of previously published novellas is the perfect Christmas present for fans of Slow Horses. Two of the stories shed further light on Slough House supremo Jackson Lamb – “a grubby Santa, putting the grot into grotto” – and his shared past with MI5 archivist Molly Doran, while the other three take us into the farther reaches of Herron’s espionage world, where washed-up boozehound John Bachelor works as a “milkman”, looking after retired assets who have “come in from other nations’ colds”. Bachelor’s needs may be simple – shelter, and enough money to pickle himself in peace – but his drunken stumbles into the murky world of double and even triple agents invariably lead to complications and the unwelcome attention of fearsome Service chief Diana Taverner. With Herron’s trademark blend of cynical humour, sinister undercurrents, suspense, irony and pathos, this is a splendid read for a dark night.

My favourite book growing up

The book that changed me as a teenager
A Tree Grows in Brooklyn by Betty Smith. My mom gave it to me at around 12 or 13, and I remember thinking it was such an adult book at the time. It gave me a protagonist to admire who thrived in spite of the setbacks in her life, and also helped put into perspective the charmed life I’d been living.

issues.title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison
issues.summary: This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attention American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery
issues.author: Sarah Moss
issues.content_html:
This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attention

American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing.

The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suzanna’s visits take increasingly constrained forms. Abjuring ordinary teenage activities, she takes the train towards the hill every Saturday, submits to searches, and follows rules about how to move and what and whom she may not touch.

Assadi’s third novel was inspired by the story of her late father, a Palestinian who escaped the Nakba as a child in 1948

Palestinian-Jewish author Hannah Lillith Assadi has won the National book award for fiction, one of the US’s most prestigious literary prizes, for her novel Paradiso 17.

Assadi’s third novel is a study of the psychic toll of displacement on migrants, through the tale of a Palestinian man who escaped the Nakba in 1948, when more than 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes by Israel. The story was inspired by her father, Sami Abdul-Fattah Al-Assadi, who fled the Nakba as a child with his family, before studying in Italy and moving to New York.

issues.title: Music Venue Trust and Fender team up for intimate London showcase gig with Unpeople
issues.summary: The venture aims to support the capital's grassroots music scene The post Music Venue Trust and Fender team up for intimate London showcase gig with Unpeople appeared first on NME .
issues.author: Damian Jones
issues.content_html:
The Music Venue Trust and Fender have teamed up for an intimate London showcase gig with up and coming Bristol band Unpeople.

The venture entitled The One. For London. aims to support London’s grassroots music scene kicking off with a concert at the dive bar Blondies in Hackney on December 1. Tickets are available to purchase here and all fans in attendance will receive a Limited Edition Fender The One. For London. t-shirt on the night.

“We all started out in small venues just like Blondies,” said Unpeople. “So it feels very special to team up with Fender and get to play a show like this, for a cause that’s very close to our hearts. Support small venues that give bands like ours a place to start. We are unpeople, you are unpeople, we are all unpeople.”

Liam Cunnah, Executive Vice President, EMEA, Fender, added: “The One. For London. is about giving back to the grassroots music venues that make Fender possible and supporting Music Venue Trust’s ongoing efforts to protect these vital spaces,” said Liam Cunnah, Executive Vice President, EMEA, Fender.

“These venues are the beating heart of the UK’s music culture, providing a platform for emerging artists to find their sound and connect with audiences. Through The One. For All. and the American Professional series, we’re celebrating the connection between artists, the instruments they play and the stages that give them a place to be heard.”

The event marks the next chapter in Fender’s collaboration with MVT, which began with a nationwide call for fans to nominate their favourite grassroots venues to win Fender gear in September, which received more than 5,000 nominations.

For the Blondies performance, Unpeople will play a Stratocaster, Telecaster and Precision Bass from Fender’s new American Professional series.

Fender will also match donations raised on the night up to a cap, with all proceeds supporting the MVT’s “vital work protecting the UK’s grassroots music venues”.

The event will also feature in an upcoming short documentary celebrating the American Professional series and the grassroots music communities that help shape emerging artists, including Unpeople.

The film will highlight “the importance of preserving these vital spaces for future generations”, according to a press release.

Elsewhere, the UK music industry recently reported a record-breaking £8.4billion generated for the economy, but sector leaders have warned NME that “growth is slowing and success is not being felt evenly” for artists, venues and beyond.

issues.title: Liam Gallagher, Bonehead and Primal Scream lead tributes on one year anniversary of Mani’s death
issues.summary: "A year ago today we lost our HERO our FRIEND the 1 n only GARY MANI MOUNFIELD" The post Liam Gallagher, Bonehead and Primal Scream lead tributes on one year anniversary of Mani’s death appeared first on NME .
issues.author: Damian Jones
issues.content_html:
Liam Gallagher, Bonehead and Primal Scream have led tributes on the anniversary of Gary “Mani” Mounfield’s death.

READ MORE: Gary “Mani” Mounfield, 1962-2025: baggy bass hero whose melodies made the Madchester movement

The Stone Roses bassist, who was also a member of Primal Scream from 1996 and 2011, passed away from respiratory issues a year ago today at the age of 63. He was laid to rest the following month at a funeral at Manchester Cathedral, which was attended by Liam Gallagher, Paul Weller, Ian Brown and more.

Liam Gallagher was one of the first to pay his respects to the Manchester music icon on the anniversary of his passing. “A year ago today we lost our HERO our FRIEND the 1 n only GARY MANI MOUNFIELD thinking of you always Rkid LG x,” he wrote.

A year ago today we lost our HERO our FRIEND the 1 n only GARY MANI MOUNFIELD thinking of you always Rkid LG x

— Liam Gallagher (@liamgallagher) November 20, 2026

The Oasis frontman helped carried Mani’s coffin during his funeral alongside Stone Roses members Reni and John Squire.

Fellow Oasis bandmate Bonehead also paid tribute to Mani posting on X: “Thinking of you today Mani,” alongside a link to the Stone Roses’ classic ‘I Wanna Be Adored’. He also posted an image of himself on his Instagram page wearing a Brazil football shirt with Mani’s name on it ahead of their concert in the country on the day of the late icon’s death.

Thinking of you today Mani. https://t.co/kHkAsSSPQs

— Paul Arthurs. (@BoneheadsPage) November 20, 2026

View this post on Instagram

Primal Scream honoured their former bandmate by posting a photo of frontman Bobby Gillespie and Mani shot by former NME photographer Kevin Cummins on their Instagram page. “One year without Mani,” they wrote.

View this post on Instagram

Former bassist Simone Marie Butler took to her Instagram Story to offer her condolences, adding: “1 year gone, always in our hearts.”

Ex-Happy Mondays singer Rowetta also paid tribute to Mani and mentioned the loss of Inspiral Carpets drummer Craig Gill, who also passed away on November 22 in 2016.

“A year without Mani. The saddest day. 10 years without Gilly. Forever Loved & Missed,” she wrote.

View this post on Instagram

Former presenter of The Word and friend Terry Christian took to Instagram to share a lengthy post with a picture of him with Mani taken at a documentary launch for former Manchester United midfielder Bryan Robson.

Christian shared that Mani “was taking the piss out of me for pursuing @waynerooney for a selfie.”

“After that i said – time we had a selfie – I even made him not do that weird pouty thing which he’d often do on photos . I’m glad I did it,” he added before concluding: “R.I.P Mani – deservedly loved in Manchester and by everyone who wver spoke to you. Authetic and real to the core,” he added.

View this post on Instagram

Many also marked Mani’s birthday, which was four days before his death, one year on with John Squire posting a video of a tree to the sound of The Stone Roses hit ‘Waterfall’. “Miss you brother,” he wrote.

View this post on Instagram

Primal Scream also paid honoured his birthday as did Simone Marie Butler who said: “You are incredibly missed dear bass brother.”

View this post on Instagram

View this post on Instagram

View this post on Instagram

Mani’s passing was documented in the recent Oasis film Don’t Look Back In Anger.

Directors Will Lovelace and Dylan Southern spoke to NMEabout the emotion running through the Oasis camp when they learned of his death ahead of their concert in Brazil.

“It wasn’t just them; it was the whole crew. The day it happened, you could feel the grief and shock amongst everyone,” Southern said.

“There was an energy in the crowd and in the stadium that night that made it pretty amazing to be there. You can see it in the film how much he meant to them. It always felt like it had to be part of the film,” Lovelace added.

issues.title: BST Hyde Park 2027: Billie Eilish announced as latest headliner
issues.summary: D'UH! After topping the bill at Glasto, Eilish will be playing another huge UK show – with new music expected by summer The post BST Hyde Park 2027: Billie Eilish announced as latest headliner appeared first on NME .
issues.author: Andrew Trendell
issues.content_html:
Billie Eilish has been announced as the latest headliner for London’s BST Hyde Park 2027. Check out full dates and ticket details below.

  • READ MORE: Billie Eilish live at Glastonbury 2022: headline set ushers in a new era for the festival

After being revealed earlier this week as one of next summer’s Glastonbury headliners alongside Harry Styles and Sam Fender, now it has emerged that she’ll be extending her stay in the UK to top the bill at the 70,000 capacity London festival when she tops the bill on Saturday July 3.

She joins previously announced headliners RAYE (now playing two nights due to phenomenal demand), Muse (who are also playing the sister Roundhay Festival in Leeds), and Bon Jovi.

Special guests and a full line-up will be revealed in the coming months, but tickets go on sale from 10am on Thursday November 26 and will be available here.

Fans are growing hopeful that 2027 will herald new music from the ‘Bad Guy’ alt-pop phenomenon, with her acclaimed third album ‘Hit Me Hard And Soft‘ arriving back in 2024, and a James Cameron-directed 3D film of the spectacular arena tour that followed, hitting cinemas back in Spring.

Speaking to NME around the movie’s release, Eilish confirmed that she and brother and collaborator FINNEAS were very much “working on new music”.

“It’s happening. It’ll be a second but we’re deep in album mode and it’s really fun,” she said. “It’s actually really fun. We’re having a really good time which maybe means it’ll be really shit because [it’s rare that I have] a good time [while making an album]… But we’re right in the middle of it and it’s feeling really good.”

Eilish also defended young fans who use mobile phones to film at gigs. “I just think that’s what it’s like,” she said. “My generation, and the generations below, we love to film stuff. All I do is film and take pictures of stuff – all of the time.”

She continued: “When I was young and would go to concerts or festivals, I would film every single minute of it – and then I would watch every single video that I took over and over until I even had the audio of the crowd memorised. I think that’s not to be pooh-poohed. An important part of the culture is that we are all on our goddamn phones! It keeps us connected. It does!”

Billie Eilish has also been confirmed to headline Roskilde 2027, with more tour dates expected to be announced in the weeks and months ahead.

issues.title: How Magic Lantern Ghosts Helped Measure the Stars
issues.summary: A nineteenth-century invention brought theatrical illusions into the observatory, changing how astronomers studied starlight. The post How Magic Lantern Ghosts Helped Measure the Stars appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: Danny Robb
issues.content_html:
In the nineteenth century, entertainers began dazzling audiences with the “magic lantern.” Operators used these projection systems to bring marvelous images to large crowds. They even performed tricks on the eye, conjuring “ghosts” onto the stage using reflections or transparent screens. But some at the time saw scientific possibilities in those ghostly images.

The rise of projection culture coincided with an increasing effort to mechanize astronomy. Astronomers had been precisely charting the positions of stars and other objects, and the next step was to study their color and brightness. German projectionist Karl Friedrich Zöllner realized that magic lanterns might help astronomers in this effort, explains historian Klaus Staubermann. He argues that Zöllner’s new scientific instrument, an astro-photometer, harnessed the subjective perception created by the magic lantern for scientific purposes.

To Zöllner, “The mind was the spectator, looking at the image and deciding what of that which was seen was illusory and what was real.”

The principles behind the “magic lantern” have a deep history, but improvements by Christiaan Huygens and others in the seventeenth century led to more widespread use. Staubermann describes how magic lanterns became popular lecture aids by the eighteenth century, as improvements to lighting and mirrors made them suitable for larger theaters. Projectionists learned new ways to control brightness and create visual effects using a variety of filters and lenses. Meanwhile, scientists were experimenting with optics, prisms, and mineralogy.

It was in this milieu that Zöllner became a projectionist and a student of photometry. He began studying illusions, trying to understand how we distinguish them from reality. He thought of the retina itself as a projection screen, Staubermann explains. To Zöllner, “The mind was the spectator,” he writes, “looking at the image and deciding what of that which was seen was illusory and what was real.”

More to Explore

The Hidden Aesthetics of Early Astrophotography

Danny Robb January 2, 2026 Behind the transformative star photographs of the 1880s lay a complex collaboration between astronomers and engravers.

It was the interplay between reality and illusion that enabled Zöllner’s photometer. The instrument employed techniques similar to those used to conjure ghosts on the stage to create artificial stars. A gas burner provided intense and steady light, which was projected as a point of light on a semi-transparent glass screen using lenses and prisms.

“For the observer with a Zöllner photometer,” Staubermann writes, “it appeared as if both stars were actually in the sky, having the same background.” The operator could control the brightness of the “ghost” star and compare it with a real one. Previously, astronomers’ perceptions of star brightness and color varied, sometimes significantly. But as they began experimenting with Zöllner’s photometer, they obtained results that agreed with each other.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

The instrument became a best seller in Europe and the United States. Astronomers added it to telescopes like the one at Leipzig Observatory. By the 1870s, Staubermann explains, “of the observatories participating in international observing programmes almost half of them had ordered a Zöllner photometer.” Papers on astro-photometry proliferated, and Zöllner himself became the first German professor of astrophysics.

Staubermann argues that the photometer didn’t quite make astro-photometry a “mechanically objective” science, however. Using it meant refining observation skills rather than eliminating the need for them. “Through the use of Zöllner’s photometer,” he writes, “observers learned how to both control and improve their visual judgement.”
