issues.title: The College Kids Who Drove a Duck Across the Americas
issues.summary: In 1961, nine young Americans set out to promote international friendship. Their adventures survive in a remarkable collection of letters. The post The College Kids Who Drove a Duck Across the Americas appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: April White
issues.content_html:
The DUKW was designed for war. The gray metal vehicle had six wheels, a rudder, and a propeller, an unlikely cross between a Jimmy deuce-and-a-half—as the standard GMC military truck was known—and a bulky metal scow. Between 1942 and 1945, more than 21,000 DUKWs came off the assembly lines in Michigan and Missouri. Called “ducks” by just about everyone, these land-water hybrids would carry troops and supplies to the beaches of Sicily and Normandy and countless other battle sites through World War II. Later they delivered the same cargo to the shores of Incheon, changing the tide of the Korean War.

And then in the summer of 1961, an aging DUKW from an Akron scrapyard became an unlikely symbol of peace in the midst of the Cold War.

“What I learn from this trip will make me appreciate life (especially with you) more.”

It was an adventure only a couple of college kids could dream up—a yearlong road trip across the Americas in a vehicle that had broken down five times on the drive from Ohio back home to New York. But “adventure was only part—a small part—of this trip,” Dan Twomey, one of nine men who participated in what they called Operation Americas, told a local newspaper. (The contingent also included his twin brother, Tom.)

For Twomey, who documented the odyssey in letters to his girlfriend Rosemarie Feuerbach, now shared by Drew University via JSTOR, the purpose was much bigger. The adventure was both a goodwill mission and a personal quest.

To the newspapers, Twomey explained that the goal was “friendship and understanding”—“meeting ordinary people, listening to their ideas and perhaps putting across the true American story was and is the sole purpose of this whole thing.”

“I think the fuller a person you are the more you can enjoy life.” Click on the letter to take a closer look. “I think the fuller a person you are the more you can enjoy life.” Click on the letter to take a closer look.

But to Feuerbach, Twomey confessed from Panama during a particularly challenging stretch of the trip that the “noble” reasons “really don’t mean as much.” “What I learn from this trip will make me appreciate life (especially with you) more,” he wrote. “I think the fuller a person you are the more you can enjoy life.”

Their journey kicked off in August 1961 with a media tour, including an interview on Today. Over the next several months, the men and their DUKW—which was christened El Pato Valiente (“The Valiant Duck”) and painted with a cheerful Donald Duck in a mortarboard—would cross the United States, zigzag through Mexico, and ping-pong around Central America before finding themselves seemingly stuck in Panama.

Along the way, the men spent much of their time visiting college campuses, where they played guitar, performed silly skits, and challenged students on the basketball court. But Twomey credited most of the trip’s successes—and most of its troubles—to the DUKW itself.

“One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look. “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look. “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look. “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look.

Everywhere they went, the odd vehicle attracted curiosity. In Mexico City, the sight of a boat with wheels caused a traffic collision: “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!” In Juchitán, Mexico, it attracted a mob. As the men navigated the DUKW through the rough, narrow back streets of the community’s poor neighborhoods, “we had a crowd of about 50 people following us,” Twomey wrote to Feuerbach. When they stopped at a basketball court for an impromptu game, “In about 10 minutes there was a crowd of two to three hundred watching. Many of the people cheered for us.” (The DUKW crew lost 38–34.) By the time they reached Guatemala in mid-October 1961, Twomey reported that “people, crowds, unusual happenings are so commonplace, I feel like I’m repeating myself.”

“We had a crowd of about 50 people following us.” Click on the letter to take a closer look. “We had a crowd of about 50 people following us.” Click on the letter to take a closer look.

Maintenance on the DUKW was also unfortunately commonplace. In the first two weeks of the trip alone, there was a brake issue in New Jersey, a flat tire in Indiana, and a busted fan belt in St. Louis. But the real trouble came just before Christmas, one hundred miles from Panama City, when a busted motor required the US Army to step in, towing the immobile vehicle to the Canal Zone.

The men, the machine, and their mascot, a German shepherd named Robin who had joined the crew in Texas, would stay much longer than they intended in Panama. They needed to raise more money, first to fix El Pato Valiente and then for boat passage to South America, bypassing the impenetrable Darién Gap. In theory their duck could swim, but they’d been warned the waters would be too rough. Eventually, though, the men became impatient and decided to set off across the Caribbean to the northern coast of Colombia.

Their planned five-day voyage was doomed almost from the beginning. “For the first few hours everything went o.k.,” Twomey wrote. “Then the rudder cable broke.” The men had to steer by hand as waves washed over the DUKW, swamping the new motor and washing the survival gear overboard. Everyone was seasick, even Robin. They continued to limp along for a couple of days. “Then it happened,” Twomey wrote.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

“A loud noise told us something had gone wrong (broken) with our propeller,” he wrote. They beached the DUKW on an island off the coast of Panama, where it would stay for a week—delaying the men still further, but attracting ever more publicity to their travels. It even caught the attention of President Kennedy, who assured one frantic parent that the US government would help her stranded son, despite the administration’s previous misgivings about the trip. With help, the men eventually made their way to Colombia, spending another five months touring South America before returning to the United States.

More than 50 years later, Matt Twomey told the story of this more-than-an-adventure in a documentary titled Duck Diaries: A Cold War Quest for Friendship Across the Americas. In interviews and images, the film brings to life the amazing stories in the Drew University archives. And it provides a lovely coda to the tale: the filmmaker is the son of Dan Twomey and Rosemarie Feuerbach, who married a year after Dan’s return. When Dan Twomey passed away in 2024, his obituary noted that his time on the DUKW and the couple’s correspondence through Operation Americas had, as Twomey had hoped in 1962, “set the tone for a life full of adventures and global interest and inquiry.”

issues.title: The Stories That Make Thanksgiving
issues.summary: Turkey or Tofurkey? Stuffing or dressing? Whatever’s on your table, these Thanksgiving stories will satisfy your curiosity. The post The Stories That Make Thanksgiving appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: The Editors
issues.content_html:
Americans are getting ready to celebrate Thanksgiving, the middle entry in the Halloween-Thanksgiving-Winter holidays trifecta. Plate up with some table talk about the origins of the holiday, the reason we eat turkey, and what really makes people so sleepy after the annual meal. Extra fixings: all stories contain free links to the supporting academic research on JSTOR. Happy Thanksgiving!

How Thanksgiving took shape

Quakers Against Thanksgiving

Livia Gershon November 24, 2025 In colonial America, government “thanksgivings” blurred faith and politics. For Quakers, rejecting them was an act of religious conviction.

Why the Pilgrims Were Actually Able to Survive

Peter C. Mancall November 28, 2019 If you were reading Bradford's version of events, you might think that the survival of the Pilgrims' settlements was often in danger.

Thanksgiving Has Been Reinvented Many Times

Matthew Wills November 1, 2019 From colonial times to the nineteenth century, Thanksgiving was very different from the holiday we know now.

The Modern Invention of Thanksgiving

Livia Gershon November 26, 2014 Thanksgiving as we know it was deliberately invented in the nineteenth century.

Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade: A History in Pictures

The Editors November 12, 2021 In 1927, the parade replaced live animals with helium balloons designed by puppeteer Tony Sarg.

Indigenous histories and living traditions

Translating Corn

Matthew Wills November 22, 2023 To most of the world, “corn” is “maize,” a word that comes from the Taíno mahizwas. Not for British colonists in North America, though.

Returning Corn, Beans, and Squash to Native American Farms

Christina Gish Hill November 24, 2020 Returning the “three sisters” to Native American farms nourishes people, land, and cultures.

How (Not) to Teach Kids about Native Cultures

Livia Gershon November 23, 2020 Even well-intentioned books for children can romanticize (or demonize) Native Americans. But better materials exist.

From turkey to tofu

Let’s Talk Turkey

Matthew Wills November 26, 2014 First of all, why the name "turkey?"

The Great American Turkey

Livia Gershon November 27, 2024 The turkey was semi-domesticated and kept in pens in the American Southwest some 2,000 years ago—but not for the reason you think.

Seven Things You Might Not Know About Cranberries

Matthew Wills November 21, 2018 They're red, tart, and mostly eaten at Thanksgiving. Love them or hate them, here are seven things you might not have known about the humble cranberry.

Vegetarian Thanksgiving Dates Back to the 1900s

Lina Zeldovich November 25, 2019 Tofu Turkey was created in 1990, but some Americans celebrated Thanksgiving with veggie dishes over a century ago.

The Real Joy of Mock Food

Livia Gershon November 8, 2019 "Wow, this really kind of tastes like turkey.”

Beyond the meal

Thanksgiving Is a Feast of Things Forgotten

Sarah McColl November 22, 2016 Thanksgiving is a feast so complex and semiotically dense that things are very often forgotten and rarely go according to plan.

What Does Thanksgiving Look Like in Prison?

Morgan Godvin November 23, 2021 Our American Prison Newspapers collection provides a peek at Thanksgiving celebrations in prisons throughout the decades.

Why Does Eating Food Make You Sleepy?

James MacDonald November 25, 2015 Your turkey is not to blame.

Synesthetic Adjectives Will Make You Eat Your Words

Chi Luu November 23, 2016 Fragrant. Sweet. Tangy. Certain synesthetic adjectives actually trigger cognitive simulations of eating.

It’s Time to Reinvent Food Waste!

Lori Miller Kase November 13, 2018 Startups worldwide convert refuse into energy, biomaterials, and more food.

A moment of gratitude

Eight Poems of Gratitude

The Editors November 23, 2020 Let us pause now and give thanks.

issues.title: How should war criminals be punished? We asked a historian for their view
issues.summary: How should we prosecute those who perpetrate war crimes? This is a challenge that the global community has confronted since the end of the First World War – with, as historian Devin Pendas tells Danny Bird, mixed results
issues.content_html:
Danny Bird: In September, Hashim Thaçi, former president of Kosovo, was convicted of war crimes committed in the Kosovo War, following a trial in The Hague. What does the case reveal about how trials of this nature have evolved over the past century?

Devin Pendas: Two things stand out. First, the principle that heads of state can be prosecuted for acts of state is now firmly established. Sovereignty traditionally meant acts of state were not crimes, even when Kaiser Wilhelm II’s trial was mooted after the First World War. Later, Nuremberg shifted that in theory, but Hitler was dead, so the principle was never established. In the 1990s, prosecutors pursuing crimes during Yugoslavia’s breakup pushed hard for it. Slobodan Milošević’s unfinished trial was the first real attempt, and Hashim Thaçi’s conviction confirms the precedent.

The second point to make is that this principle is applied unevenly. Weak powers, small countries and deposed leaders are far likelier to be prosecuted than sitting heads of state, or leaders, current or former, of great powers.

What are these courts actually prosecuting, and what separates war crimes from crimes against humanity?

International criminal law has four core crimes: war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and aggression. The first three are atrocity crimes, involving the mistreatment of civilians and non-combatants.

War crimes can be sporadic: a lieutenant who loses control and orders his men to massacre a village has committed one. Crimes against humanity must be, in the legal term, widespread or systematic, which implies deliberate policy: orders from commanders, most probably from generals or civilian leaders, rather than rogue action.

Genocide is a crime against humanity with an added ‘special intent’. Victims are targeted because they belong to a protected racial, religious, ethnic or national group (not a political one), with the intent to destroy that group in whole or in part. It turns on the perpetrators’ state of mind, which the others don’t require.

  • Read more | “I hope I would have defended the Nazis at Nuremberg”

Did prosecuting wartime atrocities begin at Nuremberg?

No. The history of war crimes prosecutions is longer and crimes against humanity were raised after the First World War, notably over the Armenian genocide [the systematic killing of up to 1.2 million people in the Ottoman empire between 1915 and 1916]. Almost all earlier trials were conducted in national courts. Nothing developed in terms of international prosecutions, or in terms of codifying crimes against humanity, until Nuremberg made them a legal category through the London Charter of 1945, the treaty that authorised the trials.

War crimes, by contrast, belong to customary law dating to the Middle Ages, with codification beginning in the 19th century and prosecutions after the American Civil War.

When did genocide become a crime in its own right?

The term was coined by Raphael Lemkin, a Polish Jewish lawyer who fled the Nazis, in a wartime book on Axis occupation policy in eastern Europe. Lemkin argued that genocide is distinct because it destroys communities, and their members, targeting something fundamental to their identity that they cannot change.

He lobbied relentlessly, visiting every politician who would see him. He wanted genocide to be prosecuted at Nuremberg, but negotiators chose crimes against humanity as a broader category. He did get it onto the new United Nations’ agenda – and its Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide was passed, making genocide prosecutable later.

How did nation-states come to accept that some crimes transcend borders?

It has been one of the biggest fights of the last 80 years. Sovereignty, the principle that states answer for their own territory, dates back at least to the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. It arose because Europe’s Wars of Religion were fuelled by Protestant and Catholic states fighting to protect co-religionists abroad, a spiral lasting around a century. It asserted that, in principle, what a state does to its citizens is nobody else’s business – though, in practice, interventions often continued.

However, the world wars in the 20th century convinced many that some crimes are so evil, and so prone to spill across borders, that they cannot be left to the caprice of individual states. They concern the international community and warrant international prosecution, at least case by case.

Suspicion persisted and still does. At Nuremberg, the Americans and Soviets agreed on little except that the precedent must not touch their domestic conduct – notably Stalin’s mass killings, and lynchings in the Jim Crow South. Their solution was to tie international jurisdiction to aggression. The real crime was invading Poland; massacring 3 million Polish Jews became an international matter because Germany invaded first.

Your own research examines the postwar Nazi trials, notably the Frankfurt Auschwitz trials of 1963–68. What do they reveal about justice, historical understanding and public memory?

Advocates of prosecuting political atrocities typically make two arguments. The first is deterrence and the second is pedagogy. On that second point, Nuremberg’s prosecutors said they were teaching the world, especially Germans, about their government’s past evil to help forge democracy and a culture of human rights.

The record is more complicated because trials draw publicity, and some react with shock and resolve while others reject them outright. Critics denounced Nuremberg as victors’ justice, even a high-grade lynching party, and Serbs said much the same of the Yugoslavia tribunal.

At the Frankfurt trials in the 1960s, many Germans concluded that the accused were singular psychopaths, unrepresentative of German society and nothing to do with them or their parents. They accepted that the perpetrators deserved punishment, but took it to mean everyone else, including those who voted for Hitler, was innocent. Trials can become an alibi: “We prosecuted 20 people. What more do you want from me?”

How did the Yugoslavia and Rwanda tribunals build on Nuremberg?

After Nuremberg, plans for a permanent international criminal court collapsed amid Cold War resistance and fears of neocolonialism. Then things began to change. The end of the Cold War coincided with the Yugoslav wars, followed by genocide in Rwanda. Opposition had weakened as post-Soviet Russia was courting the west. That opened a window to revive the Nuremberg model through tribunals. These were one-off bodies, usually created by the UN, each handling a single set of crimes.

They changed three things. First, genocide was now chargeable. Second, they prosecuted heads of state. Rwanda’s was dead, but Serbia’s Milošević was tried, and although he died in prison before a verdict, it was the first prosecution of a former head of state. After the Second World War, Hitler was dead and the Japanese emperor untried, so the question stayed open until these tribunals resolved it.

Third, they changed how eyewitnesses are treated. Testifying is traumatic. For example, you may be asked to describe how your parents were murdered when you were 12, then face cross-examination – “Were you wearing your glasses? Are you sure it was your parents?” – or worse, be accused of seeking revenge and money. At Nuremberg and Frankfurt, witnesses were left alone. Many suffered breakdowns. The new tribunals institutionalised support-staff psychologists, training for attorneys to ask hard questions without insulting witnesses – and therapy afterwards. This made testimony far more bearable.

  • Read more | Before the Nuremberg Trials, this was Winston Churchill’s shocking plan for Nazi war criminals

What can trials offer the victims?

Victim witnesses, from Nuremberg to the International Criminal Court (ICC), have mixed views. I have never met one who called it a waste of time, as they want justice and the truth told. But they are often frustrated, because defendants have rights to a defence, cross-examination and denial. Watching the man who murdered your parents say “I don’t know what this guy’s talking about” is infuriating.

Punishments often seem inadequate. International tribunals have no death penalty – nor do German courts – though Adolf Eichmann’s trial in Israel was a notable exception. Accomplices to murder in Germany often get three to seven years. A survivor may see the killer sentenced to five years, but only serving two and a half after being released early with heart trouble.

And a fair trial lets the defence tell its story: it didn’t happen, wasn’t my responsibility, wasn’t so bad, your side did it, too, etcetera. That must be allowed to happen. But for survivors, it can be traumatising, frustrating and politically damaging.

What happens after the verdict? Can trials aid reconciliation, or might they deepen divisions?

Whether reconciliation should even be a goal is controversial. Desmond Tutu championed it in South Africa, where a Truth and Reconciliation Commission offered perpetrators immunity in exchange for testimony. The idea of truth instead of justice was something many survivors found insulting.

Even where perpetrators serve time, there is an expectation that, for instance, Croats, Serbs and Bosnians will live as neighbours again. That is a great deal to ask of someone whose torturer or family’s killer is to be forgiven in the cause of ‘political stability’, as if it were just a playground scuffle.

Perpetrator communities respond in kind: “Why blame us?” Germans in the 1950s and 1960s pointed to the Allies’ firebombing of Dresden, the expulsions from eastern Europe and the mass rapes. Both sides can emerge more frustrated than satisfied, which breeds tension, visible in South Africa today. In Serbia, polling suggests most reject any primary responsibility for the wars. The trials haven’t eased that – and may have hardened it. As history lessons, they are a mixed bag at best, often counterproductive.

What do you think truth commissions or public inquiries can achieve that courtrooms cannot?

Again, the record is mixed, with South Africa being the notable case. But South America has had commissions, too, with or without trials. Both commissions and trials do well at establishing forensic truth, gathering documents and testimony in one place and publishing findings – work that would take historians decades. They have resources a lone historian lacks. They also attract public attention, prompting people to say: “I genuinely didn’t know.”

Yet there is no perfect response. Atrocity crimes hurt thousands, even millions, and are committed by institutions that may remain in power, so every solution has serious limits.

What I come back to is that sometimes you act because it is right, not because it solves a problem. You prosecute atrocities because they are evil, and prosecution is the proper response. Whether it brings stability, reconciliation or the ‘proper’ historical lessons doesn’t matter. These are bad people who did bad things, and they belong in jail.

  • Read more | The Srebrenica massacre: the worst atrocity committed on European soil since the Second World War

What can these earlier trials tell us about the possibilities and limits of justice in the century ahead?

International justice has always been contentious as everyone wants enemies prosecuted, friends spared and themselves exempt. So, rejecting international tribunals isn’t new. But we are at an inflection point, because some major powers increasingly won’t even pay lip service to the principles of international justice.

Take the United States in Vietnam where the air war, plus massacres on the ground, were hugely controversial. The My Lai prosecutions [following the massacre of hundreds of Vietnamese civilians by US Army soldiers in March 1968] were half-baked, with acquittals and pardons. But some Americans at least had the decency to be embarrassed.

About a year ago, an adviser to President Trump gave an interview saying: “We live in a world, in the real world, that is governed by strength, that is governed by force, that is governed by power. These are the iron laws of the world since the beginning of time.” This reminds me of Thucydides’ observation that the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. However Thucydides meant his words as a warning, not a model.

Those who reject the very possibility of justice have failed to learn that lesson. They are immoral and unwise.

Devin Pendas is professor of history at Boston College. He is the author of The Frankfurt Auschwitz Trial, 1963–1965: Genocide, History, and the Limits of the Law (Cambridge, 2006)

This article was first published in the December 2026 issue of HistoryExtra Magazine

issues.title: Prolonged mask exposure changes how we process facial emotions
issues.summary: A longitudinal study reveals that people adapt to reading emotions on mask-covered faces over time. The findings show improvements in identifying occluded expressions of fear and happiness, highlighting the adaptability of human social cognition.
issues.author: Karina Petrova
issues.content_html:
Humans rely heavily on facial expressions to navigate social interactions, a process that became notably more difficult when face masks became a global norm. Recent research published in Cognition and Emotion reveals that people adapt and improve their ability to read masked emotions over a period of several months. The findings suggest that our visual processing adjusts to occluded faces, and these changes relate to both daily exposure and individual mental health symptoms.

Reading emotions from the faces of others dictates how people respond in social situations. Seeing fear might prompt someone to look for a threat, while a smiling face reinforces positive behaviors. Because human beings rely heavily on the lower half of the face to decode many of these emotional states, facial coverings create a substantial barrier to everyday communication.

Initial studies during the pandemic revealed that face masks led to lower accuracy and slower reaction times when identifying emotions. It was not well understood whether prolonged exposure to masked faces would eventually lead to improved recognition skills. Past research yielded mixed results, with some data indicating no improvement in adults over time and other data suggesting young children might adapt.

In addition to visual barriers, an individual’s mental state can alter how they perceive emotions in others. Some research indicates that people experiencing depression might be better at recognizing sadness, while those with anxiety might be highly sensitive to fearful faces. Researchers wanted to know how these mood symptoms might interact with the specific challenge of reading masked faces.

The research team was led by Marie Huc and Katie Bush, both affiliated with the University of Ottawa and Carleton University. They worked alongside senior author Natalia Jaworska of the University of Ottawa Institute of Mental Health Research. Together, they designed an experiment to track whether the ability to recognize masked emotions changes over several months, and how mental well-being factors into that process.

The investigators tracked 128 Canadian adults who participated in two testing sessions spaced three to four months apart. During each session, participants completed a series of questionnaires to assess their feelings of loneliness, perceived stress, depression, and anxiety. At the second session, they also reported how many hours a day they spent wearing a mask and how much time they spent interacting with other people wearing masks.

Following the questionnaires, participants completed a computerized emotional processing task. They were shown photographs of actors displaying five distinct facial expressions, which included happiness, sadness, fear, surprise, and a neutral state. Half of the images featured the faces fully visible, while the other half had a realistic surgical mask digitally overlaid onto the lower half of the face.

Participants were instructed to identify the emotion as quickly and accurately as possible by pressing corresponding keys on their keyboards. The research team recorded both the accuracy of the responses and the exact amount of time it took for the participants to make their choice. By comparing the results from the first session to the second session, the team could evaluate changes in recognition skills over time.

The results indicated that time and practice changed how participants processed the masked faces. Over the three to four month period, accuracy improved for identifying masked fear, happiness, and sadness. Conversely, participants became slightly less accurate at identifying masked surprise.

Reaction times also shifted depending on the emotion being displayed. Participants became faster at identifying masked fear over time, but their reaction times slowed down when attempting to identify masked surprise. Recognizing a surprised expression relies heavily on the mouth region, making it particularly difficult to decode when the lower half of the face is covered.

The researchers pointed out that becoming faster and more accurate at identifying fear could serve an adaptive purpose. Recognizing threat-related cues rapidly is highly beneficial in a stressful environment. Because the testing occurred during a global health crisis, heightened vigilance toward fearful expressions may have been a natural psychological response to prolonged uncertainty.

When looking at the unmasked faces, the researchers did not see the same broad changes in accuracy or reaction time between the two testing sessions. This lack of change in the unmasked condition suggests that the improvements seen with masked faces were not simply a result of participants practicing the computer task. Instead, it indicates a specific adaptation to processing partially covered faces.

The amount of time participants spent interacting with masked individuals in their daily lives also played a role. Greater daily exposure to masked faces was associated with slower reaction times when identifying masked happiness and sadness. The researchers suggest that people who interact more often with masked individuals might develop a habit of searching for more subtle visual cues. Looking for changes around the eyes takes slightly longer to process but helps maintain high accuracy.

Mental health symptoms were also linked to how participants performed. Individuals who reported increased symptoms of depression over the study period demonstrated greater accuracy when identifying masked happy faces. Those with increased anxiety symptoms showed better accuracy for masked happy and neutral faces.

General levels of perceived stress, depression, anxiety, and loneliness decreased across the group over the three to four months. These broad mental health improvements did not directly correlate with changes in facial recognition performance. The researchers note that their sample mostly consisted of community members without formal psychiatric diagnoses, which may explain the low overall symptom scores.

The study took place during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, a period characterized by unique global stressors that may have influenced overall mental health trends. Because mask mandates were universally in place for the sampled population during testing, the researchers could not include a control group with zero mask exposure. This limits the ability to isolate the exact impact of daily mask exposure compared to general time passing.

The experimental setup relied on static photographs of facial expressions rather than dynamic videos or real-world interactions. In natural settings, people rely on head movements, vocal tone, and body language to interpret emotions, which were not available in this computer task. Future research could incorporate video clips to better capture the realities of face-to-face communication.

Finally, because the study is correlational, it cannot prove that daily mask exposure or mental health symptoms directly cause changes in visual processing skills. The results only show that these factors change in tandem. Additional studies using different methodologies would be required to establish direct cause and effect.

The study, “Changes in facial expression recognition and well-being over time,” was authored by Marie Huc, Katie Bush, Lindsay Berrigan, Sylvia Cox, and Natalia Jaworska.

issues.title: Mild sleep loss can dull how much people enjoy art and perceive beauty
issues.summary: We know poor sleep harms focus and health, but a new laboratory study suggests losing rest also saps positive emotions and quietly flattens our ability to enjoy visual art and beauty.
issues.author: Eric W. Dolan
issues.content_html:
Getting a couple of hours less sleep than usual for just two nights may subtly dull how much people enjoy artwork and perceive its beauty, according to new experimental research published in Journal of Sleep Research. In a controlled sleep-laboratory study of young adults, mild sleep restriction dampened morning alertness and positive mood while lowering ratings of abstract paintings, though it did not alter judgments based on the perceived race or gender of the artist. The findings suggest that adequate rest does more than prevent fatigue and mistakes, playing a quiet role in how people appreciate everyday aesthetic experiences.

Aesthetics refers to how people perceive and respond emotionally to beauty, art, and design in the world around them. Those responses depend partly on visual features of an object, such as symmetry or color, and partly on what the viewer brings to the moment, including cultural background, personality, and mood. Psychologists studying art appreciation frequently use abstract paintings, which rely on shapes, colors, and textures rather than recognizable everyday scenes, leaving their meaning open to personal interpretation and creating wide variation from one viewer to the next.

Health guidelines generally recommend at least seven hours of sleep per night for adults, and falling short is well known to impair attention, memory, academic performance, and job satisfaction. Losing sleep also alters emotional life, though not always in the way people assume. Rather than uniformly fueling anger or distress, a 2023 meta-analysis of 154 experimental studies found that sleep loss consistently drains positive feelings and blunts emotional engagement, whereas its effects on negative emotions are mixed and depend on how sleep is disrupted.

Since positive emotions help draw people into artistic and creative experiences, shortened sleep could make visual art feel flatter and less rewarding. Prior work directly testing sleep and art appreciation has been scarce, though a 2019 study of aesthetic perception found that when people slept poorly, their empathy had less bearing on how they judged the proportions of sculptures.

At the same time, some psychologists have proposed that sleep loss depletes the mental self-control people rely on to keep social stereotypes in check, raising the question of whether tired viewers might judge artwork differently depending on who supposedly painted it. Research on sleep and bias has examined both automatic associations and deliberate evaluations. In the domain of automatic attitudes, a 2017 laboratory study of healthy adults found that chronic sleep restriction increased unconscious negative associations with Arab-Muslim names on a rapid categorization test, whereas fully rested participants showed no such bias.

To examine how sleep shapes deliberate art appreciation and potential bias, co-first authors Ariadne D. Godinho of Baylor University and Chenlu Gao of Harvard Medical School and Mass General Brigham collaborated with Michelle R. Hebl of Rice University and senior author Michael K. Scullin, a professor of psychology and neuroscience at Baylor University who directs the Sleep Neuroscience and Cognition Lab.

“Sleep loss is known to cause performance errors and increase disease risk,” Scullin told PsyPost. “Less is known, however, about whether being well-rested benefits ‘the good things’ in life, such as our ability to enjoy artwork and experience beauty.”

The artwork experiment was part of a broader multi-week laboratory project at Baylor University examining how restricted sleep affects learning and creativity in college students. Sleep-monitoring records from the same project were also analyzed in an earlier sleep-staging study by Scullin and colleagues. Seventy-five students completed the broader protocol, and 68 healthy young adults, ranging in age from 18 to 22, finished every phase required for the artwork study. Slightly more than half of the final sample were women, and roughly 56 percent identified as non-White, including multiracial, Asian or Pacific Islander, African American, Hispanic, and other racial or ethnic backgrounds.

Eligibility was open to right-handed native English speakers aged 18 to 29 who normally needed at least seven hours of sleep a night, had no sleep disorders, and did not have extreme morning-lark or night-owl schedules. Researchers also screened out night-shift workers, frequent nappers, and people who consumed more than 300 milligrams of caffeine daily or drank caffeine regularly after 5:00 p.m. The team made the study’s data and task materials publicly available online, though the study was not preregistered.

The researchers used a counterbalanced crossover design, meaning every participant completed both a well-rested phase and a mildly sleep-restricted phase in the laboratory in a randomized order, allowing each person to serve as their own comparison. Participants began with an initial adaptation night in the lab monitored by polysomnography, an overnight recording technique that uses sensors on the scalp, face, and body to track brain waves, eye movements, muscle tension, and breathing. They then spent about a week sleeping at home while keeping a sleep log and wearing a wrist actigraph, a watch-like motion sensor that tracks daily sleep and wake patterns.

Participants returned to the sleep laboratory for two three-night stays separated by a wrist-monitored recovery break at home that averaged 5.4 nights, though individual gaps ranged from 3 to 46 nights. During the well-rested stay, lights were out for nine hours each night from 10:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m.; during the sleep-restriction stay, time in bed was trimmed to 5.5 hours per night from 1:30 a.m. to 7:00 a.m. Outside of scheduled lab testing, students could attend classes and go about normal daytime routines, though napping was prohibited and verified with the wrist monitors.

The artwork evaluation took place after the second night of each laboratory stay. Upon waking at 7:00 a.m., participants rated their current positive and negative emotions on separate 10-to-50 scales and rated their sleepiness on a 1-to-9 scale, then took 30 minutes to shower and get dressed so that sleep inertia, the grogginess that lingers right after waking, could wear off. At 7:30 a.m., they viewed 12 paintings on a computer, drawn from a pool of 24 abstract paintings split into two counterbalanced sets of 12 so no image was ever repeated across sessions.

Participants were told the paintings came from a mix of nationally exhibited professional artists and local amateurs. Each painting appeared for 15 seconds alongside a fictitious year and a fictitious artist name chosen from prior discrimination research to suggest a White or African American man or woman, such as Anna Taylor or DeShawn Williams.

After briefly describing what they believed the artist meant to convey, participants rated each piece from 1 to 7 on overall liking, beauty, colorfulness, creativity, and artistic skill. They also guessed whether the work came from an amateur or professional display venue and estimated what an art curator would need to bid in U.S. dollars to acquire it.

Overnight brain-wave recordings confirmed that the schedules worked as intended: on the night before the art task, participants slept an average of 8.04 hours when well-rested versus 5.19 hours when restricted. Reflecting built-up sleep pressure during the restricted stay, participants fell asleep faster, spent less time awake during the night, and showed higher sleep efficiency, spending 94.7 percent of their time in bed asleep compared with 90.4 percent when well-rested. Even with that consolidated sleep, two nights of restriction left participants noticeably sleepier at 7:00 a.m. and lower in positive emotions, whereas negative emotions did not differ at a statistically significant level.

This emotional pattern aligns with an earlier study of emotional reactions to film clips, which examined everyday subjective sleepiness rather than experimentally restricted sleep and aesthetic judgments of visual art. That study similarly found that sleepier viewers experienced weaker positive feelings, particularly during bittersweet scenes, while their negative emotional responses remained unchanged.

In the main analyses of the five rating scales and perceived display venues, mild sleep restriction lowered participants’ aesthetic appreciation of the abstract paintings. On the 1-to-7 scale, participants liked the artwork less when sleep-restricted, giving an average rating of 4.33 compared with 4.53 when they were well-rested. They also rated the paintings as less beautiful after restricted sleep, averaging 4.33 compared with 4.51 when well-rested, shifts of roughly a fifth of a point, or about 4 percent.

Sleep loss did not alter every judgment about the paintings, however. Differences between the well-rested and sleep-restricted sessions were not statistically significant for perceived colorfulness, creativity, the skill needed to create the work, or whether participants guessed a painting came from an amateur outlet like a local coffee shop or a professional museum. The order in which participants completed the sleep phases also had no statistically significant effect, and exploratory checks linking art ratings to time spent in specific sleep stages, such as rapid eye movement sleep, did not remain statistically significant once extreme data points were removed.

Asked what the average person should take from the findings, Scullin said, “When we’re well-rested, we experience more alertness, greater happiness, and apparently, a touch more beauty.”

“We observed a subtle effect—a 5% change in artwork ratings—small enough that most people are likely unaware that their sleep patterns influence their aesthetic experiences,” he explained. “Yet, a 5% change might accumulate across thousands of everyday interactions with scenery, artwork, architecture, music, people, and other experiences. When ‘5%’ is placed within this larger context, it seems possible that sleep loss could subtly change our quality of life without us ever realizing why.”

To explore how sleep loss connected to lower art evaluations, the researchers ran statistical mediation analyses on the 66 participants with complete questionnaire data, testing morning sleepiness, positive mood, and negative mood in separate models. For overall liking, greater alertness and higher positive mood when well-rested each independently formed an indirect statistical link between the sleep schedule and painting ratings in their respective models. Once either variable was factored in, the direct relationship between sleep condition and liking was no longer statistically significant, a pattern researchers call full mediation. Negative mood, by contrast, did not form a statistically significant link.

For beauty ratings, a different pattern emerged across the separate models. Subjective alertness and sleepiness again formed an indirect statistical pathway, with the direct effect of sleep condition on beauty ratings no longer statistically significant once sleepiness was included, whereas neither positive mood nor negative mood was a statistically significant mediator.

“It was surprising that people’s positive emotions and negative emotions did not mediate the effect of sleep restriction on beauty ratings,” Scullin noted.

In the authors’ reading, that split suggests that perceiving beauty may be tied less to a viewer’s specific mood and more to overall brain alertness and visual sensitivity to subtle artistic details. Even so, the researchers caution right alongside this analysis that morning sleepiness and mood were both measured via self-report just before the task and may overlap with one another, meaning the statistical models cannot pinpoint a strict cause-and-effect chain among alertness, emotion, and art perception.

Contrary to the team’s secondary hypothesis, ratings of the paintings did not vary at a statistically significant level based on whether the listed artist’s name suggested a White or African American man or woman. That absence of bias held both when participants were well-rested and when they were sleep-restricted, and follow-up Bayesian analyses, which weigh how strongly the evidence favors the absence of an effect, supported the conclusion that artist names did not sway evaluations. The authors suggest this outcome aligns with prior studies indicating that mild sleep loss does not consistently trigger overt, conscious discrimination, even if some tests have linked short sleep to subtler unconscious associations.

There are a few caveats to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The experiment took place in a tightly controlled laboratory setting with healthy college students aged 18 to 22 who viewed a single style of visual art on a computer screen early in the morning after two nights of mild sleep loss. Responses could differ among older adults, people facing months or years of insufficient sleep, or visitors encountering sculptures, music, and realistic paintings in everyday settings like museums. In addition, the researchers ran separate statistical tests across multiple rating scales without applying formal mathematical adjustments for multiple comparisons in order to preserve sensitivity to subtle effects, making independent replication important.

The absence of gender or racial bias in the ratings also comes with an important qualification. Artist identity was signaled solely through a printed fictitious name, and the researchers did not include a follow-up check to confirm that participants noticed the names or associated them with a specific race and gender as intended. Future studies could test whether more direct cues, such as artist photographs or short biographies in real gallery spaces, produce similar results.

Looking ahead, Scullin, who has also shared research on building healthier sleep habits in a TEDx talk, hopes to move beyond laboratory sleep restriction to test how improving rest shapes everyday well-being.

“We’re interested in how improving sleep quality can help people flourish across all their life domains,” Scullin added. “Experiencing happiness and beauty in life is one sign of flourishing, as is succeeding at work/school and having enriching social relationships. Correlational work suggests that good sleep health coincides with life satisfaction, and we’re interested in whether intervening to address insufficient sleep will make people’s lives better.”

The study, “Experimental Sleep Restriction Blunts Positive Emotions and Aesthetic Experiences When Viewing Artwork,” was authored by Ariadne D. Godinho, Chenlu Gao, Michelle R. Hebl, and Michael K. Scullin.

issues.title: The earlier kids join social media, the lower their test scores tend to be, study finds
issues.summary: When should kids get social media? A study tracking more than 5,000 Italian students’ test scores from 2nd to 10th grade found that those who joined earlier tended to fall further behind in Italian and math.
issues.author: Vladimir Hedrih
issues.content_html:
A study of high school students in Lombardy, a region in northern Italy, found that students who created a personal social media account in 6th, 7th, or 8th grade tended to score lower on standardized tests of Italian and mathematics than peers who waited until 9th grade or later. The earlier students opened an account, the larger the gap tended to be. The paper was published in Nature Human Behaviour.

The age at which children should be allowed to start using smartphones and social media has become a subject of intense debate among scientists, educators, and parents. Children are increasingly acquiring their first smartphones at around 10 or 11 years of age, often creating social media accounts before reaching the minimum age required by platforms or national regulations. This trend has raised concerns because increasing digital media use among young people has coincided with declining indicators of mental health and academic performance in many countries.

Research suggests that intensive social media use is associated with poorer sleep, reduced concentration, fewer face-to-face interactions, and lower life satisfaction. However, scientists disagree about whether social media use directly causes these problems, as findings have been inconsistent and many studies cannot establish cause-and-effect relationships.

Studies examining academic performance have generally found small negative associations between social media use and learning outcomes, although much of this research has focused on university students. Another important limitation is that researchers have typically examined how much time young people spend on social media rather than the age at which they first started using it. Consequently, despite growing campaigns encouraging parents to delay their children’s access to smartphones and social media, little is known about whether starting to use social media at an earlier age affects students’ academic achievement.

Study author Marco Gui of the University of Milano-Bicocca and colleagues wanted to estimate the impact of early social media use on students’ learning outcomes throughout their school careers. They hypothesized that early social media use would harm school performance by distracting students and displacing time they would otherwise spend on homework, sleep, or physical activity, and by exposing them to content and relationships that could harm their mental well-being. They also expected the negative effects to grow with longer exposure.

The researchers combined two data sources. The first was the EYES UP survey, a retrospective questionnaire completed by 6,609 students in 10th and 11th grade in Lombardy during the 2023–2024 school year. The second was data from INVALSI, the Italian National Institute for the Evaluation of the Education and Training System, which administers standardized tests in Italian and mathematics in grades 2, 5, 8, 10, and 13, and in English in grades 5 and 8.

The survey asked students in which grade they opened their first social media profile and received their first internet-connected smartphone, as well as when they began independently using a video game console, computer, or tablet. It also assessed how much smartphones intruded on students’ daily lives, along with their well-being, life satisfaction, and academic self-efficacy. After merging the two datasets and focusing on students born in 2007 and 2008, the analytic sample included 5,227 students.

Results showed that the median student started using a video game console in grade 4 and a tablet in grade 5. By grade 6, the median student had independent access to a computer and their own internet-connected smartphone, and 47% of students received their first smartphone that year. By the end of 8th grade, when Italian students finish lower-secondary school, 98% owned a smartphone, and most began using messaging apps when they got their smartphone or the following year, even though most such apps require users to be at least 13 or 14.

When it came to social media, 11% of students opened their first profile during primary school, 30% in 6th grade, 25% in 7th grade, and 18% in 8th grade. Only 16% waited until 9th grade, which corresponds to age 14, the minimum age for independent access under Italian law.

Students who started using social media earlier tended to score lower in Italian and mathematics, even after accounting for their exposure to other forms of technology. However, early adopters also tended to come from less-educated families, were less likely to live with both parents, and already had lower test scores before they opened a social media account.

To better isolate the role of social media, the researchers separately matched students who opened accounts in 6th, 7th, or 8th grade with students who waited until 9th grade or later, pairing them on family background, prior technology use, and 5th-grade test scores and school marks. They then tracked how each group’s test scores changed over time, a method known as difference-in-differences.

Students who opened an account in 6th grade scored about 0.22 standard deviations lower in Italian and 0.18 lower in mathematics by 8th grade than comparable students who waited. By 10th grade, the gap in Italian remained the same and the gap in mathematics grew to 0.27 standard deviations. Differences for students who started in 7th grade were in the same direction but smaller, and differences for those who started in 8th grade were smaller still, with the 8th-grade gap in mathematics not statistically significant.

The findings for students who started in 8th grade were also less robust in additional statistical checks, while the findings for those who started in 6th grade were the most robust. Early social media use was not linked to English test scores, which the authors suggest may reflect the large amount of English-language content online. Students who started in 6th or 7th grade were also more likely to repeat a grade, and all early adopters were less likely to earn top marks at the end of 8th grade and reported lower academic self-efficacy.

An exploratory analysis suggested that the pervasiveness of smartphones in students’ daily lives, such as checking their phones before bed, upon waking, or while doing homework, accounted for roughly 15% to 47% of the link between early social media use and lower test scores, depending on the subject. The authors note that this analysis was correlational.

“The findings of this study carry important implications for educators, parents and policymakers. First, they emphasize the need for more structured guidelines and digital literacy programs in schools aimed at developing appropriate awareness of social media use among young students and parents, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds. Second, they suggest the need to regulate the engagement mechanisms embedded in these platforms, particularly when they are used by minors. Moreover, in the short term, policies that delay social media access until children are cognitively mature enough to manage its potential distractions could be beneficial. Some of these policies are already in place,” the study authors concluded.

The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the links between social media use and academic performance. However, it should be noted that the size of the differences is open to interpretation. The authors note that effects above 0.2 standard deviations are considered large in education research and that a 0.2 standard deviation gap is roughly equivalent to six months of schooling, but by general benchmarks used in psychology, differences of this magnitude are considered small.

Additionally, although the authors interpret their findings as evidence of a causal effect, the study was not an experiment, and its conclusions depend on assumptions that cannot be fully verified, such as the absence of unmeasured factors like family dynamics that influence both social media use and academic performance. The age at which students first used social media was also based on their recollections, leaving room for recall bias, and the sample excluded students in short vocational programs and those who had dropped out or repeated multiple years.

The findings may also not generalize beyond northern Italy or to the social media landscape of 2019 to 2023, when the students in the study were adolescents. Two of the authors, Gui and Chiara Respi, serve on the governance board of the Patti Digitali Foundation, which advocates for a gradual approach to children’s access to digital environments.

The paper, “Longitudinal effect of early social media use on standardized learning outcomes during school career,” was authored by Marco Gui, Chiara Respi, Giovanni Abbiati, Cristiana Paladini, Sofia Ercolanoni, Francesca Milzani, Tiziana Pirola, and Giovanni Vezzoli.

issues.title: Your brain may start reacting to an emoji’s expression before your eyes even reach it
issues.summary: New eye-tracking research suggests people start registering a face emoji's expression in peripheral vision before looking directly at it, pausing slightly longer on the preceding word while finishing the overall sentence faster.
issues.author: Eric W. Dolan
issues.content_html:
When people read a text message containing a smiling face emoji, their brains may begin registering its emotional tone before their eyes even look directly at it, according to new eye-tracking research published in Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology. The experiment indicates that an upcoming positive face emoji is associated with readers pausing slightly longer on the preceding word than a neutral face emoji is, while also finishing the overall sentence slightly faster. Together, the findings provide evidence that readers take in emotional symbols alongside neighboring words in parallel rather than processing each item strictly one at a time.

Emojis are small pictorial symbols depicting faces, gestures, objects, and animals that people insert into digital messages to convey emotion and tone, serving a role similar to facial expressions in spoken conversation. People tend to be remarkably quick at reading these tiny faces: an earlier emotion-recognition experiment found that participants identified emotions 73 milliseconds faster and more accurately from emojis than from photographs of real human faces, with happy expressions recognized fastest of all.

Matching symbols can also shape how an entire message lands, as an earlier study of social media posts indicated that tweets paired with an emotionally fitting emoji were judged easier to understand and more believable than tweets with mismatched emojis or none at all.

Beyond overall message impressions, psychologists use high-speed eye-tracking cameras to examine how emojis alter the split-second mechanics of reading. As the eyes move across a line of text, sharp central vision, known as foveal vision, focuses on the word currently being read, while the surrounding area of near-peripheral vision, called the parafovea, previews upcoming characters just to the right.

When a word or symbol in that parafoveal preview alters how long the eyes dwell on the current word, researchers call it a parafoveal-on-foveal effect. Such effects sit at the center of a longstanding debate between serial reading models, which hold that people process the meaning of only one word at a time, and parallel reading models, which propose that attention spans several adjacent items simultaneously.

Recent eye-tracking experiments have shown that object emojis placed right after a matching noun, such as a wine glass symbol following the word “wine,” can speed up reading of that preceding word from parafoveal vision. Face emojis, however, do not stand in for a single concrete noun and instead carry broader social and emotional shades of meaning, with survey studies suggesting that even ostensibly neutral faces are sometimes read as slightly cold or negative. Whether the facial expression on an emoji placed in the middle of an everyday neutral sentence alters how readers process the words right before and after it had not yet been tested.

Whether a cheerful face symbol also gives readers a head start on surrounding words during natural reading was another open question, after 2025 and 2026 single-word studies by the same researchers indicated a positivity bias in which smiling emojis sped up recognition of isolated neutral words. The new research, led by Demian Stoianov as part of his doctoral work at Macquarie University and the University of Groningen, examined how facial expressions shape sentence reading.

“In our earlier experiments, we showed people an emoji and measured how quickly and accurately they could decide whether a string of letters was a real word,” Stoianov, now a postdoctoral researcher in the Forkosh Lab in the Department of Cognitive Science at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, told PsyPost. “The emoji’s emotional tone could influence their performance even though it gave them no clue to the correct answer. We wanted to know whether that influence would also show up in people’s eye movements as they read a whole sentence at their own pace. The earlier studies appeared in Cognition and Emotion (2025) and Scientific Reports (2026).”

To test this, the researchers first created 100 emotionally neutral sentences, each consisting of two independent clauses separated in the middle by a dash (for example, pairing “Did you change your hair” with “something is different”). The words directly before and after the dash were matched on length, frequency in English, spelling similarity to other words, and emotional tone. An independent prescreening group of 34 Australian university students, with an average age of 21.5, rated each dash-separated sentence online on a 5-point scale from very negative to very positive, allowing the team to select the 64 most consistently neutral sentences, which averaged about 11 words in length.

The researchers also selected 64 Apple face emojis, consisting of 32 positive and 32 neutral faces validated in standardized emoji databases, and adjusted them for uniform pixel size and brightness. Each of the 64 sentences was paired with one plausible positive face and one plausible neutral face, producing 128 versions divided into two lists so that each reader saw 64 sentences, half positive and half neutral, without seeing any sentence or emoji twice.

Fifty-one native English-speaking undergraduate psychology students at Macquarie University were recruited, with one excluded due to calibration issues and horizontal drift, leaving the preregistered final sample of 50 participants (36 women and 14 men, aged 18 to 34, with an average age of 19.5). The study’s sample size, hypotheses, and primary analyses were preregistered, and all materials and data were posted publicly on the Open Science Framework. Sitting 104 centimeters from a desktop monitor in a head-stabilized setup, participants silently read the single-line sentences with both eyes while an infrared eye tracker recorded movements 1,000 times per second, with data from the right eye analyzed. After finishing each sentence, participants rated the sentiment of either the sentence, on half of the trials, or the emoji, on the other half, on the same 5-point scale.

The team tracked both early eye-movement measures, which reflect a reader’s initial pass over a word, and late measures, which reflect rereading and sentence integration. Early measures included first-fixation duration (how long the very first glance on a word lasted), single-fixation duration (how long the glance lasted when a word was fixated only once before moving on), and gaze duration (the combined time of all consecutive initial glances on a word before leaving it). Late measures included total reading time on a word, the probability of looking back at it after leaving, and total dwell time across the full sentence.

In everyday digital communication, positive face emojis tend to be more familiar, higher in emotional arousal, less visually complex, and slightly different in how unambiguous their meaning is compared to neutral faces. To isolate the effect of positive versus neutral emotion, the statistical models adjusted for those four emoji characteristics.

When participants looked directly at the emoji itself, the expected positivity advantage emerged: positive face emojis drew shorter total reading times than neutral ones, averaging 298 versus 362 milliseconds. Positive faces also prompted fewer backward glances and shorter early fixation times, with initial glances on the emoji averaging 208 versus 226 milliseconds and first-pass gaze durations showing a similar pattern.

On the word immediately preceding the emoji, however, the pattern went in the opposite direction. Across all three early eye-tracking measures, readers paused slightly longer on the preceding word when the upcoming face in parafoveal vision was positive rather than neutral; for example, single-fixation durations averaged 196 milliseconds before a positive face compared to 192 milliseconds before a neutral face, with first-fixation and gaze durations showing similar small, statistically reliable increases in the transformed models. Late measures on that preceding word, including total reading time and backward glances, were not statistically significant.

Notably, detecting any valence effect on the preceding word depended on accounting for emoji familiarity, arousal, visual complexity, and ambiguity: in parallel models that omitted those four adjustments, differences between positive and neutral emojis were not statistically significant across the eye-tracking measures. Even with those adjustments in place, the authors describe their interpretation of the brief pause as tentative given the modest raw millisecond differences, suggesting that a cheerful face in peripheral vision may capture attention or briefly compete for mental resources while the reader finishes the current word, similar to patterns reported for emotional words in character-based scripts like Chinese.

“Our eyes sometimes land just short of where we aim them,” Stoianov explained. “We wondered whether readers who appeared to be looking at the end of a word had actually been aiming for the emoji beside it. Even after we set aside glances that landed on the word’s final letter or in the space before the emoji, we still saw the difference between positive and neutral faces.”

During initial data cleaning, very brief nearby glances were merged (about 4 percent of the data), while trials with blinks in or right next to the target region or fixations longer than 1,200 milliseconds were removed, excluding 25 percent of trials. As context for that data loss, the researchers noted that earlier mid-sentence emoji studies by members of the same team had documented high emoji-skipping rates of roughly 56 to 66 percent, depending on whether comprehension questions targeted the symbols. In their non-preregistered follow-up check for mislocated fixations, mapping eye landings character by character across a 10-space window around the emoji and incorporating adjacent blank spaces reduced data removal to about 6 percent, consistent with the view that narrow boundaries around a small symbol can inflate apparent skipping and missing data when glances land slightly to the side.

Although glances did cluster within two character positions of the emoji, breaking single-fixation times down by distance showed that the valence difference held specifically at a middle distance of 4 to 10 characters before the emoji rather than within 1 to 3 characters or beyond 10 characters. Rerunning the models after excluding fixations on the final letter of the preceding word and the space before the emoji still yielded longer first-fixation, single-fixation, and gaze durations before positive faces (with single fixations averaging 196 versus 193 milliseconds), indicating that the pause was not merely an eye-aiming artifact and supporting parallel-processing models of reading.

On the word immediately following the emoji, by contrast, differences between positive and neutral face emojis were not statistically significant across any early or late measure, including first-fixation duration, single-fixation duration, gaze duration, total reading time, and backward regressions. Greater visual complexity of the emoji was associated with slightly longer initial glances on the next word and higher arousal with shorter total reading time in the initial models, though neither relationship remained statistically significant in the character-level reanalysis.

“In our earlier experiments with words shown in isolation, a positive emoji helped people recognize the word that came next,” Stoianov said. “We expected a similar benefit here, yet we found no reliable difference on the word immediately after the emoji. One possibility is that a face between two clauses acts a little like punctuation, giving readers a moment to wrap up one thought before moving on to the next.”

Unlike studies that position an emoji at the very start of a sentence, the authors propose that ongoing grammar and meaning integration mid-sentence, combined with that clause-ending wrap-up process, may mute any emotional priming boost on the next word. Across the full sentence, however, participants finished reading trials with a positive face emoji faster overall than those with a neutral face emoji, averaging 2,523 milliseconds compared to 2,585 milliseconds, with higher emoji arousal also linked to faster sentence reading.

“The first glance at the word before the emoji lasted on average a few milliseconds longer when a positive face was coming up, and across a whole sentence, readers finished about 60 milliseconds sooner with a positive face than with a neutral one,” Stoianov noted. “These differences were statistically reliable and consistent, and we tested one emoji per sentence, so these small effects may accumulate over a conversation.”

Exploratory sentiment ratings collected after each trial aligned with those reading shifts, with participants rating positive emojis higher than neutral ones on the 5-point scale (averaging 3.1 versus 2.3). Readers also judged sentences containing positive faces more positively than the same sentences paired with neutral faces (2.9 versus 2.3), consistent with the authors’ note that some nominally neutral emojis may be interpreted as slightly negative.

Comparing those scores against the independent prescreening group’s ratings of the dash-separated versions without emojis showed that the plain dashed sentences averaged 3.0, edging out the positive-emoji versions (2.9) and scoring well above the neutral-emoji versions, which the authors suggest may indicate that adding emojis can sometimes make a plain statement come across as less sincere.

“You may start picking up on an emoji’s emotional tone before you look directly at it, as we found that readers’ eyes lingered a little longer on the word just before a positive face than before a neutral one,” Stoianov pointed out. “Also, even a face classed as neutral could give an otherwise matter-of-fact message a slightly negative tone.”

There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The experiment tested only emotionally neutral, two-clause sentences read in a laboratory setting, so facial emojis might behave differently inside messages that already carry strong positive, negative, or sarcastic meaning, and the word-level preview effect emerged only after statistically adjusting for familiarity, arousal, visual complexity, and ambiguity. In addition, the eye-tracking session itself did not include plain sentences without emojis, meaning the sentiment comparison against dash-separated text came from two separate groups of readers.

“If you’re wondering whether adding a smile will make a message sound friendlier, it matters what you’re comparing it with,” Stoianov cautioned. “Every sentence in our eye-tracking experiment contained an emoji. In a separate pretest, another group read the same sentences with a dash in place of the emoji. They rated those versions slightly more positively than the readers who saw the versions with a positive face.”

Looking ahead, the authors note that future experiments could systematically vary where emojis appear within a sentence to test how placement and clause boundaries shape subsequent word reading. Expanding beyond smiling and neutral faces to examine negative and high-arousal expressions could also test whether negative facial cues capture peripheral attention just as early.

“We’d like to know whether readers pick up on a frown as early as a smile,” Stoianov added. “One way to test this would be to let readers glimpse either expression while their eyes are still on the preceding word. As their gaze crosses an invisible boundary just before the emoji, the screen would switch to the same final face in both versions. That would let us test whether the expression in that first glimpse changes how long readers linger on the preceding word.”

The study, “The Effect of Positive Emojis on Reading: An Eye-Movement Study,” was authored by Demian Stoianov, Nenagh Kemp, Signy Wegener, and Elisabeth Beyersmann.
