issues.content_html:
It was perhaps inevitable that market-driven land use change would come to City Island; the beauty of the place is immediately apparent. Only a quarter-mile causeway separates the small island from the rest of the Bronx, one of the five boroughs of New York City, and yet City Island can seem a world away.

The former United Boat Service Yard at the foot of Carroll Street was the first major maritime property to be converted to residences, becoming in the early-1980s The Boatyard Condominiums. The managing director then of the island’s chamber of commerce told the New York Times, “If the condos do well, then the boatyards and marinas are all going to go.”

Less than 10 years later, the last sail-making loft, Rapsey & Lapthorn, founded in 1915 and a purveyor to America's Cup racing yachts, became The Sailmaker Condominium. All that was left of these two businesses was nominal references to their function before conversion to residential development. Yet, in spite of the loss of major historic waterfront industries, City Island (mostly, see “Know Before You Go”) maintains its small-town, maritime feel.

A half-mile wide and 1.5 miles long, one is never far from the water on City Island. The buildings, even the new construction, are low-rise, providing a sense of sky that is unique to waterfront communities. With only 4,417 residents (2020 Census) and a—“a” as in one—small supermarket, gas station, bank, and hardware store, it is not hard for visitors to picture themselves in a quaint New England fishing village.

The popular seafood restaurants, the principal tourist attraction, contribute to the impression. This is ironic because City Island was not a significant port for fishing vessels. City Island is known for its boat building and repair and if you want to know more about that history, the place to visit is the City Island Nautical Museum.

The museum is located in the former Public School 102 (later, P.S. 17) designed by noted academic architect C.B.J. Snyder and constructed in 1897. The museum contains a main hall gallery primarily composed of two-dimensional material; the Walsh Library with books, ephemera, and other artifacts; the Nautical Room that focuses on the island’s maritime history; a Community Room, which celebrates life on City Island; and the School Room, with an emphasis on local education.

Like many museums in sparsely populated places that have undergone substantial change, the historical museum on City Island is nostalgic, a lovingly handcrafted assemblage of what artifacts became available for exhibition and what might be reproduced (including with a photocopying machine). A larger physical space, and a much larger budget, might have resulted in a more polished presentation, but a good deal of the charm of the museum derives from the manner in which it tells the maritime and social history of City Island.

issues.title: Thypoch is launching its latest line of AF lenses with a $349 F1.4 prime for X-mount
issues.summary: The first "Sculptor" has an all-metal build and a reasonable price.
issues.author: Mitchell Clark
issues.content_html:
The first “Sculptor” has an all-metal build and a reasonable price.

When you use DPReview links to buy products, the site may earn a commission.

Earlier this year, Thypoch surprised us by becoming the first Chinese company to release an autofocus zoom lens for full-frame with its 24-50mm F2.8 “Voyager” lens. Now, the company is releasing its second autofocus lens, introducing the “Sculptor” series.

It’s a 23mm (35mm equiv) F1.4 prime for Fujifilm’s X-mount, and the company says it has a design “distinct from Thypoch’s existing lines.” It features an all-metal build, an aperture ring and, excitingly, a square lens hood.

The lens is made up of 12 elements in 10 groups, with 2 aspheric lenses, 4 ED elements and 1 high-refractive-index element. It can focus as close as 0.25m (9.8″) for a maximum reproduction of 0.13x. Thypoch says it has its “Epoch” coating to reduce the risk of flare.

Despite the metal construction, relatively fast aperture and deeply textured control rings, the lens comes in at just 283g (10oz), which is a fair bit lighter than Fujifilm and Sigma’s 23mm F1.4 offerings, though a touch heavier than Viltrox’s. However, it’s slightly shorter than all three at 71mm (2.8″) long. It accepts 52mm filters.

While there is no shortage of companies producing APS-C prime lenses, it never hurts to have another competitor in the ring. We were relatively impressed with Thypoch’s first autofocus lens, so it’s exciting to see the company continue along that path. We’ll be interested to see how its image quality compares to similar offerings from Fujifilm and Sigma.

Given its price, people may be willing to give it a bit of leeway even if it ends up not being quite as sharp as other options. Fujifilm’s 23mm F1.4 retails for $1050, while Sigma’s is $660. The Sculptor AF 23mm F1.4, meanwhile, will cost $350, and is available now.

issues.title: The disappointment factory: fear and loathing in the camera rumor mill
issues.summary: Please don't be let down by cameras that don't exist yet.
issues.author: Mitchell Clark
issues.content_html:
Please don’t be let down by cameras that don’t exist yet.

If you’re a fan of Panasonic cameras and have been hanging around the Lumix subreddit or rumors sites, it’s possible you feel a little let down by this week’s announcement. The SHX1 is, essentially, an S1II designed to be solely used by video professionals. It has a few new features, some of which are pretty cool, but for most videographers, it won’t suddenly unlock ways of shooting that were unthinkable with Panasonic’s hybrid offerings.

In short, it’s what we’ve come to expect from a camera release in 2026; a lot of the same parts, rearranged to better fit a specific audience. To me, that’s a good thing. I’m not especially disappointed by this camera.

But if you kept up with the rumor mill and read the comments from people speculating on the information that had leaked about it, the SHX1 was supposed to have an unprecedented sensor. Maybe one that could shoot 8K, and utilized the organic tech Panasonic’s been working on for over a decade to unlock a global shutter and variable ND. Or maybe it’d have a LOFIC design for crazy levels of DR. Surely, Panasonic must be doing something to completely embarrass the competition, right?

This is a scene that plays over and over before pretty much every camera launch. A few real specs leak, occasionally alongside a heady blend of misinformation and optimistic expectation, and people extrapolate it out to the moon. This next camera is going to be the best thing ever… but if it doesn’t match exactly what the commenter is imagining in their head, it’ll be a crushing disappointment. Perhaps even a reason to declare that you’re switching brands.

To put it bluntly, this feels like an unhealthy way to think about cameras, or even products in general. * Not everyone does – there are just as many people calling out this behavior (or, more likely, mocking it) as there are engaging in it, and I don’t find that it’s all that common on our site and forums, thankfully – but it’s common enough that it worries me. It’s hard to imagine a life spent on such an emotional roller coaster is a fun one.

This isn’t to say that people shouldn’t have fun daydreaming about what might be possible, or push companies to innovate. But there’s a big difference between looking at the specs of the SHX1 now that it’s officially ** announced and saying “sure, but I wish it had 8K, too,” and getting whipped into a frenzy over imagined specs of a camera that you aren’t going to buy, sometimes for weeks at a time.

Cameras are complex machines, and while there are often times where you can look at a spec sheet and have a pretty good idea of how it’ll perform, there are just as many where they end up being more than the sum of their parts. But to even begin to tell those apart, you need to actually know what the camera is first.

* I saw this a lot when I reported on tech in general, too, though in that realm people seemed to have a much firmer grasp on reality, in terms of what features products would have and what they’d cost.

** I’ve also seen many people use the word “confirmed” or “official” when referring to rumors, which is literally not the case.

issues.title: Why this Tokyo photographer sold everything and started over with manual-focus lenses
issues.summary: Marcel shares the Sony a7R V and manual-focus Voigtländer and Zeiss primes he built after selling everything, plus the lessons his grandfather taught him.
issues.author: Mathew Anderson
issues.content_html:
Marcel shares the Sony a7R V and manual-focus Voigtländer and Zeiss primes he built after selling everything, plus the lessons his grandfather taught him.

Meet Marcel

Home base: Tokyo, Japan

This week, we head to Tokyo to chat with forum member Vamp898-ng , a photographer whose love of the craft traces back to watching his grandfather shoot eagles in flight from a mountain trail, steadying a 500mm lens in an era before image stabilization.

Over 22 years, Marcel has cycled through gear obsessions and eventually sold everything to start over – arriving at a setup built almost entirely around manual-focus primes from Voigtländer and Zeiss for his Sony a7R V. His big question for much of his photography: what photos would he want to show his grandchildren someday?

Our What’s in your bag? community spotlight series features readers sharing their favorite gear and photography, including from past DReview collaborators. See below for what today’s guest has to share.

Have your photography featured on the DPReview homepage! Find out how.

What’s in Marcel’s bag

Favorite camera(s):Sony a7R V

“The a7R V has a lot of room for cropping, so I don’t have to use zoom lenses or large tele. It has a big, comfortable grip and a large, high-resolution EVF, which is perfect for fast and precise manual focus.”

Favorite lens(s): “All of my lenses are from either Voigtländer or Zeiss. If I leave the house without knowing what is going to happen, I will have the following with me:

  • Voigtländer APO-LANTAR 50mm F2 (mounted on the camera)
  • Voigtländer APO-LANTHAR 35mm F2
  • Voigtländer Nokton 75mm F1.5

If I know the shooting conditions beforehand, I take the Zeiss Sonnar 135mm F2.8 (C/Y).

I only have one accessory: the Voigtländer VM-E Close Focus Adapter II. I love it because it enables me to use all M-Mount lenses, like the Zeiss C Sonnar 50mm F1.5, which was love at first sight for me.”

What got you started, and how long have you been a photographer?

“My Grandfather was a photographer, and I was the first (and only) of his grandchildren who showed interest in his work. He taught me with a Zeiss Ikon Icarex 35 and a Tessar 50mm F2.8, promising I would get that camera if my photos got good enough. It was fully analog, so no battery, not even a light meter. I had to use a Zeiss Ikon Ikophot to meter the light, and he even wanted me to guess the shutter speed for the aperture I wanted before measuring, because relying on the light meter was simply too slow.

While many people today think of analog photography as a way to slow down intentionally, they probably think of a rangefinder. He taught me how to get as fast as possible with that camera. “The subject might not wait for you”. It was an SLR; it can shoot fast if the photographer knows how to, and he wanted me to pull it off.

After roughly three months, he deemed me worthy to get the whole set. The Icarex, the Tessar 50mm F2.8, the Ikophot, and a nice book called Mit der Kamera auf du by Alexander Spoerl to continue learning. It’s an amazing book whose tricks I still use today.”

How has your photography changed since you started?

“As soon as I got my first job (16 years ago), I had a co-worker who was a travel photographer with years of experience. He showed me amazing images from India and Ireland. As someone just getting his first job, world travel with a full-frame SLR (he used the original Canon EOS 5D) was an unthinkable dream.

Then I got into gear wars, comparing 100% crops of lenses and cameras over and over again, looking for the best comparison tool. This is probably the darkest era for me personally because I spent more time researching than shooting.

I started realizing that what I do didn’t feel right to me when I was working with a portrait photographer who told me, “You have to get better-looking models,” after showing him a photo of my girlfriend.

That single sentence changed a lot for me because, even though there are a lot of famous exceptions, he wasn’t wrong. I soon realized that this was not what I wanted to do. I sold everything I owned and started again. With a set of fully manual, fixed-focal-length lenses, taking photos purely of what I wanted to photograph.”

What’s so special about Voigtländer?

“Cosina Co., Ltd. (the company that makes Voigtländer and a lot of Zeiss lenses) is not getting enough love, and it seems people have a hard time understanding their lens lineups (like the difference between Nokton (Vintage), Nokton Classic and so on) and sometimes end up with a lens they are not happy with, even though the lens does exactly what it was built for.

Cosina is the only maker brave enough to offer the same lens in different versions. All their products are handmade in Japan with insane, full-metal build quality. As far as I know, they are also the only maker that does not artificially inflate prices based on gray imports and currency exchange rates. They are a small, traditional lens maker who works out of a love for lenses and photography.”

What places of interest do you shoot?

“One thing that felt unique to me was shooting the Formula E Race in Berlin. I stumbled into that by accident. I noticed you couldn’t buy tickets for the press stand, and I just wanted to know how you get into these stands (I did not intend to shoot there), and they looked at my SIGMA Sports 120-300mm F2.8, whispered to each other, and then put a band on my wrist and told me to get in.

Because I had a SIGMA SD Quattro at that point whose AF was absolutely not up for the job, I remembered what I learned from my grandfather and shot the whole race in MF.”

What have you learned?

“As I am shooting with manual lenses only, fast, precise MF is of utmost importance. I disabled the MF assist (the focus loupe that triggers as soon as you turn the focus wheel) because it slows me down. You lose control over framing; if the subject moves, you can’t refocus, as all you see is a magnified blurry mess, and so on.

Choose the lenses you want to use, then find a body to attach them to. And always think about how you want to use a lens. Do you really want a lens with harsh bokeh that is razor-sharp edge-to-edge for wide-open portrait shots? If not, be brave enough to choose the lens with the bokeh you prefer, even if it might not be as sharp on a test chart.

Don’t know what lenses you might want to use? Start with one that has the focal length roughly equal to your sensor diagonal. You’ll eventually end up owning most focal lengths anyway, so it doesn’t really matter which you’ll start with. If you ask me, I’d always recommend a used full-frame camera with a 50mm lens.”

Marcel really enjoyed participating in this spotlight article and would love to hear what you think of his photography and to answer any of your questions in the comments below.

issues.title: Capture One adds wired tethering for the Hasselblad X2D II 100C
issues.summary: The feature follows July’s native Raw support and requires X2D II 100C firmware 1.4.15.7 and Capture One 16.9.1.
issues.author: Dale Baskin
issues.content_html:
The feature follows July’s native Raw support and requires X2D II 100C firmware 1.4.15.7 and Capture One 16.9.1.

Hasselblad has released firmware version 1.4.15.7 for the X2D II 100C, adding support for wired tethered shooting in Capture One. Tethering is available in Capture One 16.9.1 for desktop and Capture One Mobile 4.3.0. This marks the second stage of a partnership the two companies announced in July.

What the update adds

With the camera connected via USB, each 100MP frame appears in Capture One at full resolution as soon as it’s captured, so focus and exposure can be checked while it is still live. Capture One’s full editing toolset is available while shooting, and adjustments applied to the first frame carry over to subsequent captures.

“You pick up your camera, you plug in, and it just works,” said Capture One chief executive Rafael Orta.

This release only adds tethered shooting for the X2D II 100C. The X2D 100C and CFV 100C digital back, which gained native Raw support in Capture One in July, weren’t included in today’s announcement.

A complicated history

Historically, Hasselblad support had been missing from Capture One, a result of the old rivalry between Hasselblad and Phase One, Capture One’s former parent company, which competed for the same medium format customers.

That changed in July, when Capture One added native support for Hasselblad’s .3FR Raw files in version 16.8.3, covering the X2D II 100C, X2D 100C and CFV 100C, along with dedicated lens profiles for XCD lenses. At the time, the companies said tethering would follow later in 2026.

Bronius Rudnickas, Hasselblad’s global marketing manager, said tethering was one of the top requests from photographers after the collaboration was announced.

Availability

Firmware 1.4.15.7 for the X2D II 100C is available now for download from Hasselblad. Tethering support is available in Capture One 16.9.1 and Capture One Mobile 4.3.0. Capture One is also offering Hasselblad camera owners a 90-day trial of the software.

issues.title: The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City
issues.summary: From The Bass in Miami Beach to the murals of Wynwood, the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is heavily inspired by the local arts scene.
issues.author: Rhea Nayyar
issues.content_html:
After 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.

As fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach.

“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” said Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.

“It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!”

While not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center, which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life.

“We were as delighted as anyone else to find PAMM in what feels like the biggest video game of all time,” said Alexa Ferra, PAMM's senior director of marketing and communications, in an email to Hyperallergic.

Ferra attached a photo someone sent her from the game showing the PAMM dupe and some gummy bear-inspired sculptures installed in the shallow water.

“It's a testament to our stunning Herzog & de Meuron building, and goes to show if you stick around long enough, you'll pop up in the unlikeliest — but inevitable — of places.” Ferra added.

Other references to Miami's arts and culture scene include Leonida's Stockyard neighborhood, which directly channels the street murals and warehouse-lined roads of the Wynwood Arts District. It was reported earlier this summer that Rockstar Games had hired over 50 real street artists to design the in-game murals across Stockyard. Users shared they've spotted the works of street artist Ahol Sniffs Glue (David Anasagasti), among others.

Miami-raised contemporary photographer Josh Aronson also took notice of GTA 6's inclusion of his installation at the Catalina Hotel & Beach Club in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2024, which Rockstar Games incorporated in Vice City's own Catalina Hotel. From Aronson's Florida Boys (2020–) photo series, the photo “Spring” (2024) was made into an enormous sublimated fabric print that hung from the second-story window of the hotel.

The same printed photo, which features a group of cheerful young men photographed from above while floating in water, is shown at Vice City's Catalina Hotel.

“Florida Boys is my own imagined version of Florida, so I love that it gets to live on in another imagined Florida,” Aronson told Hyperallergic. “The installation at the Catalina was temporary, but in Vice City, someone might stumble upon it years from now. It’s a reminder of the wild ways we encounter art today, and how a work can find new life long after it comes down.”

GTA6's pre-holiday release comes just before Miami Art Week begins early next month. Those dropping in can find some of Aronson's installations on view beyond Vice City at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens and the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami, and also pay homage to the cultural venues and districts that inspired Leonida.

issues.title: A View From the Easel: Rei Xiao
issues.summary: “I love that my roommate’s cat, Astrid, whom I appointed as my studio assistant, can always come and join me when I am painting.”
issues.author: Lakshmi Rivera Amin
issues.content_html:
Welcome to the 364thinstallment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Rei Xiao paints a world of surreal, feline figuration into being while navigating the artist visa system and managing their studio assistant (a dignified cat named Astrid).

Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.

Rei Xiao, Brooklyn, New York

How long have you been working in this space?

Two years.

Describe an average day in your studio.

I work from my apartment. The most predictable parts of my studio day start with putting on my sunscreen and painting clothes. It’s a very small space that I paint in, so I usually have to push stuff aside when I start, like my painting cart, stool, and trash bin.

I, then, turn on my air purifier, open the lids of my palettes, scrape paints from the previous session, and play either TV shows I’m familiar with or podcasts hosted by comedians in the background. The day usually ends with my cleaning the palette, emptying and wiping my brush cleaning tank, and diligently washing my brushes. Then I wash my face and go to sleep.

issues.summary: Plus: Joyce Awards winners announced, Agnes Gund's gift to art in schools, and Derrick Adams and LEGO make a splash in Miami.
issues.author: Valentina Di Liscia
issues.content_html:
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

Laura Hoptman Wins CCS Bard Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence

The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College announced Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in New York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.

So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.

“The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”

issues.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’’s Vice City Pays Homage to the Bass, Among More Art Easter Eggs
issues.summary: The game even rendered a riff on 'Miami Mountain', a tower of boulders by Ugo Rondinone installed outside the Bass.
issues.author: Tessa Solomon
issues.content_html:
The new Grand Theft Auto arrived this week, the messianic reward after 13 long years, offering the best-rendered version of the series’ standing promise: anything, within the scope of its metropolis and the player’s imagination. I watched my cousin paint a house for his avatar’s girlfriend, then hop in a car and drive to the Bass Museum. Or rather, to the Vice City Museum of Art, the faithful replica of it in Vice City, the game’s fictional Miami.

Rockstar teased that Grand Theft Auto VI would boast the franchise’s sharpest graphics yet, and the claim was not exaggerated. The Vice Museum of Art captures the Bass’s signature civic Art Deco style: a pale limestone facade (the real stuff was quarried in the Florida Keys) and, as far as I could tell, even the carved decorative relief around the entry. It’s a far cry from the series’ earliest entries, when a building like this would have been a smooth beige box; here, the facade looks textured. We parked and admired its public art: a riff on Miami Mountain, a tower of boulders by Ugo Rondinone permanently installed in Collins Park, outside the Bass. Part of Rondinone’s “Mountain” series, it’s made of garishly clashing fluorescent rocks stacked high and probably visible from space. The Vice City version has swapped stone for emojis: winking, crying, smiling.

Vice City may be hiding another Easter egg for art heads. Months ago, a screenshot circulated online from an expansion for Grand Theft Auto Online, showing a new character in a shirt with an “Art Oregano” logo. It’s a safe bet that it’s a nod to Art Basel Miami Beach, held at the Miami Beach Convention Center, since it’s set in the same font as the fair’s. The herby homage was well received. “I hope he’ll be in GTA 6 having his own little art studio or something,” wrote one Reddit user. Another added, “I can’t wait to wear this shirt to Art Basel this year, if I can pull myself away from GTA6.”

Art Basel Miami Beach runs December 4-6; keep an eye out for Art Oregano shirts. And, perhaps, as players make it further into the notoriously long game, a new version of Art Oregano may appear.

I couldn’t personally verify whether the game includes a replica of the fair, with NPCs entering and exiting, as the Vice Museum did. We’d spent the momentous night doing relatively mundane things, like comparing paint colors, which confirms what the think pieces have already noted: these characters can do coke and rob banks and make chaos, but viral clips suggest they’d rather dream of having enough money to buy a car and go for a long drive.

Before I left, my cousin regretfully canceled our plans to visit the Guggenheim on Saturday. He has to work.

issues.title: Judge Allows Lawsuit Over Allegedly Stolen Fra Angelico to Move Forward
issues.summary: The ruling is good news for the Bich heirs, though there's still a long way to go. The judge hasn't decided who owns the painting, or even whether it was stolen.
issues.author: Daniel Cassady
issues.content_html:
A New York judge has refused to throw out a lawsuit over a 15th-century Fra Angelico painting that the heirs to the Bic pen fortune say was stolen by their family chauffeur and later sold by the late art dealer Richard Feigen.

In a decision dated October 26 and filed on November 16, New York Supreme Court Justice James G. Clynes rejected an attempt by Feigen’s estate and associated businesses to get the case dismissed. Their main argument? The family had waited too long to sue.

“No family should lose a treasured work of art simply because the people who handled this stolen property were sophisticated dealmakers,” Luke Nikas, a lawyer for the Bich family, told ARTnews. The Bich family is determined to recover what belongs to them, and today’s decision is an important step toward achieving that result.” The ruling is good news for the Bich heirs, though there’s still a long way to go. The judge hasn’t decided who owns the painting, or even whether it was stolen.

As ARTnews reported in April, the dispute centers on Saint Sixtus (ca. 1453–55), a painting by the Italian Renaissance master that Baron Marcel Bich, the founder of Bic, bought at Sotheby’s in 1972 for £130,000. The painting eventually passed to his son Bruno, who kept it in his Fifth Avenue apartment in Manhattan. Then, around 2006, it disappeared.

According to a lawsuit filed in March by Bruno’s three sons, Gonzalve, Charles, and Guillaume, the family’s chauffeur, Roy Morrow, stole the painting and sold it to Feigen for $3 million. The family says Morrow had no paperwork proving the painting was his, but Feigen bought it anyway and promptly insured it for $8.5 million, nearly three times what he’d paid.

Feigen, one of New York’s best-known Old Master dealers before his death in 2021, later consigned the painting to Christie’s. In 2018, it was sold for $5.4 million to Chilean billionaire Álvaro Saieh and his wife, Ana Guzmán.

The Bich brothers say they didn’t learn where the painting ended up until 2023. They asked for it back the following year, but Saieh and Guzmán refused. So the brothers sued, demanding the painting’s return, along with damages and money from its sale.

Feigen’s representatives tell a different story. In March, lawyers for his estate told Reuters that Morrow had signed a bill of sale saying he owned the painting. The Saiehs, meanwhile, have said they bought it in good faith, relying on Christie’s research.

Which brings us to the latest ruling.

Feigen’s lawyers argued that the family had simply waited too long to bring its claims. After all, Feigen bought the painting in 2006 and sold it in 2018. The brothers didn’t file their lawsuit until March 2026.

But stolen art can be a tricky business under New York law. Generally, when someone buys a stolen artwork in good faith, the clock doesn’t start ticking on a claim for its return until the rightful owner demands it back and the buyer refuses.

Things get more complicated when someone is accused of knowingly dealing in stolen property. The clock can start earlier, and Clynes said there were too many unanswered questions about Feigen’s purchase to settle the issue now.

The judge also rejected, for now, an argument that the family had dragged its feet for so long that allowing the case to continue would be unfair. Lawyers call that laches. Both arguments can come up again later.

Feigen’s side did score one win. The judge dismissed claims against his revocable trust and its trustees because the family hadn’t shown enough to connect the trust to the money from the painting’s sale. The brothers can bring those claims again if they find more evidence.

issues.title: How do Artworks Acquire Value? New York Art Dealers David Nolan and Anton Svyatsky Weigh In.
issues.summary: An art world veteran and a relative newcomer offer their perspectives on the role of the art collector in today's market.
issues.author: Lmiller
issues.content_html:
How do artworks acquire value? I discussed this complex question with two New York art dealers during Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America.

David Nolan, whose eponymous gallery has been open since 1987, gave the view of an art world veteran; Anton Svyatsky, who opened Management in 2023, provided a newer perspective.

Along the way, we discussed the role of the collector in sustaining value, the challenges of pricing artworks by emerging artists, the ways in which influence and market value have become decoupled, the casino that is the auction house and the zoo that is the art fair.

At our talk on Friday, November 13 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, Svyatsky insisted that collectors need to see themselves as responsible for an artist’s value, rather than depend on dealers and institutions for that function. This shift in perspective, and a return to collecting artists in depth, may well be the key to ridding the art world of speculators. Nolan recalled the immense changes that took place during the 1980s, and the increasing attention paid to artworks’ financial value.

Speaking of casinos, a flask emerged at the mention of the new partnership between Artnet and Kalshi—you can catch that moment and other choice ones in the video of the talk above.

issues.title: Working Mothers Face Pervasive Discrimination in London Art World, Study Finds
issues.summary: For many, having children comes at a professional cost
issues.author: Anne Doran
issues.content_html:
Despite the contemporary art world’s increased attention to women’s experiences and the politics of care in its public-facing programming, working mothers employed by London’s galleries and auction houses face widespread discrimination, according to a new study. As reported by the Art Newspapertoday, a survey of 50 employees working in the UK capital’s commercial art sector has found that, for many, having children comes at considerable professional cost.

The study, conducted by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi and published today in the European Journal of Cultural Studies, sought to ask to what extent pregnancy and maternity affected career progression among art world workers. Moving beyond previous studies centered on fine artists or senior directors, it focused non-artist roles such as sales, administration, and marketing.

Roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s research, which also included 12 in-depth interviews, reveals an industry “marred by implicit and explicit expectations that often result in workers needing to choose between their careers and being parents,” they write. Three quarters of respondents felt that motherhood had impeded career advancement, while 20 percent said they had been explicitly denied promotion.

The authors found poor and sometimes illegal practices across the industry, including employees being “managed” out of their roles while on maternity leave. Such practices, they note, are made possible by a lack of formal human resource structures—only half of the respondence worked for organizations with dedicated HR staff, and just 60 percent said their workplace had a specific parental leave policy—as well as the art market’s pervasive culture of secrecy.

Class and wealth also play a role in shaping employee experience, the study found. For junior employees on modest salaries, the cost of childcare can make travel and attendance at evening events difficult and increase the likelihood of discrimination on the job. At the same time, a lack of resources makes challenging such discrimination unaffordable.

Roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s study spanned small galleries to multinational auction houses and found problems across the board. As they say in their report, “A lack of accountability pervades the sector.”

issues.author: Grace Ebert
issues.content_html:
Model and ballet dancer Sheena Liam brings her understanding of poise, elegance, and graceful bodily movements to a more fixed medium. For the past several years, the artist has been stitching tender portraits of women with long, three-dimensional braids that cascade off the fabric. Occasionally, a single loose thread appears to have slipped out of its plait as it drifts across a protagonist’s cheek.

Liam’s latest works are on view this month in her solo exhibition, The Unbearable Lightness. Several pieces feature figures sporting the same striped bodysuit with an open back, and the methodical pattern on the garment evokes both a sense of precision and rhythm depicted in the scenes. Dancers grasp hands in a circle, clutch each other at the waist, and quietly stretch in solitude, their movements steady and self-determined.

Created across the last eight years, this body of work extends Liam’s interest in women’s labor and how the slow, careful process of stitching can also be an act of defiance in an increasingly digital, fast-paced world. Each piece begins with an underlying sketch that the artist then covers in thread and typically finishes with sleek braids and quick snips of the remaining loose ends.

The Unbearable Lightness opens today at Item Gallery in Paris and runs through December 19. Follow Liam’s latest on Instagram.

issues.summary: Gunnarsson emphasizes profound tonal shifts and incredible vistas on the Reykjanes Peninsula. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
Along the rugged volcanic coast of Iceland’s Reykjanes Peninsula, Vilhelm Gunnarsson captures striking storm surf amid natural contrasts. Dark rocks and beaches send foamy waves into high definition, highlighting the forces that physically shape the artist’s home country. Using black-and-white, an approach inspired by fellow artist Ragnar Axelsson, Gunnarsson emphasizes profound tonal shifts and incredible vistas.

Doubling as a press photographer and a member of a local rescue team, Gunnarsson is accustomed to working in a range of conditions. He captured these images during or just after a storm, when the waves are at their highest. Once you see an otherworldly face emerging from one of the crests, which the photographer describes as a ghost, you won’t be able to unsee it. Explore a larger archive on Instagram.

issues.title: A New Jean-Michel Basquiat Documentary Considers the Artist Behind the Work
issues.summary: "He was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat." Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article A New Jean-Michel Basquiat Documentary Considers the Artist Behind the Work appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Grace Ebert
issues.content_html:
A forthcoming documentary spotlights the life and work of luminary artist Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960-1988). Directed by Quinn Whitney Wilson and Viridiana Lieberman for Netflix, the feature film is the first project authorized by the artist’s two younger sisters, Lisane Basquiat and Jeanine Heriveaux, who helm his estate.

In a trailer, the siblings describe their brother’s energetic approach to life and how the story typically told about his meteoric rise omits so much of who he really was. Simply titled Jean-Michel Basquiat, the film features archival footage and audio, along with never-before-seen works and commentary from his family. The documentary seeks to venture beyond the mythology that’s come to surround Basquiat, who died of an accidental overdose at just 27 and whose work has continued to captivate the art world.

As one sister says in the trailer, “he was unapologetically Jean-Michel Basquiat.” The documentary will be available for streaming globally on December 11.

issues.title: Yoshitomo Nara’s Beloved Wide-Eyed Figures Return to New York
issues.summary: A blockbuster solo show in New York has people lining up down the street. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Yoshitomo Nara’s Beloved Wide-Eyed Figures Return to New York appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Grace Ebert
issues.content_html:
The first time I encountered Yoshitomo Nara’s work was when I opened the mailbox as an angsty teenager. A friend a few years older had recently visited the Walker Art Center, where she bought a postcard printed with two of the artist’s portraits and scribbled a note to her friend (me) still stuck in their tiny Wisconsin hometown. As is wont to happen to teenagers on the cusp of adulthood, I took that postcard as a sort of guiding light—a reminder that the world was bigger than the tractors and small-town gossip I was surrounded by—and promptly cut and taped the works to fit within my clear phone case. I carried this pair of strange characters everywhere I went for years after.

Nara also was born and raised in a rural region, albeit on the other side of the globe. The artist has described his childhood in Aomori on the northern tip of Japan’s main island as solitary and removed from the culture of the cities, instead flanked by the endless expanse of the Pacific Ocean and the snowy ridges of the Hakkōda Mountains. These early years indelibly informed his sensibility, and even in his most emotionally charged works, there’s a deep sense of calm that comes from immersion in nature.

In his first solo presentation in New York in almost a decade, Nara takes over two of David Zwirner’s galleries. The self-titled exhibition includes nearly 100 works from the last several decades, spanning paintings, drawings, and monumental bronze sculptures. Central are the artist’s signature childlike figures with large heads and eyes and an underlying sense of innocence, their skeptical, bored, and even rebellious expressions providing a necessary counterbalance—one that also spoke to my teenage sensitivities.

Profoundly enigmatic, Nara’s works are also instantly recognizable, relatable, and broadly appealing. According to the gallery, 4,000 visitors lined up to see the exhibition on opening night, with 26,000 attending in the first week alone.

Ranging in scale from intimate miniatures to larger-than-life, Nara’s two-dimensional portraits emerge from soft, pastel-hued palettes. Several also often contain pithy phrases that hearken to our collective challenges. Both “world peace” and “tomorrow’s far away” drip with longing and speak to the artist’s broader concern for the contentious state of human relations.

Introducing clay into his practice also emerged from unease and grief, when Nara picked up the earthen material after the 2011 Tōhoku earthquake. The disastrous event killed nearly 20,000 people and injured and displaced many more around the artist’s hometown. In the moment, the tactile medium offered a reprieve the canvas couldn’t.

In the exhibition, Nara’s monochromatic bronzes, coated in white urethane paint, capture these forays into three-dimensions and evoke the icy, snow-blanketed landscapes of his youth. Based on smaller ceramic prototypes, the sculptures bear the traces of the handmade, as if he had sculpted each head with an enormous thumb.

As an exhibition statement says, Nara’s overarching impulse is simple: he “creates art in order to express and communicate what he feels unable to convey in words, and his distinctive body of work has evolved through his ongoing search to identify what is uniquely his: his upbringing in rural northern Japan at a particular moment in time and, above all, his profound concern for humanity, including those outside mainstream society.”

The artist recently wrapped up a large-scale project at the Hirshorn Sculpture Garden, and next fall, the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art will host a major retrospective of his work. Until then, see Yoshitomo Nara through December 12 in New York.

issues.title: 20 New Artist Auction Records Set in November 2026
issues.summary: More than $2 billion worth of art has been auctioned off in New York this week during the annual marquee sale season. This was a week shaped by major collections, including those of philanthropist and Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) trustee Agnes Gund, artist Jeff Koons , and Argentine collectors Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and Carlos Pedro Blaquier, whose holdings of Impressionist and modern art were a
issues.author: Annabel Downes
issues.content_html:
More than $2 billion worth of art has been auctioned off in New York this week during the annual marquee sale season. This was a week shaped by major collections, including those of philanthropist and Museum of Modern Art (MoMA) trustee Agnes Gund, artist Jeff Koons, and Argentine collectors Nelly Arrieta de Blaquier and Carlos Pedro Blaquier, whose holdings of Impressionist and modern art were among the season’s biggest draws.

Christie’s 20th-century evening sale brought in $626.6 million with fees (all listed prices include fees), up from $471.7 million at its equivalent sale last November. The auction was led by Wassily Kandinsky’s Betonte Ecken (1922–23), which sold for $85.8 million and nearly doubled the artist’s previous auction record. Another star lot, Gustav Klimt’s Litzlbergkeller (1915–16), fetched $82.3 million, while Fernando Botero was among six artists to set new records that evening. The strong sale followed a banner Wednesday that saw the highest ever total for the Impressionist and Modern Art Day and Works on Paper sales at the auction house.


Sotheby’s, meanwhile, brought in $777.8 million across two back-to-back evening sales on Wednesday, its highest total for a single evening and surpassing the $706 million achieved during comparable sales last November. The first, “Legendary: The Blaquier-Arrieta Collection,” was a dedicated sale of 12 Impressionist works assembled by the Argentine couple, which realized $412 million. It was led by Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), which fetched $190.4 million, setting a new auction record for the artist and becoming the second-most-expensive work ever sold at Sotheby’s. The subsequent Modern Evening sale brought in $365.8 million, setting records for Mary Cassatt and Aaron Douglas. Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening Auction also produced a slew of auction records for artists including Tomma Abts and Jonas Wood.

Elsewhere, Phillips’s modern and contemporary evening sale brought in $104.4 million, up 55 percent year over year, led by Amedeo Modigliani’s Tête (1911), which fetched $44.6 million. Bonhams’ 20th- and 21st-century evening sale totaled $10 million, led by George Condo’s Big Face (2015) at $3.4 million, while a dedicated sale of five Constantin Brâncuși bronzes realized $15.1 million.

Major single-owner collections continue to power these marquee auctions, with exceptional works and strong provenance continuing to attract buyers despite uneven bidding across the wider market.

Here, we spotlight 20 artist records set during the season. All prices include fees.


Vincent van Gogh

Châtaigniers en fleurs, 1890

Sold for $190.4 million (Estimate: $180 million)

Sotheby’s

Painted just four days after Van Gogh’s arrival in Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, Châtaigniers en fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees) (1890) captures a sunlit village street lined with flowering chestnut trees. Three women carrying parasols gather beneath the trees, while a large house rises in the background. The painting belongs to the final, extraordinarily prolific months of the artist’s life, following his departure from a psychiatric hospital in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. He died in July 1890, just two months after arriving in Auvers.

Owned by the Blaquier-Arrieta family since 1975, the painting became the subject of a restitution claim shortly before the auction. Descendants of former owners Hedwig and Samuel Fischer alleged that it had been sold under duress during Nazi persecution in the 1930s. An undisclosed agreement between the heirs and the sellers allowed the sale to proceed.

At Sotheby’s New York this week, Châtaigniers en fleurs sold for $190.4 million, with veteran dealer William Acquavella winning the bidding. The result marked the fourth-highest price ever achieved for an artwork at auction, surpassing van Gogh’s previous record of $117.2 million, set by Verger avec cyprès (1888) from Paul Allen’s collection at Christie’s New York in 2022.

Wassily Kandinsky

Betonte Ecken, 1922–1923

Sold for $85.8 million (Estimate: $60 million–$80 million)

Christie’s

Kandinsky’s auction record has almost doubled in a single evening, thanks to the sale of Betonte Ecken (1922–23). The painting was consigned by the Nahmad family, prominent art dealers and collectors known for their extensive Pablo Picasso holdings and galleries in London and New York. The family acquired it for $1 million at Sotheby’s New York in 1986. It had previously sold at the same auction house in 1964 for $61,000. In 1929, it became the first known Kandinsky painting acquired by Hilla Rebay, the German artist and collector who later advised Solomon R. Guggenheim on building his collection of abstract art.

Kandinsky painted Betonte Ecken shortly after joining the Bauhaus in Weimar, Germany, in 1922, at the invitation of its founder, Walter Gropius. Measuring just over four feet square, the work marks his shift away from gestural abstraction towards sharply defined geometric forms, reflecting the influence of Suprematism and Constructivism. Its title, translated as “Accentuated corners,” refers to the intersecting lines and colorful shapes that draw attention to the painting’s four corners.

Betonte Ecken, which was backed by a guarantee, sold for $85.8 million at Christie’s New York, against an $80 million high estimate. The result surpassed Kandinsky’s previous auction record of $44.8 million, set by Murnau mit Kirche II (1910) at Sotheby’s London in 2023.


Sam Francis

Towards Disappearance I, 1958

Sold for $17.13 million (Estimate: $15 million–$20 million)

Sotheby’s

Painted in 1958 at his studio in Arcueil, France, Towards Disappearance I (1958) dates to one of the most celebrated periods of Sam Francis’s career. Spanning more than 10 feet in length, the monumental canvas is one of just seven works in the artist’s celebrated “Disappearance” series, three of which are held in major institutional collections, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Across an expansive white ground, clusters of Francis’s signature cobalt blue are punctuated by bursts of yellow and vermilion, reflecting the artist’s exploration of color, space, and the expressive possibilities of abstraction.

“When I paint, I try to create the feeling of being in it,” Francis remarked in 1956. Having begun painting in 1944, in his early twenties, Francis drew inspiration from Abstract Expressionists, particularly the organic forms and monumental scale of Clyfford Still’s canvases and restrained compositions of Mark Rothko. Though he never aligned himself with a single artistic movement, these influences were further shaped by his West Coast roots and his move to France.

Acquired by collectors Richard C. and Elizabeth Hedreen at Sotheby’s New York in 1999 for $3.41 million—then an artist record—Towards Disappearance I returned to Sotheby’s this week, selling for $17.1 million against a high estimate of $20 million. The result surpassed Francis’s previous record of $13.6 million, set by Composition in Blue and Black (1955) at Christie’s New York in 2022.


Yayoi Kusama

No. 3P.B., 1960

Sold for $15.1 million. (Estimate: $10 million–$15 million)

Sotheby’s

Just three months after Yayoi Kusama’s death at age 97, an early painting from her celebrated “Infinity Nets” series has set a new auction record for the Japanese artist. No. 3P.B. (1960) was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1961 annual exhibition, one of Kusama’s earliest institutional presentations in the United States.

Kusama began her “Infinity Nets” series in 1958, shortly after moving from Japan to New York. Inspired in part by the rippling sea she observed during her journey across the Pacific, the paintings feature repeated loops of paint extending across large canvases. No. 3P.B. is an early example, its dense crimson brushstrokes creating a network of overlapping forms. The repetition that defines the series would remain central to Kusama’s practice for more than six decades.

No. 3P.B. sold for $15.1 million at Sotheby’s New York, against a $15 million high estimate. The result surpassed Kusama’s previous auction record of $10.5 million, set by another early “Infinity Net” painting, Untitled (Nets) (1959), at Phillips New York in 2022.


Aaron Douglas

Harriet Tubman, 1931

Sold for $14.48 million (Estimate: $2.5 million–$3.5 million

Sotheby’s

Works by Douglas rarely appear at auction. Measuring six feet wide, his painting Harriet Tubman (1931) portrays the abolitionist who helped enslaved African Americans escape to freedom. Commissioned by philanthropist Alfred K. Stern for Bennett College in Greensboro, North Carolina, the painting spent the past two decades on loan to the North Carolina Museum of Art. The historically Black women’s college consigned the work, with proceeds set to support the institution’s future growth, including its Women’s Health Initiative, which aims to address healthcare disparities and advance health equity for women.

In the 1920s, Douglas moved from Kansas to New York, where he became a leading figure of the Harlem Renaissance. The painting depicts Tubman breaking a chain above a group of onlookers, in a composition reminiscent of Eugène Delacroix’s Liberty Leading the People (1830). Douglas described Tubman as “a heroic leader breaking the shackles of bondage and pressing on toward a new day.”

Harriet Tubman sold for $14.48 million, far exceeding its $3.5 million high estimate. The result shattered Douglas’s previous auction record of $600,000, set by Building More Stately Mansions (1944) at Swann Galleries New York in 2008.


Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem

Hercules and Achelous, 1590

Sold for $13.9 million (Estimate: $12 million–$18 million)

Christie’s

Nearly two decades after setting Cornelis Cornelisz van Haarlem’s auction record, Hercules and Achelous (1590) has broken its own record. Among the Dutch Mannerist painter’s largest and most ambitious works, the painting depicts Hercules wrestling the river god Achelous, a scene drawn from Book IX of Ovid’s Metamorphoses.

Born in Haarlem, the Netherlands, in 1562, Cornelis became one of the city’s leading painters, known for his dramatic compositions and muscular, contorted figures. By 1590, he had received some of Haarlem’s most prestigious commissions. The exceptional scale of Hercules and Achelous, painted on a canvas assembled from three pieces of fabric, suggests it was created for a specific patron rather than the open market. One possible early owner was Jacob Rauwart, among the wealthiest art collectors in late 16th-century Amsterdam.

The oil painting sold for $13.9 million at Christie’s 20th Century Evening Sale, against an $18 million high estimate. The result surpassed the artist’s previous auction record of $8.11 million, set by the same painting at Christie’s New York in 2008.

Wifredo Lam

Ogue Orisa (Eggue Orissa, l'herbe des dieux), 1943

Sold for $11.6 million (Estimate: $10 million–$15 million)

Christie’s

Painted following Wifredo Lam’s return to Cuba in 1941, Ogue Orisa (1943) reflects the artist’s growing engagement with his Afro-Caribbean heritage. Having encountered Surrealism through Picasso and André Breton in Paris, Lam developed a distinctive visual language combining European modernism with Afro-Cuban spirituality. In Ogue Orisa, a hybrid figure emerges among sugarcane stalks and tobacco leaves, its elongated body and doubled, mask-like head reflecting the artist’s exploration of metamorphosis and identity.

The painting was included in “Wifredo Lam: When I Don’t Sleep, I Dream,” which opened at MoMA in November 2025, where it was credited to prominent collectors Clarissa and Edgar Bronfman Jr. The retrospective was the first in the United States to survey the full trajectory of Lam’s career, highlighting his contributions to modernism and the influence of Afro-Caribbean culture on his practice.

The sellers purchased the work for $1.32 million at Sotheby’s New York in 1997. The painting returned to auction at Christie’s New York this week, selling for $11.6 million against a $15 million high estimate. The result surpassed Lam’s previous auction record of $9.6 million, achieved for OMI OBINI (1943) at Sotheby’s New York in 2020.


Jonas Wood

Japanese Garden with Moon and Stars, 2020

Sold for $6.32 million (Estimate: $3 million–$5 million)

Sotheby’s

Wood, who is based in Los Angeles, brings his signature flattened perspective and densely layered patterns to the traditional landscape genre in Japanese Garden with Moon and Stars (2020). The painting transforms the carefully cultivated terrain of a Japanese garden into an intricate arrangement of shapes, textures, and saturated colors beneath a star-speckled sky.

Best known for his depictions of domestic interiors, houseplants, and ceramics, Wood regularly exhibits with galleries including David Zwirner, Karma, and David Kordansky. Japanese Garden with Moon and Stars was acquired from Gagosian in 2020. The work sold for $6.83 million at Sotheby’s New York, exceeding its $5 million high estimate and narrowly surpassing Wood’s previous auction record of $6.51 million, set by Two Tables with Floral Pattern (2013) at Christie’s New York in May 2021.

Fernando Botero

Horse, 2006

Sold for $5.2 million. (Estimate: $3 million–$5 million)

Christie’s

While living in New York in the 1960s, Botero first turned his attention from painting to sculpture. “I wanted to do sculpture in bronze, but I really couldn’t afford it at that point,” he recalled. Following his move to Paris in 1973, growing international recognition enabled him to pursue the medium in earnest.

The Colombian artist became known for his distinctive, rounded figures, a signature style that extended across painting and sculpture. After decades of experimenting with equine forms, Botero created Horse (2006), combining exaggerated proportions with balance and monumentality. His fascination with horses stemmed from his childhood in Medellín, where they were integral to daily life. One of an edition of three, this particular sculpture made its public exhibition debut in 2007, when it was displayed prominently beneath Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate. In October, Opera Gallery presented the late artist’s first solo exhibition in London in over a decade.

At Christie’s this week, Horse (2006) sold for $5.2 million, narrowly surpassing Botero’s previous auction record of $5.1 million, achieved for his 1979 painting The Musicians at Christie’s New York in 2023, just two months after the artist’s death. The previous auction high for one of Botero’s bronze sculptures was $4.9 million, achieved for a different, marginally smaller sculpture also titled Horse (1992) at Sotheby’s New York in 2024.

Hans Bellmer

Jointure de boules (La Poupée), 1934-1936

Sold for $1.7 million (Estimate: $1.5 million–$2.5 million)

Christie’s

One of only two surviving original sculptural variants of Hans Bellmer’s celebrated doll constructions, Jointure de boules (La Poupée) (1934–36) is among the rarest works by the German Surrealist to appear at auction. Combining painting, sculpture, and assemblage, the unique relief belongs to the body of work that came to define Bellmer’s career. The other surviving sculptural variant is held in the collection of the Centre Pompidou in Paris.

Bellmer began creating his unsettling, fragmented dolls in Berlin in 1933, partly in response to the Nazis’ rise to power. Photographs of his first doll, published in his 1934 book La Poupée, caught the attention of André Breton and the Parisian Surrealists. At their invitation, Bellmer created Jointure de boules (La Poupée) for the landmark “Exposition surréaliste d’objets” at Galerie Charles Ratton in Paris in 1936, the first exhibition devoted to the Surrealist object.

Held in the same collection since 2000, the work sold for $1.7 million at Christie’s New York this week, against a high estimate of $2.5 million. It marked the first time a Bellmer work had surpassed $1 million at auction, exceeding his previous record of $942,000, achieved for the 1959 oil painting Les Bas rayés at Sotheby’s New York in 2025.

Firelei Báez

Encyclopedia of gestures (Jeu du monde), 2023

Sold for $1.32 million (Estimate: $600,000–$800,000)

Sotheby’s

Dominican-American artist Firelei Báez set a new auction record with Encyclopedia of gestures (Jeu du monde) (2023), a large-scale painting that draws on the history of European colonialism in the Caribbean. The work depicts a brightly colored, hybrid figure with feathered limbs and a flower-like head, painted over an enlarged section of Le Jeu du Monde, a geographical game published by French cartographer Pierre Du Val in 1645. The painting was included in Báez’s first European solo exhibition, “Trust Memory over History,” presented at the Louisiana Museum of Modern Art in Denmark and Kunstmuseum Wolfsburg in Germany between 2023 and 2024.

Born in the Dominican Republic in 1981 and now based in New York, Báez joined Hauser & Wirth’s roster in 2023. She has since held two exhibitions with the gallery, including a 2026 New York show during the city’s May art week.

Encyclopedia of gestures (Jeu du monde) sold for $1.32 million at Sotheby’s New York, exceeding its $800,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Báez’s previous auction record of $1.11 million, set by Untitled(Colonization in America, Visual History Wall Map, Prepared by Civic Education Service) (2021) at Christie’s New York in November 2025.

Jim Nutt

Loom, 1999

Sold for $1.1 million (Estimate $250,000–$350,000)

Christie’s

A painting that famed patron Agnes Gund once described as “my Mona Lisa” has set a new auction record for Chicago Imagist Jim Nutt. Loom (1999), a small-scale portrait of an anonymous woman with exaggerated facial features, was a highlight of the philanthropist and Museum of Modern Art trustee’s collection. Gund acquired the work from Chicago’s Karen Lennox Gallery in 2000.

A founding member of The Hairy Who, the Chicago artist collective that emerged in the 1960s, Nutt initially became known for his unconventional depictions of the human figure. By the late 1980s, he had turned his attention to portraits of women, often featuring distorted proportions and unusual facial features. Working with small brushes and thinned acrylic paint, Nutt can spend up to a year on a single painting. Loom was included in his 2011 retrospective, “Coming Into Character,” at the Museum of Contemporary Art Chicago.

Loom sold for $1.1 million at Christie’s New York, more than tripling its $350,000 high estimate. The result exceeded Nutt’s previous auction record of $966,094, set by Tooth at Bukowskis Stockholm in 2022. The painting was part of a sale of works from Gund’s collection benefiting the Gund Art Foundation, which realized $25.7 million in total.

Antonio Santín

Trampolín, 2025

Sold for $486,400 (Estimate: $100,000–$150,000)

Christie’s

Spanish artist Antonio Santín creates remarkably lifelike paintings of ornamental carpets entirely from oil paint. He applies tens of thousands of fine threads and dots using syringes powered by an air compressor, before shaping them with brushes and needles. His Trampolín (2025), a nearly 8-foot-tall painting in cobalt blue and ivory, captures the texture and folds of a woven rug in such detail that it could easily be mistaken for the real thing.

Trained as a sculptor in Madrid and Athens, Santín began painting carpets in 2011 after photographing a model concealed beneath a rug in her apartment. The experiment inspired a series of paintings in which carpets appear to bulge and fold, suggesting the presence of something underneath. In more recent works, including Trampolín, Santín has moved away from reproducing existing rugs and instead invents his own patterns. The artist is scheduled to present a solo exhibition with Marc Straus in New York in 2027.

Trampolín sold for $486,400 at Christie’s New York, more than tripling its $150,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Santín’s previous auction record of $324,000, set by Sonora (2022) at Sotheby’s in 2024.

Julia Jo

One Fell Swoop, 2026

Sold for $409,600 (Estimate: $30,000–$50,000)

Christie’s

Brooklyn-based artist Julia Jo’s new auction record came at the close of Christie’s evening auction. Her large-scale abstract painting One Fell Swoop (2026), created earlier this year, was the final lot of the sale. Measuring 70 square inches, the work was donated to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless, a New York nonprofit founded in 1981.

Born in Seoul in 1991, Jo grew up between South Korea and the United States before earning her MFA from Parsons in 2019. Her paintings begin with figures drawn directly in oil, often depicting moments of intimacy or conflict, which she gradually obscures beneath layers of color. In recent works, she has incorporated oil sticks and pastels, building compositions in which traces of the human body remain visible within the abstraction. Represented by Charles Moffett in New York and Ronchini in London, Jo was featured in Artsy’s 5 Artists on Our Radar in May 2025.

One Fell Swoop sold for $409,600 at Christie’s New York, more than eight times its $50,000 high estimate. The result topped Jo’s previous auction record of $203,200, set by Rhyme or Reason (2022) at Christie’s New York in 2025.

Tomma Abts

Hebo, 2013

Sold for $281,600 (Estimate: $180,000–$250,000)

Sotheby’s

German-born artist Abts has worked almost exclusively with the same small canvas dimensions, approximately 20 by 15 inches, since 1998. Hebo (2013) follows this format, combining scarlet, coral, and amber tones in a tightly composed geometric abstraction. The painting was included in the Turner Prize winner’s 2018–19 solo exhibition at the Art Institute of Chicago, her first solo museum exhibition of paintings in the United States in a decade.

Working without preparatory sketches, Abts builds her compositions intuitively, layering arcs, polygons, and stripes to create an illusion of depth and movement. Represented by David Zwirner since 2005, her work is held in major collections including MoMA and Tate.

Hebo sold for $281,600 at Sotheby’s New York, exceeding its $250,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Abts’s previous auction record of $278,671, set at Sotheby’s London in 2018.

Alvaro Barrington

Musician, beat of their own drum, 2021

Sold for $129,000 (Estimate: $40,000–$60,000)

Phillips

Multidisciplinary artist Alvaro Barrington has set a new auction record with Musician, beat of their own drum (2021), a work that reflects his interest in the connections between Caribbean culture, migration, and artistic expression. Born in Venezuela to Grenadian and Haitian parents and raised between the Caribbean and New York, Barrington draws on his upbringing to explore questions of identity, community, and belonging.

Although he considers himself primarily a painter, Barrington works across a range of media. Musician, beat of their own drum, for example, combines yarn, acrylic, locks, a drum, and chains on burlap, housed in a frame made by the artist. This fall, Barrington has also presented work with High Line Art in New York, alongside his first solo exhibition on the African continent at Limbo Museum in Accra, which runs through February 1, 2027. The exhibition features paintings, sculptures, and site-specific installations made in collaboration with local artisans and fabricators.

Musician, beat of their own drum sold for $129,000 at Phillips, more than doubling its $60,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Barrington’s previous auction record of $89,361, set by Black Power (2021) at Christie’s London in 2025.

Irene Rice Pereira

Painting in Three Planes, 1945

Sold for $128,000 (Estimate: $20,000–$30,000)

Sotheby’s

American abstract artist Irene Rice Pereira set a new auction record with Painting in Three Planes (1945), a box assemblage made with oil and porcelain fluid on glass and Masonite. The work was offered from the collection of Vicki and David Cox in Sotheby’s Modern Day Auction in New York.

Born in Massachusetts in 1902, Pereira studied at the Art Students League in New York, where she was introduced to Cubism and Constructivism. A leading advocate of Bauhaus ideas in the United States, she helped establish the Design Laboratory in 1935, a school that encouraged experimentation with industrial materials and modern design. By the late 1930s, she had turned toward geometric abstraction, incorporating glass, plastic, and metallic pigments to explore the effects of light and transparency. She later worked at the Museum of Non-Objective Painting (now the Guggenheim Museum) as a museum assistant, and participated in Peggy Guggenheim’s landmark “31 Women” exhibition in 1943.

Painting in Three Planes sold for $128,000 at Sotheby’s New York, more than four times its $30,000 high estimate. The result topped Pereira’s previous auction record of $100,000, set by Untitled (Squares) (1944) at Capsule Gallery Auction in New York in 2021.

Sofía Bassi

Quijote triunfante, 1973

Sold for $121,600 (Estimate: $25,000–$35,000)

Sotheby’s

Mexican Surrealist Sofía Bassi’s new auction record came with Quijote triunfante (1973), amid growing interest in her work. The result follows her first European solo exhibition, “Floating Between Earth and Sky,” at Pippy Houldsworth Gallery in London, which ran through November 14. The exhibition introduced European audiences to an artist who, despite her associations with fellow Mexican Surrealists Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo, has remained relatively little known outside her home country.

Born in 1913, Bassi began painting in her fifties. Her work took a darker turn during her imprisonment in Acapulco between 1968 and 1972, after she pleaded guilty to the murder of her son-in-law. Interest in her work has also grown in Mexico this year, with Mexico City’s Georgina Pounds Gallery mounting a major exhibition of her paintings in the spring.

Quijote triunfante sold for $121,600 at Sotheby’s New York, more than tripling its $35,000 high estimate. The result surpassed Bassi’s previous auction record of 800,000 Mexican pesos (approximately $46,000), set by Muñeca Reina (1974) at Morton Subastas in Mexico in May 2026.

Marc Sijan

Seated Security Guard, 2007

Sold for (Estimate: $15,000–$20,000)

Bonhams

Serbian-American sculptor Marc Sijan is known for his hyperrealistic depictions of everyday people. Seated Security Guard (2007) is part of a series of lifelike figures that have frequently commanded some of his highest prices at auction. The sculpture was acquired directly from the artist in 2008.

Born in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in 1946 to a family of Serbian descent, Sijan creates his sculptures using plaster molds taken from live models, which he casts in polyester resin. He then applies layers of oil paint and varnish to reproduce the appearance of human skin, paying close attention to details such as wrinkles, veins, and facial expressions. His work is held in collections including the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and the Milwaukee Art Museum.

The 56-inch-tall sculpture sold for $108,200 at Bonhams, more than five times its $20,000 high estimate. The result broke Sijan’s previous auction record of $69,850, set by Standing Security Guard (2013) at Phillips New York in 2025. While his security guard sculptures have fetched his highest prices at auction, figures depicting butlers and bathers have also featured among his top sales.

Hugo McCloud

Untitled, 2014

Sold for $92,880 (Estimate: $30,000–$40,000)

Bonhams

Brooklyn-based artist Hugo McCloud is known for creating large-scale abstract paintings using unconventional industrial materials. His To Be Titled (2014) is made from aluminum foil, aluminum coating, and oil on tar paper.

Born in Palo Alto, California, in 1980, McCloud is self-taught and has a background in industrial design. His practice explores themes of labor, class, and the relationship between people and their surroundings, incorporating materials ranging from tar and metal to discarded plastic bags. Represented by Sean Kelly in New York, McCloud currently has a solo exhibition, “to everything there is a season,” at the Memorial Art Gallery in Rochester, New York, on view through January 3, 2027.

To Be Titled sold for $92,880 at Phillips’s Modern & Contemporary Art auction, more than doubling its $40,000 high estimate. The result broke McCloud’s previous auction record of $77,400, set by Untitled (2015) at Phillips in New York in 2026.

issues.title: The 5 Best Booths at Frieze Abu Dhabi 2026
issues.summary: Against a backdrop of uncertainty in the Middle East—particularly surrounding the volatile Iran conflict—the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi opened with a noticeably robust security presence. issues.author: Arun Kakar
issues.content_html:
Against a backdrop of uncertainty in the Middle East—particularly surrounding the volatile Iran conflict—the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi opened with a noticeably robust security presence. Inside the art fair venue, Manarat Al Saadiyat, however, the mood was decidedly upbeat. Collectors, curators, and art enthusiasts filled the aisles during the VIP preview, bringing a lively energy to a fair making a defiant debut at a complicated moment for the region.

Taking place from November 19th to 22nd, the fair marks a new chapter for Abu Dhabi’s art scene. Frieze announced late last year that it would take over Abu Dhabi Art, which launched in 2009 and, over 17 editions, grew into one of the region’s leading art fairs. Now organized in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism, the event brings together 89 exhibitors from 37 countries, combining international heavyweights with established and emerging galleries from across the Middle East, North Africa, and South Asia. It is a noticeably smaller affair than last year’s Abu Dhabi Art, which featured 142 galleries, suggesting a more tightly focused approach under Frieze’s stewardship.

Its arrival comes at a particularly crowded point in the international art calendar. Frieze London and Art Basel Paris in October were followed by major fairs in cities from Turin, to Mumbai, to Shanghai, to Tokyo. In that context, the pressure is on for fairs to offer something genuinely distinctive.

“We have so many fairs around the world. The fair calendar is just unbelievable,” art advisor Diane Abela told Artsy. “The aim, I think, of Frieze Abu Dhabi is to create a unique platform and a unique fair.”

And there is a sense that the timing is right for Abu Dhabi. The cultural ambitions that have been taking shape on Saadiyat Island—where the fair is based—for years are increasingly coming to fruition. The Louvre Abu Dhabi, which opened in 2017, has since been joined by the Zayed National Museum, the Natural History Museum Abu Dhabi, and teamLab Phenomena, while the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi is scheduled to open on December 11th. What was once a bold vision for a cultural district is now, quite literally, taking shape in stone, steel, and glass.

For Frieze, the challenge is to make the most of this momentum while carving out a place in an already packed calendar. Judging by the energy of its opening day, it has made a promising start.

Here are five standout booths from the inaugural edition of Frieze Abu Dhabi.

Taymour Grahne Projects

Booth G1

With works by Ala Younis

Dubai-based Taymour Grahne Projects’ intimate solo booth of works by Jordanian artist Ala Younis was among the busiest at the fair during its opening hours. Featured in the curated Global Futures section dedicated to artists that engage with the histories of the U.A.E., the presentation comprises intricate mosaics from Younis’s ongoing “Climate Conditions” series. These works pay tribute to Abu Dhabi’s modernist apartment blocks and office buildings from the 1970s and ’80s, and visitors could be seen pointing to individual works, recognizing the buildings depicted in them.

Trained as an architect, Younis lived in Abu Dhabi for several years and became fascinated by how these buildings were designed to withstand the region’s extreme climate. Works depict tiled façades, recessed windows, and shaded balconies, and are painstakingly composed of hand-cut stone mosaics. It’s a tactile and poignant way to depict these otherwise unassuming structures, preserving a part of the city’s architectural history amid its rapid development.

As gallery founder Taymour Grahne explained, mosaic is “a way to sort of monumentalize these older buildings in the city of Abu Dhabi,” using a medium that can endure for centuries.

The works are offered in editions of two, priced at $18,000 each, with an additional artist’s proof. Grahne reported strong sales during the fair’s opening, with first editions selling out and second editions also finding buyers, which included several U.A.E.-based collectors.

Galerist

Booth B4

With works by Semiha Berksoy, İpek Duben, Elif Uras, and Margaret R. Thompson

Istanbul’s Galerist brings together four generations of women artists for a vibrant presentation exploring identity, memory, and self-representation. Framed by striking terra-cotta red walls, the booth reflects the gallery’s 25th-anniversary exhibition program, which has been dedicated entirely to solo presentations by women artists.

At its center is Margaret R. Thompson’s large triptych Firmament’s Gate (2026), a richly layered composition incorporating oil paint, earth, mica, volcanic rock dust, and turmeric. Gallery director Müge Tümen Çubukçu explained that the New Mexico–based artist developed the work for an exhibition in Istanbul, where she drew inspiration from the city’s layered history, collecting water from the Bosphorus and spices from local markets as part of her research. The resulting composition is filled with swirling, otherworldly forms that evoke spirituality and the unconscious.

Nearby, sculptural ceramic vessels by Turkish artist Elif Uras draw on ancient Mesopotamian tear bottles, traditionally associated with women mourning absent or deceased husbands. Their intricate, mottled surfaces reflect the artist’s longstanding engagement with decorative traditions and what Çubukçu described as “the idea of invisible female labor in society.”

The presentation also features works by two pioneering Turkish artists. A triptych of İpek Duben’s “Şerife” paintings depicts headless, figureless garments that explore women’s social status and repression, alongside 1980s self-portraits. Meanwhile, celebrated late opera singer and painter Semiha Berksoy is represented by three works spanning more than four decades, including the expressive portraits Behice Siyavuşoğlu (1957) and Hayrünissa Binzet (1960). Works across the booth are priced between €10,000 ($10,992) and €400,000 ($439,704).
