issues.author: David Brown
issues.content_html: For many people a trip to the zoo is an opportunity to see favorite animals like gorillas, giraffes and lions. But in Alburquerque, New Mexico, U.S., visitors can add spiders, scorpions and ants to their must-see list at the ABQ BioPark BUGarium. The facility also includes an aquarium, traditional zoo and botanic garden. The BUGarium was closed for a year and reopened in October 2026 following a $1.45 million renovation. Insects are the largest group of animals on Earth, and ecologically essential as pollinators and the base of many food chains. Famed entomologist E.O. Wilson once said: “If we were to wipe out insects alone — just that group alone — on this planet, which we are trying hard to do, the rest of life and humanity with it would mostly disappear from the land. And within a few months.” The BUGarium exists to educate the public about the importance of insects. “Whether they’re pollinating plants, recycling nutrients, controlling pests, or supporting entire food webs, these animals are essential to healthy ecosystems,” said ABQ BioPark Associate Director Matthew Peterson in a statement. Bugs are not always an easy sell. “Guests come to the BUGarium with a wide spectrum of attitudes ranging from disgust and horror to fascination and awe,” Alexandra Miller, the curator of entomology at the ABQ BioPark told Mongabay in an email. “We hope guests learn how important arthropods are to ecosystems around the world, what they can do to support native populations, and that arthropods require specialized care…This article was originally published on Mongabay

issues.title: Philippine corn farmers investigate links between chemical farming and soil erosion
issues.summary: LAKE SEBU, Philippines — To the untrained eye, a handful of soil might appear to be a monotone brown. But to farmer Welna Sumulde, who grew up among generations of Indigenous T’boli farmers on the Philippines island of Mindanao, the slightest change in the color of the soil is a whisper from the land, a […]
issues.author: Geela Garcia
issues.content_html: LAKE SEBU, Philippines — To the untrained eye, a handful of soil might appear to be a monotone brown. But to farmer Welna Sumulde, who grew up among generations of Indigenous T’boli farmers on the Philippines island of Mindanao, the slightest change in the color of the soil is a whisper from the land, a warning of its degradation. “Around 2023, we observed changes in our soil. The color became lighter, the leaves looked different, and the cassava we harvest became smaller. We also observed fewer living organisms on our soil,” Samulde told Mongabay. Samulde and other farmers in her community also thought changes in the soil might hold answers to a troubling puzzle: Why do fish keep dying in nearby Lake Sebu, a lake that lies in the natural basin below their upland farms? They said they began to suspect that soil erosion from surrounding corn farms was speeding up siltation in the lake — and that changes in farming practices were accelerating erosion. With the help of NGOs and scientists, the farmers were able to test this hypothesis. MASIPAG Mindanao coordinator Leo XL Fuentes, in yellow, conducts a soil test alongside farmers of the Lem Bulul Farmers Association. The farmers are comparing soil fertility and pH between traditional and chemical corn farms. Image by Geela Garcia for Mongabay. issues.title: Indigenous protesters board soy and oil barges on Brazilian Amazon river
issues.summary: Hundreds of Indigenous protesters on several small boats and canoes stopped and boarded barges carrying soybeans and fuel on Brazil’s Tapajós River in the eastern Amazon. The demonstrations on Nov. 14 and 15 were to demand protection for the river amid industrial expansion and legal recognition of Indigenous territories in the region. The two-day demonstration […]
issues.author: Shanna Hanbury
issues.content_html: Hundreds of Indigenous protesters on several small boats and canoes stopped and boarded barges carrying soybeans and fuel on Brazil’s Tapajós River in the eastern Amazon. The demonstrations on Nov. 14 and 15 were to demand protection for the river amid industrial expansion and legal recognition of Indigenous territories in the region. The two-day demonstration near Santarém, in Pará state, drew more than 650 protesters. “Our children need this river, just as we need this river,” Jackson Tapajós, executive secretary of the Tupinambá Indigenous Council who participated in the protest, told Mongabay by phone. Smoke in the air from nearby forest fires was so thick that protesters could not see the barges approach until they were close, he said. Indigenous women negotiated with armed security guards after approaching the fuel barge on Nov. 14, explaining that the group was peacefully protesting. The guards allowed them to board but stayed with them, Tapajós told Mongabay. “We managed to talk to some of these guards … but they were by our side the whole time, the whole time with their guns, so that creates a lot of tension,” Tapajós said. The Tapajós River is an export artery for the region, carrying large amounts of soybeans and corn from Brazil’s agricultural heartland to ports on the Amazon River, which ultimately connect to international trade routes via the Atlantic. According to the Ministry of Ports and Airports, 16.8 million metric tons of cargo was moved through the waterway in 2025, up 14.3% from 2024.…This article was originally published on Mongabay

issues.title: It’s time to put Africa’s forest communities on the map (commentary)
issues.summary: The U.N. General Assembly’s recent adoption of a new standard world map, more accurately reflecting the true size of Africa than depicted in the Eurocentric 16th-century Mercator projection, is great news and a welcome reminder that multilateralism isn’t dead yet. It also doesn’t tell the whole story. We’re not talking about how the continent was […]
issues.author: Georges Thierry HandjaJoe Eisen
issues.content_html: The U.N. General Assembly’s recent adoption of a new standard world map, more accurately reflecting the true size of Africa than depicted in the Eurocentric 16th-century Mercator projection, is great news and a welcome reminder that multilateralism isn’t dead yet. It also doesn’t tell the whole story. We’re not talking about how the continent was carved up between the former colonial powers through such events as the Berlin conference of 1884-1885, though the social, economic and political impacts of the often straight and artificial lines drawn on those maps are still felt today. No, we’re talking about how maps of Central African states are still used by foreign interests and political elites as tools to perpetuate power — with control of natural resources and the benefits they generate tending to flow outwards and upwards — rather than to the people living in these areas. Resource map of the Congo Basin. Graphic courtesy of Earth Insight. Today, much of the Congo Basin, the world’s second largest rainforest, resembles a patchwork of extractive industry concessions, strictly protected areas and an ever-increasing array of carbon offset projects which our organization has documented. These have largely failed to stem deforestation and biodiversity loss, while delivering few or no benefits to local populations, and in many cases, causing severe impacts on human rights and food security. issues.title: Unanswered questions linger after on-field CSU football incidents
issues.summary: There are unanswered questions for Colorado State after a couple of on-field incidents with the football team this season.
issues.content_html:
As Colorado State's 2026 football season nears a conclusion, there are unanswered questions around the program.

A couple of notable incidents have occurred during the season without clear final resolutions.

In an Oct. 3 game against Oregon State, CSU coach Jim Mora took play-calling duties away from defensive coordinator Tyson Summers. Mora then says Summers left the sideline and Summers was fired after the game.

It's unclear if Summers is still being paid by CSU or if there was a buyout payment. The Coloradoan submitted an open records request in November for resignation settlements and nondisclosure agreements at the university, but none for Summers were found. A Coloradoan request for comment sent to CSU the morning of Nov. 20 for information on potential payment agreements with Summers had not been answered as of 2 p.m. He is not listed on CSU's online compensation report.

Another incident took place Nov. 7 during Boise State's 64-38 win over the Rams.

Reporter Jon Tritsch of 9News posted a video showing CSU offensive lineman Toriyan Johnson and strength and conditioning coach Shelton Bynum in an altercation.

Colorado State football is at a place where the care level is high but so is the tension… and may have reached a tipping point.
It is heated before halftime with Boise State up 29-10.#CSURamspic.twitter.com/ecw52KdCNc

— Jon Tritsch (@hometownJT) November 8, 2026

Mora addressed the incident on Nov. 9 in a regularly scheduled press conference.

"I looked at it and I didn’t like it. I didn’t like what I saw. I understood it, but I still don’t like it. It’s not what we are going to be as a program. I will say this, as I said Saturday night, it’s a passionate game, it’s an intense game. It’s a lot of alphas playing it, but that doesn’t excuse the behavior," Mora said. "Those two guys have worked together now for four years and are very, very close. So, we’ve addressed it internally and everyone understands that’s not how we’re going to represent CSU and CSU football at all. It’s just not acceptable."

It is unclear what Bynum's role with the team currently is. He is currently still listed on CSU's football staff page. The Coloradoan asked about his status with the team but was not provided an answer.

"The university generally does not comment on individual personnel matters," a statement from CSU Senior Director of Strategic Communications and Storytelling Ryan Pfeifer said in reply to a Coloradoan request for comment on Bynum's status with the program. Bynum declined to comment when reached by phone.

Bynum joined Mora at CSU after Mora was hired away from UConn. Bynum spent the previous four seasons on staff at UConn, where Johnson previously played as well.

CSU plays at Fresno State at 5:30 p.m. Mountain on Nov. 21. The Rams finish the season Nov. 28 at home against an opponent to be announced for the Pac-12's flex week.

CSU is 3-7 in Mora's first year with the Rams and has lost seven of its last eight games.

Sports reporter Kevin Lytle can be found on social media on X, Instagram and Threads@Kevin_Lytle and on Bluesky.

issues.title: 'I just have to reiterate the power that we have as riders' - Lombardia protest ringleader Ben Healy emboldened as he calls for change on rider safety
issues.summary: The Irishman was the driving force behind the Il Lombardia protest
issues.author: Owen Rogers
issues.content_html:
The five minute delay before the start of Il Lombardia at the close of the European season demonstrated the power riders have in forcing better safety in races, according to Ben Healy (EF Education-EasyPost).

Rider safety has been the hottest topic in road cycling since the terrible death of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal in the summer. And when that incident was followed by a series of further near-misses during the Italian autumn Classics, something had to give.

Healy was the driving force behind what he calls a 'stand' rather than a protest, the peloton delaying the start of Il Lombardia, the season’s final Monument, by five minutes. But, as powerful as the delay was, and as hard hitting and articulate as Remco Evenepoel’s (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) words were, the demonstration was an example of the power riders have.

"I think we just really wanted to show as riders the power that we had, and that we're not happy," he told Cyclingnews in a café close to the bustle of the Rouleur Live show, where he was fulfilling sponsor commitments.

"We didn't want to just go at the Lombardia organisers, for instance. You know that's why we chose to do a five-minute stand before the race actually started, and just delay the race, and just show that if this continues, that this is what we can do if we choose to."

After the shock of Tarling’s death, a meeting of the UCI’s Professional Cycling Council addressed some safety issues, while calls and ideas came from all angles. But the incidents at the autumn Classics, including when a police motorbike rode head-on toward the peloton at Tre Valli Varesine, aggravated what was already an active talking point, and some sort of rider action was all but inevitable.

"I think after that happened [with Tarling] everyone expected something to change, you know, and when we went to Italy, there were what, three cars on the course in separate races over three or four days? And that was pretty clear then that nothing had changed," Healy said.

"There has to be a process to make things safer. And I mean, for sure, the UCI is aware of it, but I don't know how aware they are, they’re not on the ground every single race. This is clearly something that is recurring, and it just shouldn't happen ever, having a car on the course, let's just hope the UCI will listen and work with us to make change."

If Lombardia was the example of what unity within the peloton can do in bringing an issue to notice, Healy prefers not to commit to what might happen if and when such a dangerous situation occurs again, or worse, should another rider die.

"I just really hope it doesn't come to that, you know? I just have to reiterate the power that we have as riders and ultimately what we can do if we choose to.

"Mistakes can be made, and as long as we're working towards making racing safer, I think that's the most important thing. We don't want to point blame or, like, kick and scream, it’s about being productive and working together to improve the sport for everyone."

issues.title: Shirin van Anrooij to make cyclo-cross debut with Canyon-SRAM alongside Zoe Backstedt next week
issues.summary: Dutch rider preparing with Briton in Spain for next round of the UCI World Cup in Czechia on Friday
issues.author: Laura Weislo
issues.content_html:
Shirin van Anrooij will make her debut with Canyon-SRAM in the upcoming UCI Cyclo-cross World Cup in Ostrava, Czechia, next week, racing alongside Zoe Bäckstedt at the start of a 13-race schedule, the team announced on Friday.

Van Anrooij, a former under-23 and junior cyclo-cross world champion, forged a special agreement with Lidl-Trek to end her contract two months early to join Canyon-SRAM for the off-road season.

She has been training in Malaga, Spain alongside her new teammate and former under-23 cyclo-cross rival Bäckstedt in preparation for the intensive campaign of 11 World Cups, the National Championships and culminating with the World Championships in Oostende, Belgium in January.

"I'm just really excited and looking forward to starting the season because we've been watching CX racing on TV for a couple of weeks now, and I'm really curious to see how it is amongst the girls again," Van Anrooij said in the team press release.

"I think Zoe and I are having a good preparation camp here in Malaga, so I can't wait to be on the start line myself, and to see where my level is at."

Van Anrooij was forced to sit out the 2024-2025 cyclo-cross season after undergoing surgery for iliac artery endofibrosis. She returned to the dirt in November last year, completing 13 races and landing on two World Cup podiums.

"I'm hoping that I'll reach my best level in cyclo-cross again, and then I'll just have to discover what results this will bring me," Van Anrooij said.

"I think the biggest goals are, for sure, the Christmas period with a lot of races that I really like – Koksijde, Zonhoven, Gavere, and then the World Championships in Oostende. Worlds is always a big goal for everyone, but I especially look forward to that, with it being a race on the sand in Belgium."

After her first year racing in the elite fields last season, with nine races from the end of December through Worlds, Bäckstedt is looking forward to a longer campaign. "I'm really excited for this cyclo-cross season. It feels like it's been two years since I properly raced CX as last year was an extremely short season for me.

"It's super fun having Shirin as my teammate. Already for training, it's been really beneficial for me to follow her and learn from her. I'm now excited to do our first race together."

Although both riders have goals for the early part of the 2027 road season, Canyon-SRAM's performance director Dan Fleeman supports their off-road ambitions.

"I think cyclo-cross offers several important benefits. From a physical perspective, it develops the ability to repeatedly produce high-intensity efforts, accelerate out of corners, change pace and deal with constantly changing demands. It also requires a high level of anaerobic capacity and the ability to recover quickly between efforts.

"Technically, the benefits are equally important. CX develops bike handling, balance, coordination and the ability to make decisions under pressure. Riders are constantly adapting to different terrain and conditions, managing their effort and finding the quickest way through a course.

"Also, I think that there is a mental benefit. CX is an incredibly demanding discipline where you have to be prepared to push yourself outside your comfort zone, deal with mistakes, and keep fighting throughout a race."

Their calendar has been designed to focus only on the major races, skipping the Superprestige, X2O Trofee, and HG Cross.

"The main consideration is quality over quantity. The World Cup offers the highest level of competition, the best opportunities to measure ourselves against the world's leading riders, and the experience of racing on some of the biggest stages in cyclo-cross.

"We also have to consider the overall demands of the season. Both riders have important road objectives, so we don't want to overload the programme with racing simply for the sake of racing. We would rather be selective, target the important events, and make sure that they arrive at them in good physical condition."

issues.title: From plumbing to Picnic PostNL – The Dutch team's newest recruit with dreams of Amstel Gold Race and riding with Wout van Aert
issues.summary: 23-year-old Tour de Limousin stage winner Daan Depuydt is Dutch squad's ninth signing of the 2027 season
issues.author: Dani Ostanek
issues.content_html:
The lowest-ranked team in the WorldTour last year, Picnic PostNL, have made plenty of changes to their roster next season, with nine new faces and counting.

Joining the Dutch team in their quest for more success in 2027 is Belgian racer Daan Depuydt, who comes on board from Continental squad Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions.

The 23-year-old, who previously raced at amateur level, enjoyed several standout rides this year, including a Tour de Limousin stage win and three top-10 finishes at the Tour de Wallonie. His rise to the WorldTour has been a rapid one, given he was working as a plumber just a few years ago.

Depuydt, who also did odd jobs as a gardener and electrician, told Sporza that, "Actually, I was never really consciously focused on landing a professional contract. I just raced because I enjoyed it."

He primarily raced on the mountain bike as a junior, picking up four Belgian titles before struggling with back injuries. On the road, he raced in Belgium with amateur squad VP Consulting before catching the eye of Baloise-Het Poetsbureau – Sven Nys' team – with a stage win at the Triptyque Ardennais in 2025.

He hit the ground running this year, with June's Tour de Wallonie only the second UCI-ranked race of his career after the Antwerp Port Epic in May.

"I was riding there with broken ribs, because I had a bad fall 2 days before the opening stage," he told Sporza. In August, there was another top ride in Limousin, where he finished second on the opening day before winning stage 3.

"After my second place in the opening stage, I wanted to win one of the remaining 3 stages at all costs. And in the third stage, I struck gold," he said.

"After the opening stage, I suddenly started receiving messages from teams. But I never thought I'd actually secure a spot – especially after reading an article about how many riders were still without a team for the season."

Soudal-QuickStep were among the teams to show interest, though they were already full for 2027. Choosing Picnic PostNL was a no-brainer, he said, despite recent reports of a 'culture of fear' at the team.

"When the moment finally came to put pen to paper with Picnic PostNL, I didn’t have to think twice. I had a good feeling right from the start of our conversations. They prioritise the riders' interests and are always open to feedback," he said.

"Sure, it’s a strict team, but name me one WorldTour team that isn't. As a team, you have expectations of your riders, and vice versa. That dynamic can – and should – be a bit strict, provided it’s handled fairly."

Depuydt sees himself as a puncheur who excels on shorter climbs while also sprinting well from a small group. He's hoping to race on his home training roads at Amstel Gold Race next season, and is dreaming of racing alongside his idol, Wout van Aert – a goal which shows just how far he's come since his plumbing days.

"I see myself as a puncheur. Short climbs suit me thanks to my past as a mountain biker. But I have also noticed this year that I am fast. I am not a pure sprinter; I am too light for that. But after a tough race, I can finish well in a reduced group," he said.

"I've never ridden a race with Wout. I would think it's really cool if that happens next year. If we stand at the start of a race together, I will look for Wout and ride behind him for a bit to take a look at him.

"If I could just follow him for a little while on a climb, that would be a huge dream come true."

issues.title: WorldTour team ignored by new Collective Cycling Group reform project
issues.summary: Question marks raised over inclusivity of the coalition as Human Powered Health weren't even approached to join new bid to reshape pro cycling's economics
issues.author: Patrick Fletcher
issues.content_html:
The nascent Collective Cycling Group (CCG), a coalition of teams bidding to overhaul cycling’s economic model, did not seek the involvement of all the WorldTour teams, with Human Powered Health telling Cyclingnews they were ignored by the project.

The CCG, which is the new version of the failed One Cycling movement, launched publicly on Wednesday, with 24 teams coming together in a bid to "unlock the value potential of professional cycling".

Not all 32 teams from across the men’s and women’s WorldTour agreed to sign up to the new company, with Tadej Pogačar’s UAE Team Emirates the most notable of the teams who have declined to be involved.

However, one WorldTour team, Human Powered Health, were not even approached.

A spokesperson for the US outfit, which has operated in the Women’s WorldTour since 2022, told Cyclingnews that senior management were not made aware of the CCG nor of any opportunity to take part in such a project.

The complete overlooking of an established WorldTour team raises early question marks over the unity of the CCG, which was described by its CEO Oliver Ciesla as a “broad and inclusive initiative”.

Furthermore, it was not billed as a closed shop, with the announcement stating that discussions with other teams are ongoing.

The project is largely made up of WorldTour teams but two second-division men’s outfits, Pinarello-Q36.5 and Tudor Pro Cycling are shareholders in the company, too.

Contacted on Friday in relation to Human Powered Health's position, a spokesperson for the Collective Cycling Group said: "CCG has brought together a significant group of leading professional cycling teams, and we are open for that group to grow over time."

He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performanc
issues.author: Sam Cunningham
issues.content_html:
The 30-year-old former England star combines Twitch streaming with working to return to the top as a player

Consider the training regime Dele Alli has followed since he left Como 18 months ago and it becomes clear why he takes exception to suggestions he has given up on football in favour of becoming an internet personality.

He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach who has worked with players including Trevoh Chalobah. They spend four days on the pitch and days in between in the gym. A typical day begins at 9am with an hour of activation and stretching before Dele heads to non-league Windsor & Eton at 11am, where he trains on the pitches and uses the facilities. Then it’s back home to use his own oxygen chamber and sauna for a recovery session.
