issues.title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
issues.summary: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn't stay private.
issues.author: Dan Goodin
issues.content_html:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of AWS access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

issues.title: Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded
issues.summary: A recent brightening turned out to be from a star orbiting inside another.
issues.author: Jacek Krywko
issues.content_html:
In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act.

In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it's really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.”

Shared envelopes

Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges.

issues.content_html:
SpaceX's successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA's path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.

For SpaceX's purposes, Saturday's mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX's deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon.

Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX's existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship.

issues.title: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.
issues.summary: CTIA said jamming test showed "interference... up to two and a half miles away."
issues.author: Jon Brodkin
issues.content_html:
The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.

Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:

The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.

CTIA said the pilot test shows "that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications."

issues.title: Plastic Propaganda: How Industry Turns School Kids into Plastic Consumers
issues.summary: Our new report found that the plastic industry influences schools in the very same communities it pollutes. The post Plastic Propaganda: How Industry Turns School Kids into Plastic Consumers appeared first on The Revelator .
issues.author: Madison Dennis
issues.content_html:
Reduce, Reuse, Recycle. This mantra was taught, chanted, sung, and posted across our childhoods, teaching us that to save the planet — and avoid being “litterbugs” — we just had to put our plastic waste in the little blue bin. Why worry about plastic pollution when we have recycling? Just do your part, we were taught, and the problem will go away.

We didn’t know such a simple fix was too good to be true.

Flash forward, and today it’s abundantly clear that plastic pollution is an urgent global crisis — and, spoiler, recycling can’t fix it. After all, only 9% of all plastics ever created have been recycled.

So how did we get here?

It turns out the plastic industry has been pulling the strings on our perception of plastic for decades, and children and teens are among their prime targets. Alarmingly, their marketing doesn’t stop with the ads we see online or hear on TV and radio. A new report from our organization, Plastic Pollution Coalition, uncovers how the plastic industry — including some of the largest fossil fuel, petrochemical, and plastic producers in the world — is influencing K-12 public education to create a positive view of plastic, ensuring future profits.

Plastic producers have known since plastics were first mass-produced in the 1940s and 1950s that plastics accumulate in the environment and cannot be recycled efficiently or at any meaningful scale. Since the 1970s industry executives have known that microplastics could infiltrate the human body; plastic pollutes people and the environment and can have terrifying health consequences.

The real solution is simple: Stop making so much plastic.

Yet the interconnected plastics, fossil fuel, and petrochemical industries have poured millions of dollars into ads and public relations campaigns that pushed the convenience and necessity of plastic, misled the public on the effectiveness of plastic recycling, and blamed individuals for the pollution they themselves created.

By their own admission, these materials constitute “propaganda.”

“It is propaganda but the resource management messages are important,” said Jean Salter, former vice of president of communications at American Plastics Council, when discussing a video depicting a pyrolysis (“chemical recycling”) plant.

Industry propaganda goes back decades.

“People start pollution, people can stop it,” said the infamous Keep America Beautiful “Crying Indian” public service announcement of the 1970s. Keep America Beautiful — formed by packaging and beverage industry giants with current members including Coca-Cola, Dow, and Marlboro — also popularized the term “litterbug.”

And take the Society of Plastics Engineers, an association of professionals in the plastics industry launched in 1919. In the United States their foundation runs educational programming with the mission of “changing the perception of plastics one classroom at a time.” For example, their “Wonders of Plastics” essay contest, an initiative of local SPE sections, asks students to write about topics such as “How Plastics Benefit Humankind,” “Myths about the Bad Reputation of Plastics,” and “What Plastics Have Done for Me.”

One of their key educational programs is PlastiVan. This trademarked program brings plastic-themed activities schools across the country to “spark scientific curiosity in students while increasing their knowledge of the contribution plastics make to modern life; encouraging them to seek careers in engineering.” Since 2014 the Society of Plastics Engineers reports that PlastiVan has reached over 140,000 students and was present in 68 cities in 2025 alone.

This propaganda would be bad enough, but alarmingly, we found that many of the schools reportedly targeted by the plastic industry’s education efforts are in communities where plastic facilities are already present, polluting both young minds and young bodies.

In Beaver County, Pennsylvania, the Shell Polymers Monaca — a massive ethane “cracker” and polyethylene production facility — has received more than 60 violations for illegal levels of air and water pollution since its construction began in 2017. Meanwhile Shell funded programs at six nearby elementary schools to “help enable the circular economy by demonstrating the importance of recycling.” Shell even bought a new basketball court for one of the schools as a “prize” for learning the “right way to recycle.”

By incentivizing educators to distribute their materials, the plastic industry peddles deceptive messages aimed at building future consumers and workers, ensuring support for local facilities, and curbing meaningful policy interventions. This propaganda playbook, borrowed from the likes of Big Tobacco and Big Coal, exploits decentralized curriculum decision-making and lack of sufficient public education funding.

When schools don’t have the funding they need, it can force teachers to turn to the most accessible resources that align with their curriculum standards. In swoops the plastic industry, equipped with (often free to use) materials, attractively labeled as “STEM” (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Math).

What they don’t want you to know is that those detrimental funding gaps can partially result from tax concessions that benefit the plastic industry. Schools get a large portion of their funding from property taxes, so when the local plastic facility receives massive property tax credits or exemptions, there can be serious consequences for local schools.

Kids often develop unique perspectives of our world and hold us adults to a higher standard. This has the powerful potential to shift our markets, policy, and culture. The plastic industry sees this opportunity and is manipulating it for their profit gains.

Plastic pollution threatens the life and wellbeing of children. Children living near polluting facilities are especially vulnerable to toxic exposures and their associated life-long impacts. Allowing the plastics industry to control the story taught in schools about the plastic pollution crisis puts students at risk and hurts our ability to tackle this global crisis.

The ideal situation? We immediately ramp up funding for schools so teachers and students have access to the resources they need without a profit-driven quid-pro-quo.

The realistic situation? We expose this insidious issue and hold the plastic industry accountable for their deceptive marketing. We get creative and work together to distribute educational materials that tell the truth about plastics and equip students with the critical-thinking skills to see through the bias. We call on school boards and superintendents to reject plastic propaganda in their schools. We require curriculum source transparency.

After half a century of getting the (plastic) wool pulled over our eyes, we’ve had enough. Students, and all people, deserve science-backed information on plastic pollution, not industry talking points.

We need to work together to get the plastic industry expelled from our classrooms. if you know of plastic industry influence in schools near you, report it and help us put plastic propaganda on the map.

Previously in The Revelator:

Why The Ocean Cleanup Hasn’t Solved the Plastic Pollution Crisis

issues.title: Overfishing Exemplified: The Sad Story of Canadian Cod
issues.summary: In this excerpt from the new book Why Sustainable Seafood Matters , we learn how refrigeration changed the world for people — and fish. The post Overfishing Exemplified: The Sad Story of Canadian Cod appeared first on The Revelator .
issues.author: Dr. David Shiffman
issues.content_html:
Adapted from Why Sustainable Seafood Matters: Making Environmentally Conscious Choices(Johns Hopkins University Press)

People used to think that the oceans were so vast that we could take anything that we wanted out of them, and we’d never have an impact. That all changed after Canadian cod were overfished.

The presence of so many fish played a larger-than-commonly-appreciated role in European desires to colonize North America. If you’ve never heard this before, I recommend reading Mark Kurlansky’s aptly titled Cod: A Biography of the Fish That Changed the World. Kurlansky writes:

“…in 1497, five years after Columbus first stumbled across the Caribbean, Giovanni Cabot sailed from Bristol…Cabot found land, though it wasn’t Asia. It was a vast, rocky coastline that was ideal for salting and drying fish, by a sea that was teeming with cod. Cabot reported on the cod as evidence of the wealth on the new land.”

There were so many cod in the water that early Newfoundlanders didn’t have to use bait, they simply lowered baskets into the ocean on a rope, waited a few seconds, and hauled in baskets full of cod!

As fishing technology increased, so did catch, for many years. From the 1850s to the 1950s, cod catch steadily increased from about 100,000 tons a year to about 300,000 tons a year.

Everything changed with the invention of a revolutionary new technology. Can you guess what it is? It’s not a new kind of fishing gear, and it’s not a new kind of boat engine. I bet you have it in your home. Give up?

That’s right, the revolutionary new technology is refrigeration. This allowed larger boats to stay at sea longer, keeping fish fresh without having to go to shore to offload their catch before it spoiled. As Kurlansky put it, “[Frozen vegetable company] Birdseye undeniably changed our civilization.” Annual catch soon doubled to over 600,000 tons a year, and climbed higher still, reaching a peak of just over 800,000 tons in the 1970s. Soon after, no matter how hard we fished, there just weren’t enough cod. By the 1980s, catch was down to pre-World War II levels despite many more (and much larger) boats on the water fishing for longer, and in 1992 the Canadian government took the once-unthinkable step of closing the cod fishery. Cod populations still haven’t recovered, the few that were left weren’t able to have enough babies to replenish once-vast stocks.


By Lamiot – Own work , CC BY-SA 3.0, Link

As you might imagine, this isn’t just bad for cod, but for the entire marine ecosystem — losing that much biomass has a major disruption, the full effects of which we still don’t fully understand.

And it’s also bad for the human beings who depended on this once-abundant natural resource. The socioeconomic impact of the cod fishery collapse on Atlantic Canada can still be felt today, decades later. Historic fishing communities that were once among the world’s most prosperous are struggling. Some have pivoted to tourism, taking advantage of Atlantic Canada’s beautiful coastline — I personally loved my visits to Lunenburg, Nova Scotia, and St. Johns, Newfoundland! But many once-vibrant once-thriving communities are gone or are full of people on welfare who still feel left behind and bitter. Cod still haven’t recovered, but some former fishermen earnestly believe that they only reason they aren’t catching cod is because the evil government said they’re not allowed.

The cultural aspect of fishing is important, and it’s why I open my lectures on overfishing with a musical interlude, playing “Fishermen’s Lament” by the Canadian folk band Great Big Sea. I encourage you to listen to the haunting melody yourself:

Can you imagine a song with that kind of emotion behind it being written about, say, the 2023 bankruptcy and closing of Bed, Bath, and Beyond? I certainly can’t.

This is one of the reasons why discussions of what to do about fisheries management get so heated. Some jobs are more than what you do for income, they’re a calling, they’re who you are, and the presence of those jobs in the community is who we are as a people. A similar dynamic occurs in U.S. politics with respect to coal miners and their outsized role in discussions of transitions to renewable energy — in the 2016 presidential election, it was pointed out that many more people work for the UPMC hospital system in my hometown of Pittsburgh (around 100,000 jobs) than work for all the coal mines in the whole state of West Virginia (around 10,000 jobs), but you’d never know that from the tone and relative focus of some of the media coverage and political speeches.

But back to overfishing. You may be wondering why no one noticed that something was wrong before it was too late. Part of the answer is that nothing like this had ever happened before, at least not on this scale, to a natural resource that was so important and so well known. Many people truly did not understand that it was even possible to collapse a resource that had supported communities for centuries.

But also, some people absolutely did notice and absolutely tried to sound the alarm. One, Ransom A (RAM) Myers, was a Canadian scientist who tried to get the government reduce fishing pressure while there were still enough cod left to recover the stocks. He was ridiculed, threatened, and ultimately ignored. But he followed the data and never backed down, notably titling one of his PowerPoint presentations “I am right and here’s why.” One of my professional societies named a conference plenary address after him and his courageous, though ultimately unsuccessful, calls to action.

Previously in The Revelator:

A Promise to a Utah Prairie Dog

issues.title: The Revelator Gallery: November 2026 Exhibit
issues.summary: Creative artists and photographers celebrate the changing seasons around the globe. The post The Revelator Gallery: November 2026 Exhibit appeared first on The Revelator .
issues.author: Colleen M. Crary, Ph.D.
issues.content_html:
The art and photography in this month’s Gallery reflect the voices of people who want to capture the magnificent, and often curious, “wow” moments when we see something in nature that delights and surprises us. Many of the animals and plants they share speak to cultural traditions that have ancient meanings or are symbolic of heritage. These artistic visions have the power to inspire viewers to take action to preserve nature’s mystery and magic.

“I dried some yellow molly ( Paeonia daurica subsp. mlokosewitschii) golden flowers on a plate that I had purchased that was a very beautiful dark grey color. The match of colors was my inspiration. The bird is a crow. I use elements from Petrykivka Ukrainian folk technique of painting.”

“Please support City of Goodness, an international charity that provides comprehensive care for children, mothers, older women and animals in Ukraine.”

“Upstate New York sports lots of planted sunflowers in late summer. These remained longer than most, lasting into the peak of autumn’s color.”

“Over the summer, a doe would often hide her twin fawns in our intentionally overgrown yard. The fawns were unseeable when lying down, but would occasionally stretch their legs, and here I caught them grooming each other.”

See more of Jim’s work at longing4nature.com. “I am a retired physicist who, after a career with the government in Washington D.C., returned like some Odysseus to Ithaca, New York — hometown to my wife and site of a rewarding post-graduate stint at Cornell scores of years ago. Actually, I’ve retired twice, the second time from running an all-volunteer nonprofit watershed group in southern Maryland. This website is a retirement project aimed to salve a creative itch.”

“I recently began exploring wildlife photography because I enjoy discovering the small details and moments in nature that are easy to overlook. These photographs reflect that interest and my appreciation for the wildlife around me.”

Anupam Ditta, Wildlife Photographer & Writer
Kolkata, India
Portfolio: https://anupamdutta.in/
Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/duttanupam/

“These birds of paradise look like “floraraptors,” because of the perfect backlight and low camera angle (yes, I was on my belly), emerging from a Jurassic jungle (even though flowering plants did not appear until the Cretaceous period). I used a simple point & shoot camera in an Orange County, California, garden.”

Artist Barri Hitchen is inspired by the unique beauty of The Somerset Levels, a vast, low-lying coastal plain and wetland area in Somerset, England. He is especially interested in the visually and spiritually rich waterways and wetlands. Born in Hampstead, London, Barri is a Fauvist painter in the naive tradition, working in mixed-media, using blocks of color. A graduate of the Fitzwymarc School, and the University of Essex-East 15 Acting School, he is also an actor/director and makes independent short films.

“We were thrilled to see this during our holiday in Scotland, out in the back of our lodge near Ben Nevis.”

“Hedgehogs come into our garden every night between March-October. They’re not easy to photograph because it’s usually dark when they arrive, so when I do see one, I try to get a good photo if I can. I love to see them snuffling around the garden — they’re very docile and tend to freeze rather than run away, so they’re fun to be around.”

Claire comments, “Not often you see birds this big in England or Scotland, so have to take a photo!”

Note: Claire and Chris Sandys are the producers of The Silent Why Podcast, where loss and grief are explored and discussed, asking the question: Can hope be found in every type of loss?

The Revelator Gallery Archives

Each monthly exhibit is archived here in chronological order with links and listed under each new exhibit, so your work can be seen and enjoyed moving forward. And don’t be shy about submitting more work so we can spotlight uplifting artists and photographers each month who are inspired by wildlife and nature. October 2026 Exhibit: https://therevelator.org/gallery-oct2026/September 2026 Exhibit:https://therevelator.org/environmental-gallery-sept2026/August 2026 Exhibit: https://therevelator.org/environmental-gallery/Guidelines to get your masterpiece into the Revelator Gallery:
    • Original photos and art from you
    • No AI-generated or enhanced images
    • Images can be horizontal, square, or vertical
    • We accept only .jpgs and .png files
    • THERE’S NO LIMIT on how many submissions you send.
    • One image and description per email. No Exceptions.
    • No people in the images, just wildlife and landscapes (animals, plants and trees, insects, sea life…)

Send your submissions to ccrary@biologicaldiversity.org with the following information:

    • Your name
    • Title of image (if applicable)
    • Species of wildlife (if known)
    • The location (where it was created)
    • A brief description of what inspired you to capture or create this image
    • Medium: Photography (many types, be specific), painting, drawing, pottery, sculpture, textiles/fabric art, mixed media, glass, etc.
    • Let us know if you want us to include a specific copyright notice “©”

All submissions are considered intended for publication; submission does not guarantee publication. Monthly galleries will be distributed to our partner publications under a Creative Commons license, but you retain the copyright on your individual images. There’s no prize or payment, just bragging rights.
